Issue #114: order_cells: a smaller upstream index, and two more orderings

pyflwdir's flat next-downstream-index representation is what my own work is
built on, and keeping the ordering separate from the kernels that read it is the
part I have got the most out of: every kernel becomes one sweep over a sequence.
Working at scale on that design turned up two things that may be useful back
here. The first is a pull request, #115. The second is a question.

## 1. The fix: store the upstream index sparse

`core.idxs_seq` starts by building `core.upstream_matrix`, one row per cell and
`d` columns, `d` being the largest number of cells draining into any one cell.
A six cell example, `-1` being both nodata and padding:

```
idxs_ds = [2, 2, 3, 3, 3, -1]        cell 3 drains to itself, cell 5 is nodata

upstream_matrix, shape (6, 2)        upstream_csr
   cell 0: [-1, -1]                     indptr  = [0, 0, 0, 2, 4, 4, 4]
   cell 1: [-1, -1]                     idxs_us = [0, 1, 2, 4]
   cell 2: [ 0,  1]
   cell 3: [ 2,  4]                     upstream cells of cell 2:
   cell 4: [-1, -1]                     idxs_us[indptr[2]:indptr[3]] -> [0, 1]
   cell 5: [-1, -1]
```

The dense matrix reserves `d` slots for every cell of the raster, up to 8 on D8,
while the average cell has just under one upstream cell and nodata cells have
none. So nearly all of it is padding. The CSR form on the right stores one entry
per upstream cell plus `n + 1` offsets, and the walk reads it with no other
change: same traversal, same sequence element by element, verified cell by cell
on the test rasters and by hash on the billion-cell one.

What that buys follows from the shapes alone: the dense matrix spends its space
on the worst case at every cell, the sparse form on the links that exist, so the
saving is machine-independent arithmetic. On the Rhine example the index shrinks
about five-fold; on a 1.33 billion cell window of MERIT Hydro it goes from
39.7 GiB, more than a 32 GiB machine holds, to 7.2 GiB. Building the sequence
also gets faster, since most of what the old build wrote was padding.

That is the whole of #115: one function added, `idxs_seq` switched to read it,
tests and a CHANGELOG line.

## 2. The question: two more orderings, worth carrying?

`order_cells("dfs")`, depth-first from the pits (Braun and Willett, 2013), and
`order_cells("topo")` from the headwaters (Kahn, 1962), which needs only a count
per cell and builds no upstream index at all. Both return a down- to upstream
sequence like the existing two and treat pits and nodata the same way. Cells on
a loop are left out by every ordering; the one divergence is that `topo` keeps
the valid cells upstream of a loop or of a nodata cell, which `walk` and `dfs`
drop. On data where every cell drains to an outlet, all five cover the same
cells. Implemented and tested on
https://github.com/hellolulujiang/pyflwdir/tree/orderings.

My answer would be yes to `dfs` and take-or-leave on `topo`. The reasoning is
below; the decision is yours, since the documenting, testing and maintaining
would be too.

The case for `dfs` is that its cost is small and fixed while its gain grows with
the raster. Its sequence keeps each cell close to the cell it drains into, so
the accumulation kernels walk memory locally instead of jumping across the
raster. On a raster small enough to sit in cache that buys nothing, and its
`accuflux` runs 0.6 ms behind the others on the Rhine example. On the billion
cell window it makes `accuflux` almost twice as fast, 3.4 s against 6.2. And an
ordering is built once, cached, then read by every later kernel call, so on that
window `dfs` is ahead of the walk in total from the first call. Separately, it
is the only ordering that lays each basin out as one contiguous slice of the
sequence, which is the partition half of #85, for free.

`topo` is the cheapest of the five to build and the lightest, having no upstream
index. Use an ordering for up to three `accuflux` calls and `topo` comes out
ahead of `dfs`; use it more and `dfs` does.

One caveat before the table. Everything was timed on my personal MacBook (an
Apple M1 Max, numba 0.63.1, against `main` at be5deb7), which keeps running
other work: absolute times move by tens of percent with that load, and the cores
share memory bandwidth, so treat the milliseconds and seconds as indicative. The
row order and the ratios were stable every time I reran, and the sizes above are
arithmetic, not measurement:

| ordering | build, 1.33e9 cells | `accuflux`, 1.33e9 | `accuflux`, Rhine |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| `sort`, in the library | 55 s | 6.3 s | 1.0 ms |
| `walk`, in the library | 28 s | 6.2 s | 1.0 ms |
| `walk` with #115 | 11 s | 6.2 s | 1.0 ms |
| `dfs` | 10 s | 3.4 s | 1.6 ms |
| `topo` | 8 s | 4.2 s | 1.0 ms |

The full tables, the figures, and the mechanism that makes `dfs` slowest on the
small raster and fastest on the large one are in the notebook, which runs
against this repository's own example data:
https://github.com/hellolulujiang/pyflwdir/blob/orderings/examples/ordering.ipynb

### References

Braun, J. and Willett, S. D. (2013). A very efficient O(n), implicit and
parallel method to solve the stream power equation. *Geomorphology*, 180-181,
170-179.

Kahn, A. B. (1962). Topological sorting of large networks. *Communications of
the ACM*, 5(11), 558-562.

*(Both orderings come from [FlowTopo](https://github.com/hellolulujiang/flowtopo),
MIT; its breadth-first sequence builder is pyflwdir's, credited in the source.)*

Implement a Directed Resource Wait-For Graph (WFG) $G_{\text{wfg}} = (V, E)$ and Tarjan's Strongly Connected Components (SCC) cycle detection algorithm to identify total and partial deadlocks in $\mathcal{O}(|V| + |E|)$ time complexity.

- **Deadlock Cycle Predicate:**

$$\mathcal{D}_{\text{deadlock}} \iff \exists C \subseteq G_{\text{wfg}} \mid C = \langle G_1, G_2, \dots, G_k, G_1 \rangle$$

Issue #5285: [Feature Request] Infisical provider: resolve secrets recursively across folders (or support paths in the reference syntax)

### What problem will this feature address?

The Infisical secrets provider (introduced in v0.30.0) is a great addition — thank you! However, its current design makes it hard to use for anyone who organizes secrets with **Infisical folders**, which is a core Infisical feature (secrets are scoped by environment **and** path, with nested folders supported everywhere in Infisical: CLI, API, Terraform, K8s operator).

Current limitations:

1. **One provider = one Secret Path.** Each provider instance is bound to a single project + environment + secret path (default `/`). Referencing secrets living in different folders requires creating a separate provider for each folder.
2. **No path in the reference syntax.** The syntax is `${{vault.<provider>.<SECRET_NAME>}}`, e.g. `${{vault.infisical-prod.API_KEY}}`. Unlike the Vault provider (`<path>:<field>`) or the Scaleway provider (`[folder/]<secret-name>`), there is no way to point at a specific folder in the reference itself.
3. **No recursion.** Secrets stored in subfolders under the configured Secret Path are not picked up.

For users managing a large number of secrets organized into many folders/subfolders, the only options today are:

- Creating one Dokploy provider per Infisical folder (unmanageable beyond a handful of folders), or
- Flattening the whole Infisical project structure to `/`, losing the organization that Infisical itself encourages.

### Describe the solution you'd like

The ideal solution would make the reference syntax **folder-agnostic**, with path support as a fallback if recursion is not feasible:

**Primary — folder-agnostic resolution (recursive):**
The provider resolves `${{vault.my-infisical.API_KEY}}` regardless of which folder or subfolder the secret lives in. Concretely: the provider would fetch secrets from the entire folder tree under the configured Secret Path (recursively), exactly like the Infisical CLI already does with `infisical run --path=/backend --recursive`, which injects secrets from the folder *and all its subfolders*. This keeps the reference syntax simple and untouched — no need to know or care where a secret is stored.

Note: this would require secret names to be unique across the resolved tree (or a documented precedence rule for duplicates), which seems like a reasonable constraint since it is the same one the CLI applies.

**Secondary — path in the reference syntax (fallback):**
If recursion is not an option, then at least allow pointing at a specific folder in the reference, consistent with the precedent already set by the Scaleway provider:
```text
${{vault.my-infisical.backend/API_KEY}}
```
or Vault-style:
```text
${{vault.my-infisical.API_KEY:backend}}
```
This is more verbose and less convenient to use than the recursive approach, but it would at least make the integration usable with an organized folder structure.

Infisical exposes everything needed for both options via its API (e.g. `GET /api/v3/secrets/raw` with `secretPath` + `recursive=true`).

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Honestly, none of the available workarounds is a real alternative for this use case:

- **One provider per folder**: technically possible, but with many folders and subfolders it becomes cluttered and painful to maintain (each needs its own Machine Identity credentials + config), and it multiplies the provider list in the UI.
- **Bypassing the integration**: wrapping the start command with the Infisical CLI (`infisical run --env=prod --path=/backend --recursive -- ...`). This works, but it defeats the purpose of the native Dokploy integration (visibility in the UI, centralized management, no extra CLI dependency in every image).
- **Infisical Secret Syncs**: pushing secrets from Infisical to another target and pointing Dokploy at that — adds another moving part instead of using the native integration.
- **Flattening the Infisical structure**: losing the folder organization entirely, which contradicts how Infisical itself is designed to be used.

That is why the two solutions described above (recursive/folder-agnostic resolution as the ideal, path-in-reference as a fallback) are really the only ones that would make the integration usable at scale.

### Additional context

- Infisical folders documentation: https://infisical.com/docs/documentation/platform/secrets-mgmt/folders
- Infisical API for reading secrets at a path (supports `recursive`): https://infisical.com/docs/api-reference/endpoints/secrets/read
- Infisical CLI `--path` / `--recursive` behavior for reference: https://infisical.com/docs/cli/commands/secrets
- The Scaleway provider already supports `[folder/]<secret-name>` in its reference syntax, so there is in-repo precedent for path-aware references.
- Related upstream issue that introduced secrets providers: #2768

Issue #171: GLM-5.3 high optimisation findings

# Claude of Duty — Optimization Analysis (`develop`, cb0f72a)

## Context

A ~85k-line browser FPS (Three.js r185, WebGL2, no runtime deps but `three`). The codebase is **unusually disciplined about performance already**: preallocated scratch vectors everywhere, typed-array A* with a reused heap, pooled impact/HUD/event payloads, A* rationed to 2 solves/frame, AI LOD with frustum culling and relevance tiers, corpse TTL despawn, shader pre-warm (measured, pixel-gated), CSM caster culling with texel snapping, change-gated DOM writes (`setStyle`), pooled `getHudState()` objects, and telemetry emits gated behind `ctx.has('telemetry')`. My findings below are what remains — mostly small, plus two structural boot-time wins.

---

## Findings (ranked by expected impact)

### 1. World GLB is parsed on the main thread — `src/world/index.js:137–148`
The visual level is a **9.4 MB gzipped** (≈ likely 20–30 MB decoded) GLB, fetched → gunzipped via `DecompressionStream` → `GLTFLoader.parseAsync` **on the main thread**. Decompression itself is stream-based (good), but `parseAsync` of a decoded multi-megabyte GLB (JSON chunk parse + accessor decode + buffer view slicing) is a single long main-thread block during boot. Options:
- Parse in a Web Worker (three's GLTFLoader can be hosted in a worker; textures are procedural here, which makes it easier than the general case), or
- Split the level into a "boot district" + streamed districts.

### 2. Visual GLB is written uncompressed by `GLTFExporter` — `tools/export-world.mjs:~50`
Only *transport* gzip is applied; geometry is raw float32 (meshoptimizer is used for the *collision* LOD only, and `meshoptimizer` is already a dependency). Adding `EXT_meshopt_compression` + vertex quantization at export would shrink the payload dramatically (typically 3–6×), cut `parseAsync` decode time, reduce GPU memory, and speed first paint. Cost: shipping the ~small meshopt decoder at runtime (offline, local WASM — allowed under the no-CDN rule since it's a committed asset).

### 3. All CSM cascades re-render every frame — `src/render/csm.js:333–351`
`update()` already texel-snaps each cascade fit, and the AI LOD tier explicitly removes distant agents from the shadow cascades (`src/ai/index.js:36`). Yet `render()` clears and redraws every cascade unconditionally. With a static sun and a snapped fit, a cascade is stable unless (a) its fit moved ≥ 1 texel or (b) a dynamic caster entered its volume. A "dirty" flag per cascade — set on texel-boundary crossing of the fit, or when any dynamic caster (agents, particles, debris, ragdolls) intersects its frustum — would let the far cascades (the expensive, large-radius ones at `ultra` / 2048px maps) skip most frames. This is one of the few remaining multi-ms/frame candidates in the steady state.

### 4. `EventBus.emit` allocates on every emit — `src/core/registry.js` (`Array.from(set)`)
`emit()` copies the handler Set into a fresh array on *every* event. `weapon:fire`, `bullet:tracer`, `damage:dealt`, `player:footstep`, `weapon:shell` all fire at high rate during combat (a shotgun blast emits several). Fix without the copy: iterate the live Set with a dispatch-in-progress flag and a small pending-unsubscribe queue drained after the loop (handlers may only mutate the set via that queue mid-dispatch). Small per-emit cost, but it's the single remaining per-event allocator on the hottest cross-subsystem path.

### 5. Two fresh objects per bullet impact — `src/physics/index.js:768–774` + `src/weapons/ballistics.js:127–135`
`fireBullet()` does `{ rng: this.rng, ...opts }` (spread-allocates a new object per call) and the caller in `ballistics.js` already builds a fresh literal per hit. Pool the opts object in `BallisticsSim` and pass `rng` as a parameter or sticky field: `phys.fireBullet(pooledOpts)`.

### 6. Redundant `camera.updateMatrixWorld()` — 3× per frame
Called in `src/audio/index.js:250` (`update`), `src/sky/index.js:499` (`lateUpdate`), and `src/render/index.js:1221`. Three's `updateMatrixWorld` recomposes and recurses children unconditionally, so this is 3× the work for identical output. Centralize: one call in the engine frame loop (or keep only render's) and have audio/sky read `matrixWorld` directly.

### 7. Per-frame string formatting in the HUD — `src/ui/index.js:645–647`
`this.hudVisible.toFixed(3)` is computed **before** `setStyle`'s change gate, so three strings are allocated every frame even when the opacity hasn't changed. Compare the cached float first, format only on change (the `setStyle` cache key already exists — just move the `toFixed` behind a float-equality check).

### 8. Minor / micro
- `level.json` fetched with `cache: 'no-store'` (`src/world/index.js:57`) — defeats the browser cache on every boot; if the hash-in-URL convention is used for the GLBs, the manifest could be too.
- `for (const mesh of this.lodGroups)` in the per-frame `world.update` (`src/world/index.js:306`) — iterator allocation per frame; use an index loop like the rest of the codebase does.
- `saturationCurve` key string (`src/audio/dsp.js:231`) is built per voice creation — fine as-is, only noting it's the only per-call string key left in the audio path.

---

## Checked and found already optimal (non-findings)

Worth recording so nobody re-litigates them: no `Math.random()` in gameplay; no `new THREE.*` inside any `update`/`fixedUpdate`/`lateUpdate` anywhere in `src/`; A* working set in preallocated `Float32Array`/`Int32Array` with stamp-based visited marking; impact/HUD/tracer/shell payloads pooled; corpse + squad despawn prevents unbounded wave growth; `renderer.compileAsync` + pixel-neutral prewarm eliminates shader-compile stalls; patcher material walk is `_patched`-Set-cached; DOM writes are change-gated; disposal paths remove all global listeners; lint (`oxlint --deny-warnings`) and the vitest suite are green.

## Recommended priority

1. **#2 (meshopt-compress the visual GLB)** — best effort/impact ratio; shrinks #1's problem too.

LayerFS currently acknowledges live-process visibility without guaranteeing that an acknowledged snapshot survives an OS crash or power loss. v0.3.0 should introduce an explicit, tested durability contract, starting with **durable public Commit**: after Commit returns successfully, the published snapshot, its dependencies, and the corresponding history/head changes survive the supported crash and recovery scenarios.

Harden the legacy `%role setting` flow so it cannot publish a self-assignable reaction-role panel for a role that the invoking administrator is not allowed to manage or that BeanBot itself cannot assign.

The current setup command checks that the caller has the `Manage Roles` permission bit, but `GetRoleAsync(...)` will resolve any guild role by mention/name. It does not enforce Discord role hierarchy for the caller, reject `@everyone`/managed roles, or prove that BeanBot can actually manage the selected role. The command also only requires BeanBot's `Embed Links` permission before setup.

That leaves both a security boundary and a reliability gap in the legacy reaction-role path.

## Current behavior

On current `develop`:

- `AdministrativeModule.RoleSetting()` is guild-only and requires the invoking member to have `GuildPermission.ManageRoles`.
- BeanBot is only prechecked for `GuildPermission.EmbedLinks`.
- `GetRoleAsync(...)` resolves a role from `Context.Guild.Roles` and accepts it as long as the mention/name resolves unambiguously.
- The selected role ID is then persisted into the reaction-role configuration after the panel message and reactions are created.
- `RoleReactService.HandleReactionAsync(...)` later looks up that persisted role and directly calls `AddRoleAsync(...)` / `RemoveRoleAsync(...)` when a member toggles the configured reaction.

There is currently no setup-time validation that the selected role is:

- below the invoking member's highest role (unless the invoker is the guild owner);
- below BeanBot's highest role;
- not `@everyone`;
- not a Discord/integration-managed role; and
- assignable with BeanBot's current `Manage Roles` capability.

## Why this matters

### Security

Discord's `Manage Roles` permission does not by itself allow a member to manage roles at or above their own highest role. The current BeanBot command checks the permission bit but not that target-role hierarchy rule.

That means a member who has `Manage Roles` on a lower role can potentially configure a higher role that **BeanBot** is allowed to assign. Once the panel is published, ordinary members can react and cause BeanBot to grant that higher role. BeanBot should not become a way to bypass the invoking administrator's normal Discord role-management boundary.

### Reliability

Even without malicious intent, setup can currently succeed for roles BeanBot cannot mutate, such as `@everyone`, integration-managed roles, or roles at/above BeanBot's highest role. The panel can therefore look valid and be persisted even though every later reaction produces a doomed role mutation.

Failing at setup with a precise explanation is much better than publishing a permanently broken panel.

This is distinct from existing work:

- #138 validates assignability for the **new dropdown role-menu feature** and explicitly preserves the legacy reaction-role system rather than fixing it.
- #139 improves reaction-role failure diagnostics after an operation fails.
- #160 coordinates rapid add/remove mutations.
- #170 bounds the legacy reaction-role settings cache.

Introduce a repository-local evaluator used by the legacy setup flow. Prefer a pure/internal value-based policy that can be covered deterministically without constructing a live Discord client.

For a selected target role, validate at minimum:

- the role is not the guild's `@everyone` role;
- the role is not managed by Discord or an integration;
- BeanBot currently has `Manage Roles`;
- the target role is strictly below BeanBot's highest role;
- the invoking member is the guild owner **or** the target role is strictly below the invoking member's highest role.

Use Discord's actual hierarchy semantics; do not treat the `Administrator` permission bit as a bypass for role hierarchy when Discord itself would not.

Return a structured reason/status rather than a bare boolean so the command can give concise actionable feedback and tests can prove the exact policy.

### 2. Reject invalid targets before creating/persisting the panel

Apply the policy immediately after role resolution and before the role/emote pair is accepted.

If the role is not authorized/assignable:

- stop the setup attempt safely;
- tell the invoking administrator why the target cannot be used, without dumping internal state;
- do not create/persist a reaction-role configuration for that target;
- preserve the existing best-effort cleanup of setup prompts.

A hierarchy/permission rejection is a normal validation result, not an exception path.

### 3. Make BeanBot's required permissions truthful

At minimum, setup should account for:

- `Manage Roles` for eventual role mutation;
- `Embed Links` for the panel; and
- any reaction permission actually required to add the configured control reactions.

Use the smallest approach consistent with existing Discord.Net command preconditions. Avoid duplicating checks when one canonical assignability policy can own the hierarchy logic.

Persisted panels can outlive role hierarchy changes. Before `RoleReactService` calls `AddRoleAsync` / `RemoveRoleAsync`, re-check the **current BeanBot-side** assignability conditions that can change after setup (role still exists, not managed, below BeanBot, BeanBot still has `Manage Roles`).

- skip the doomed Discord mutation;
- emit structured diagnostics using the existing safe reaction-r

Issue #121: Redesign scoring walk: one recursive function with an explicit ABSENT sentinel

## Why

`core/scoring.py` answers the question "one side has a value, the other does not" in three separate places, each with its own copy of the schema-tree walk:

1. **`_score_object`** -- key in gold but not extracted goes to `_omission_results`, the reverse goes to `_hallucination_results`, both present goes to `_score_node`.
2. **`_score_container_type_error`** -- a container whose value is `None` on one side is turned into omissions / hallucinations, expanded per field if the present side has the right shape, otherwise one node-level result.
3. **`_omission_results` / `_hallucination_results`** -- line-for-line mirrors that each re-implement the object and array traversal for a one-sided subtree, including the both-empty rule and the negative-index rule.

Three walkers over the same tree means a reader can never settle on one rule for what an omission or hallucination is. It also hides an inconsistency: "absent" means two different things depending on the node. A missing key at a leaf reaches the comparator as `None` and is fixed up afterwards by `reclassify_nulls`; a missing key at a container is caught by the type-error function and never reaches a comparator.

PR #120 (inline `_score_container`) and the follow-ups discussed there (file reorder, `name` on `SchemaNode`, merging the two one-sided helpers, extracting array scaffolding) reduce the duplication but do not remove the three-homes problem. This issue is the full redesign.

## Proposed design

One recursive function with an explicit sentinel for "no value here", so every node handles the same 2x2 table in one place:

```python
ABSENT = object()  # distinct from None, which is a real JSON null

def _score(node: SchemaNode, gold: object, extracted: object) -> list[FieldResult]:
    if node.skip:
        return [_skipped(node, gold, extracted)]
    if gold is ABSENT and extracted is ABSENT:
        return []
    if gold is ABSENT or extracted is ABSENT:
        status = "omission" if extracted is ABSENT else "hallucination"
        present = gold if extracted is ABSENT else extracted
        return _one_sided(node, present, status)
    if node.comparator.name or not node.children:
        return [_score_leaf(node, gold, extracted)]
    if not _both_have_shape(node.json_type, gold, extracted):
        return [_shape_mismatch(node, gold, extracted)]
    if node.json_type == "object":
        return [
            r
            for child in node.children
            for r in _score(child, gold.get(child.name, ABSENT), extracted.get(child.name, ABSENT))
        ]
    return _score_array(node, gold, extracted)  # strategies return pairs; each pair goes back through _score
```

`_one_sided` still needs to know that an object expands into its present children and an array into its elements, but it is one small function next to the match path, not two mirrored ones far away.

What this removes:

- `_omission_results` and `_hallucination_results` -- replaced by `_one_sided`.
- The if/elif presence chain in `_score_object` -- becomes one recursive call per child.
- The absent branches of `_score_container_type_error` -- only "both present, wrong shape" remains.

What this depends on:

- `SchemaNode.name` (also fixes #114, the dotted-property-name bug). Do that first as its own PR.
- Array strategies returning an alignment (matched index pairs + unmatched leftovers on each side) rather than scoring inline, so `_score_array` can route every pair back through `_score`. Hungarian already has the scored pairs for its cost matrix; let it hand those back so pending batch-comparator fields are not scored twice.

## Decisions the redesign forces

These are currently answered inconsistently or by accident. Each needs an explicit choice, written down in the docstring, before coding.

- **Missing key vs explicit `null`.** Same kind of absence or not? Today: leaf says "comparator decides, post-processor may reclassify"; container says "absent". The user-facing `NullHandling` policy should remain the single knob.
- **Empty array on one side, key missing on the other.** Today: one node-level omission / hallucination. Keep, or expand to nothing (zero elements)?
- **Both sides empty (`{}` vs `{}`, `[]` vs `[]`).** Today: one node-level `match`. Keep.
- **Extra extracted elements.** Today: distinct negative indices (`tags[-1]`, `tags[-2]`, ...). Keep.
- **Extracted key not in schema.** Today: one hallucination with the whole value, not expanded. Keep (there is no schema to expand against). Related: #113 (gold key not in schema).
- **Skip field absent on both sides.** Today: still emits a `skipped` result. Keep.

## Scope

- Do it as **one PR**, not incrementally. The intermediate states (some paths unified, some not) are harder to read than either end.
- Precision / recall / F1 depend on exact field counts. Before starting, snapshot `score_record` output over the existing test fixtures and the example notebooks, and diff after. Every intentional change in counts must be listed in the PR description.
- Existing 470 tests are the regression net. Expect to touch only tests that pin a behaviour changed by one of the decisions above.

## Alternative

If the redesign is not worth the risk right now, the incremental path is: file reorder -> `SchemaNode.name` (#114) -> merge the two one-sided helpers -> extract array scaffolding. That gets most of the readability win and leaves `_score_object` and the type-error function as the two remaining homes.

- #113 gold key not in schema
- #114 property name containing a dot
- #115 `_score_object` edge-case tests

Issue #9: Global dependency-aware cache for heavy geometry and modeling operations

Type

Enhancement

Problem and context

Interactive procedural modeling is slowed by repeated solver evaluations, surface-coordinate lookups, mesh modifiers, and boolean operations. Rebuilding similar `BuildPart` operation chains after changing one parameter should reuse every still-valid intermediate result.

The cache must be a global capability spanning modules such as geometry, solver, ML, RBL, and chain. It must support in-memory reuse by default and opt-in persistence to disk across Blender sessions.

Evidence / affected code

- `blender_cad/geometry.py`: `Face.at()` delegates to `_at_uv()`, projection detection, metric walking, and repeated triangle searches.
- `blender_cad/geometry.py`: `Face` currently keeps only per-instance UV projection state; it has no result cache for resolved `(u, v, offsets, projection)` inputs.
- `blender_cad/solver.py`: `Solver._CACHE` is process-local and its key is assembled from registered solver calls and initial error.
- `blender_cad/ml.py`: ML already caches structural builds and text measurements, but this is isolated from other modules.
- `blender_cad/modifiers.py`: `add()`, `_apply_boolean()`, `extrude()`, `bevel()`, deformation, and wrapping perform expensive Blender/BMesh work without reusable operation results.

## Description

Roadmap Phase 4 → Analytics & Monitoring → **#74 Create custom metrics and KPIs** has no tracking issue. It is the remaining gap in a section whose other three items have shipped: #339 (analytics dashboard, roadmap #71), #340 (real-time performance monitoring, #72) and #341 (configurable alerting, #73).

Those three cover *fixed*, developer-defined metrics. #74 is about letting an operator define a metric **without a code change** — pick a source, an aggregation, a window and a dimension, name it, and have it appear in the dashboard and be alertable.

## Background

What exists today:

- `packages/api/rest/src/services/monitoring/` — `transaction-monitoring.service.ts`, `monitoring-alert.service.ts`, `alert-evaluator.ts`, `transaction-rule-engine.ts`, and a channel dispatcher with webhook and notification channels
- `packages/api/rest/src/routes/monitoring/` — `transactions.ts` and `alerts.ts`

`alert-evaluator.ts` and `transaction-rule-engine.ts` already evaluate conditions over transaction data, which is the closest existing analogue and the natural thing to generalize rather than duplicate.

What is missing is the definition layer: every metric is currently hardcoded, so adding one means editing a service, opening a PR and redeploying.

## Requirements

### Metric definition model
- [ ] A `metric_definitions` table and a typed model: `id`, `userId`/`orgId`, `name`, `description`, `source`, `aggregation`, `window`, `dimensions`, `filters`, `unit`, `enabled`
- [ ] Sources drawn from what the DevKit already records: transactions, wallet events, DeFi positions, oracle prices, automation executions, API request logs
- [ ] Aggregations: `count`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `p50`/`p95`/`p99`, `rate`, `distinct_count`
- [ ] Rolling windows (`5m`, `1h`, `24h`, `7d`, `30d`) and calendar windows (day/week/month to date)
- [ ] Dimensions/group-by: asset, protocol, network, wallet, user, team, endpoint
- [ ] Derived metrics — a definition may reference other definitions in an arithmetic expression (e.g. `failed_tx / total_tx`). Detect and reject cycles

### Evaluation
- [ ] A `MetricsService` that compiles a definition into a parameterized Supabase query — never string-concatenated SQL
- [ ] Reuse the caching layer from #343 with a TTL derived from the window; a `30d` metric must not be recomputed per request
- [ ] Scheduled materialization for expensive definitions, with on-demand evaluation for cheap ones
- [ ] Backfill: computing a newly created definition over existing history

### KPI targets
- [ ] Attach a target/threshold and direction (higher-is-better / lower-is-better) to a definition
- [ ] Expose current value, target, delta vs. previous period, and trend

### API
- [ ] `POST/GET/PATCH/DELETE /api/v1/metrics/definitions` — full CRUD, scoped to the owner
- [ ] `GET /api/v1/metrics/:id/value` — current value, optional dimension filters
- [ ] `GET /api/v1/metrics/:id/series` — time series for charting, with explicit bucket size
- [ ] `POST /api/v1/metrics/preview` — evaluate an unsaved definition, so the UI can validate before saving

### Integration
- [ ] Custom metrics selectable as an alert source in `monitoring-alert.service.ts`, reusing the existing channel dispatcher rather than adding a parallel one
- [ ] Custom metrics renderable in the #339 dashboard
- [ ] Definitions exportable/importable as JSON so an environment's KPI set is reproducible

### Guardrails
- [ ] Per-user caps on definition count and on evaluation cost; reject a definition whose estimated scan exceeds a limit
- [ ] Query timeouts, so one expensive metric cannot stall the monitoring API
- [ ] Audit-log create/update/delete via the #334 audit logging

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] An operator can define "average swap size in USD, per protocol, 24h rolling" through the API with no code change, and read its value
- [ ] A derived metric referencing two other definitions evaluates correctly; a cyclic definition is rejected at save time
- [ ] An alert rule can target a custom metric and fires through the existing channels
- [ ] Repeated reads inside the TTL are served from cache
- [ ] A definition with an unsupported source or aggregation is rejected with a clear validation error
- [ ] A user cannot read or modify another user's definitions
- [ ] `preview` evaluates without persisting
- [ ] Tests cover each aggregation, each window type, dimension grouping and cycle detection

## Problem Statement

Gloom's executable prototype can extract a small function graph from C or textual LLVM IR, run basic graph algorithms, export JSON, and render a self-contained viewer. A maintainer on the project Graphify-Labs/graphify (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #3253: Semantic subagents receive only doc files, so doc→code edges are structurally impossible (extraction-spec's code-file and ID-collision instructions are unreachable)

## Summary

In the Claude Code skill pipeline, semantic-extraction subagents are only ever handed `document`/`paper`/`image` files. Code files go exclusively to the AST pass. As a result a subagent has no way to construct a valid AST node ID for any code symbol, and **doc→code edges are structurally impossible in a default run** — not merely rare.

This is the *input-side* cause of the disconnected-subgraph symptom in #1254. That issue proposes reconciling two ID spaces after the fact; this one is that the pipeline never gives the extractor the chance to emit a cross-domain edge in the first place. It is also the concrete answer to the question in #537 (yes — a subagent can only relate files inside its own `FILE_LIST`).

Two instructions in `references/extraction-spec.md` are unreachable in the default flow as a direct consequence:

- Line 17: *"Code files: focus on semantic edges AST cannot find (call relationships, shared data, arch patterns). Do not re-extract imports - AST already has those."* — code files are never in `FILE_LIST`, so this guidance never applies.
- Line 61: the node-ID rule ends with *"This must match the ID the AST extractor generates"* — the subagent is asked to produce IDs that collide with AST IDs, but is shown no code paths from which to derive them.

## Mechanism

`SKILL.md:232` (Step 3 Part B0) selects the semantic corpus:

```python
all_files = [f for cat in ('document', 'paper', 'image') for f in detect['files'].get(cat, [])]
```

with the rationale at `SKILL.md:229`: *"Only content files go to semantic extraction. Code is already covered structurally by the AST pass (Part A); flattening every category here makes subagents re-read every source file (#1392)."*

Avoiding re-reads is right, but the current split throws away the code **inventory** along with the code **contents**. The subagent needs the former (paths + symbol names, to build target IDs) and not the latter.

## Measurement (graphify 0.9.53)

A private TypeScript repo, 46 code files + 5 doc files, built through the skill pipeline (AST + one semantic subagent chunk), undirected, then `--update`.

Graph: **385 nodes, 741 edges, 13 communities.** Health check clean — no dangling, missing, self-loop, or collapsed edges.

Edges by source zone:

| zone pair | edges |
|---|---|
| `src/**` ↔ `src/**` | 592 |
| docs ↔ docs | 48 |
| dashboard file ↔ docs | 8 |
| dashboard ↔ dashboard | 6 |
| docs ↔ other (`package.json`, `tsconfig.json`) | 3 |
| other ↔ other | 84 |
| **docs ↔ `src/**`** | **0** |

Connected components: **6** — 243 nodes (pure `src/`), 61 (docs + dashboard), 54 (`package.json`), 25 (`tsconfig.json`), and two singletons. The code island and the documentation island share no edge.

Narrowing to the case that matters for traversal: of **38** doc-derived concept/rationale nodes (architectural rules and design rationale extracted from `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/`), **0** have an edge into any `src/**` symbol. `graphify path "<rule concept>" "<the function that implements it>"` returns no path for every pair tested, even though the source document names that function explicitly in prose.

## The control that isolates the cause

One file in the corpus, `public/index.html`, was classified as a `document` and therefore landed *in the doc chunk*. Its JavaScript functions were extracted as `file_type: "code"` nodes, and they carry **8 edges to doc concepts** — the only meaningful cross-domain edges in the graph.

Cross-domain linkage appears exactly where the extractor had both sides in front of it, and nowhere else. The limitation is file visibility, not model capability or ID formatting.

## Suggested fixes

1. **Pass a code inventory to doc chunks.** After Part A, the AST result already holds every code node's `id`, `label`, and `source_file`. Handing the subagent a compact index (id + label + path, no source text) would let it emit `implements` / `references` edges with IDs guaranteed to collide correctly — no re-reading of source files, so #1392's concern is preserved.
2. **Post-AST linking pass.** A cheap deterministic sweep: for each doc node, look for verbatim symbol/path mentions in its source span and emit `references` edges to the matching AST nodes, marked `INFERRED`.
3. **At minimum, correct the spec.** If cross-domain edges stay out of scope, `references/extraction-spec.md:17` and the ID-collision sentence at `:61` should say plainly that code files are not part of a semantic chunk in the default flow, so the instructions stop implying a capability the pipeline does not provide.

Option 1 seems the smallest change with the largest effect, and it would let #1254's post-processing workaround be retired rather than reimplemented per project.

## Environment

- graphify 0.9.53 (`uv tool install graphifyy`), Python 3.12, Linux
- Claude Code skill pipeline, no `GEMINI_API_KEY`/`GOOGLE_API_KEY` set (host agent dispatched `general-purpose` subagents)
- Undirected graph; corpus 46 code + 5 doc files, ~37k words

Related: #1254 (cross-domain edge generation / ID alignment), #537 (subagent connection scope), #2383 (markdown routed to the LLM rather than the structural extractor).

Issue #1331: fix(core): SearchIndex build follows directory symlinks without cycle detection

Problem
`SearchIndex::build` in `crates/cadis-core/src/search_index.rs:23-58` walks with `stack: Vec<PathBuf>`, `fs::read_dir` + `entry.metadata()` (follows symlink) + `if meta.is_dir() { stack.push(path) }`. A symlink directory pointing to an ancestor (`mkdir a; ln -s .. a/loop`) creates infinite loop and stack growth until OOM. No `visited` set for `(device,inode)` and `SKIP_DIRS` only checks name not canonical target.

Actual Output
`SearchIndex::build(root)` on crafted workspace hangs on first `file.search` (index build is lazy per `search_index_cache` in `crates/cadis-core/src/lib.rs:389`). Daemon blocks indexing, no `file.search` response, CPU/memory exhausted.

How to Fix
Use `symlink_metadata()` to detect symlink, skip pushing if `file_type.is_symlink()` (simple fix), or track `visited: HashSet<(u64,u64)>` via `MetadataExt::dev/ino` on Unix + path dedup on Windows. Also ensure `SKIP_DIRS` is checked on symlink target canonical name. Add `max_files`/`max_dirs` guard and return early if exceeded.

Expected Output
`SearchIndex::build` on looped symlink returns with finite `file_count`, does not hang; symlinked dirs are skipped or deduped; `cargo test -p cadis-core -- test_build_ignores_symlink_cycle` passes.

Critical Level
Medium (DoS via crafted workspace)

My Confidence
High

Why Matters?
`file.search` is model-facing; the agent can trigger indexing of any granted workspace. A malicious workspace or accidental symlink (common in monorepos) can DoS the daemon via the first search, blocking all subsequent tool calls.

Evidence: `crates/cadis-core/src/search_index.rs:23-58`, `crates/cadis-core/src/lib.rs:389 search_index_cache`
Validation: `cargo test -p cadis-core -- search_index` add `test_build_ignores_symlink_cycle` using `std::os::unix::fs::symlink`.

Issue #141: 🚀 Gthulhu 2026 Roadmap — Claim2Core: from Kubernetes ResourceClaims to Linux task scheduling

# Gthulhu 2026 Roadmap — Claim2Core

> **DRA chooses what and where; Gthulhu controls how it actually runs.**

Gthulhu is evolving into a **node-runtime execution plane** that closes the gap between Kubernetes resource allocation and Linux task scheduling.

The central research and engineering question is:

> **How do we turn allocated resources into delivered workload performance?**

Kubernetes can decide that a workload receives a GPU, NIC, CPU set, Node, NUMA domain, or other device. That does not automatically guarantee that the workload's critical Linux threads receive the CPU service, locality, responsiveness, or isolation required to deliver its SLO.

Gthulhu should not reimplement kube-scheduler, DRA, or Kueue. Instead, it should consume their decisions and translate them into a verifiable runtime execution contract using `sched_ext`, eBPF, and node-local telemetry.

## Positioning

```text
Kueue / Workload API
  admission, quota, fair sharing
            │
            ▼
kube-scheduler / DRA
  Node + GPU/NIC/CPU + topology allocation
            │
            ▼
Gthulhu Runtime Plane
  Claim → Pod/cgroup → TGID/TID → runtime policy
            │
            ▼
sched_ext + eBPF
  DSQ / slice / weight / locality / preemption
            │
            ▼
Delivered workload SLO
  latency / throughput / jitter / utilization
            │
            └──────── feedback ────────┐
                                       │
                                       └── runtime / scaling decisions
```

The responsibility boundary should remain explicit:

| Layer | Typical timescale | Core question |
|---|---:|---|
| Kueue / workload admission | seconds → minutes | Can this workload start now? |
| kube-scheduler / DRA | milliseconds → seconds | Which Node/device/topology should it receive? |
| Gthulhu / `sched_ext` | microseconds → milliseconds | Which workload threads run when and on which CPUs? |

## Core design principle: allocation is the source of truth

`ResourceSlice` represents **inventory**. It tells us what devices exist or are exposed by a Node.

For workload execution, the source of truth must be the **actual allocation** recorded by the workload's `ResourceClaim.status.allocation`, then traced into the runtime task identity.

The target lineage is:

```text
Workload / PodGroup UID
  → Pod UID
  → ResourceClaim UID + generation
  → allocated driver / pool / device
  → NUMA / PCIe / network topology
  → Pod cgroup
  → TGID / TID / starttime
  → sched_ext DSQ / BPF-map entry
  → observed runtime metrics
  → workload SLO
```

Related groundwork:

- #133 — separate ResourceSlice inventory discovery from real DRA allocation binding and move DRA handling to modern API semantics.
- #134 — add preview / explain / provenance so we can prove which tasks a policy targets and what reaches the runtime scheduler.
- #135 — completed TID-aware process scanning, removing a major blocker for Claim-to-Task binding.

## Flagship: Claim2Core

**Claim2Core: Closing the Gap Between Kubernetes Device Allocation and Linux Task Scheduling**

The first useful execution contract should map an allocated device/topology envelope into a runtime execution domain without violating ownership boundaries.

Example:

```text
ExecutionDomain
  Claim: <resource-claim-uid>
  Pod: <pod-uid>
  NUMA: 0
  CPUs: 0-15
  GPU: <device>
  NIC: <device>
  DSQ: claim-uid/domain-0
```

Within that domain, Gthulhu may control ordering, dispatch queues, weight, time slice, and locality — but it **must never move a task outside the CPU set or resource envelope established by Kubernetes / DRA / cgroups**.

## Roadmap

### Phase 1 — Correct DRA semantics

Goal: make the existing DRA path correct and explicitly separate inventory from allocation.

- [ ] use `resource.k8s.io/v1` semantics for ResourceSlice discovery
- [ ] support `nodeName`, `nodeSelector`, `allNodes`, and per-device node selection
- [ ] separate DeviceClass semantics from DRA driver identity
- [ ] use modern device attribute shape
- [ ] make naming/comments explicit: ResourceSlice = inventory, ResourceClaim = allocation
- [ ] add unit tests for the supported node-selection forms

Tracking: #133

### Phase 2 — Read-only ResourceClaim observer

Goal: establish **Claim → workload → Node/device** binding without changing scheduling behavior.

Introduce an internal binding model similar to:

```go
type ClaimDeviceBinding struct {
    ClaimUID        types.UID
    ClaimGeneration int64
    PodUID          types.UID
    NodeName        string
    Driver          string
    Pool            string
    Device          string
    NUMANodes       []int
    PCIeRoot        string
    PCIBusID        string
}
```

Requirements:

- [ ] observe allocated ResourceClaims
- [ ] associate allocation with Pod / workload identity
- [ ] cache the resolved binding node-locally
- [ ] invalidate on claim reallocation / deletion / generation change
- [ ] do **not** place Kubernetes API calls in the scheduler hot path

### Phase 3 — Claim-to-Task preview and provenance

Goal: prove what Gthulhu intends to schedule before mutating the kernel/runtime state.

Target preview:

```text
Claim
  → Pod
  → cgroup
  → TGID/TID/starttime
  → proposed execution class
  → proposed runtime policy
```

Requirements:

- [ ] dry-run preview must not write to the BPF map
- [ ] return matched TGID/TID, `comm`, cgroup, Pod UID, and node
- [ ] deterministic conflict detection
- [ ] monotonic policy generation
- [ ] intended-vs-actual BPF state verification
- [ ] removal verification after task exit / policy deletion / claim release

## What

Add a provider-neutral **Issue Hierarchy Reconciler** that keeps each repository navigable through one Repository Wayfinder and native GitHub parent/sub-issue relationships without creating a manually synchronized mega-issue.

GitHub supports nested sub-issues, parent/progress fields in Projects, and separate blocked-by/blocking dependencies. Use those native relations rather than parsing Markdown checklists:

- https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/adding-sub-issues
- https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/creating-issue-dependencies

## Domain language

**Repository Wayfinder**: the stable navigation root for one repository's bounded programs. It summarizes purpose and rules but never duplicates child status.

**Scope Tree**: native parent/sub-issue containment. One child contributes to one parent's outcome.

**Dependency Graph**: native blocked-by/blocking relations. It describes execution prerequisites and is not inferred from the Scope Tree.

**Hierarchy Receipt**: durable evidence for create, attach, detach, reorder, reparent, refuse, or reconcile operations against an exact GitHub revision.

## Why

Flat `ready-for-agent` queues hide programs, duplicate work, and make navigation expensive. Hand-maintained epic checklists drift because issue state, dependencies, PRs, and ownership change independently. Gaia needs a reconciler that proposes or repairs native relationships while refusing ambiguous restructuring.

## Invariants

- Each repository has at most one active Repository Wayfinder for a declared scope.
- A sub-issue has one scope parent; the Scope Tree is acyclic.
- Parenthood means containment only. It never implies blocking, supervision, authority, priority, or execution order.
- Dependencies, Responsibility Trees, DAGs, PR links, and artifact provenance remain separately typed graphs.
- Every issue remains self-contained: what, why, owner, plan, evidence, next gate, ETA basis, blockers, metrics, and acceptance live on the issue itself.
- The Wayfinder body never mirrors child status or a manual progress checklist; GitHub's native sub-issue progress is authoritative.
- Reparenting uses exact-read compare-and-set semantics, preserves history, and produces one receipt under concurrent replay.
- Gaia proposes rather than guesses when an issue could belong to multiple parents.
- Recommended depth is four; deeper structures require measured navigation benefit. GitHub's hard limits remain 100 children per parent and eight nested levels.
- Cross-repository containment is allowed only when the parent explicitly owns that multi-repository outcome; otherwise each repository keeps its own Wayfinder and uses dependency links.

## Block-driven reframing

When progress is blocked, the reconciler may derive exactly one advisory decision: KEEP, SPLIT, COALESCE, or ESCALATE. The decision is based on exact issue revisions, outcomes, acceptance criteria, authority, ownership, dependencies, linked PRs, and blocker evidence.

- **KEEP:** the issue still represents one independently verifiable outcome and splitting would only add coordination debt.
- **SPLIT:** distinct sub-outcomes have independently testable acceptance, different owners or authority, or independent dependency paths, and one blocked part is preventing safe progress on another. Create self-contained child issues; keep the original as the parent outcome until all required children produce terminal receipts.
- **COALESCE:** multiple issues provably describe the same durable outcome and acceptance boundary. Select one canonical issue, mark the others as superseded or duplicate with bidirectional links, and preserve every PR, receipt, decision, and comment by reference. Never paste bodies together as if history were interchangeable.
- **ESCALATE:** scopes overlap but acceptance, authority, atomicity, ownership, or intended outcome is ambiguous.

Issue #201: Add node-local tactic timeout overrides

## Problem

Tactic-timeout policy is currently expressed in terms of build entry points:

```toml
[build.root_tactic_timeouts]
"src/AppScript.sml" = 30.0
```

A root timeout applies to the root-package portion of that entry point's dependency closure. If several entry points reach the same theory, their contracts are merged using the minimum timeout. An explicit override on an unselected root may therefore constrain a shared dependency in the selected build.

That is useful as an entry-point contract, but it cannot express a different and common requirement:

> this particular theory contains an unusually slow tactic and needs a larger timeout, without changing the timeout of its dependencies, its consumers, or unrelated builds.

For example, given:

```text
AppTheory -> SlowTheory -> BaseTheory
```

we should be able to assign `SlowTheory` 30 seconds while `AppTheory` and `BaseTheory` retain the ordinary 2.5-second timeout.

## Proposed configuration

Add node-local timeout overrides, keyed by concrete theory-script source path. For example:

```toml
[build]
tactic_timeout = 2.5

[build.theory_tactic_timeouts]
"src/SlowScript.sml" = 30.0
```

The exact table name is open to bikeshedding; `theory_tactic_timeouts` is intended to distinguish these from the existing entry-point/closure-based `root_tactic_timeouts`.

## Semantics

A node-local override should:

- apply only to the named theory-script node;
- not propagate to that node's dependencies;
- not propagate to theories which depend on that node;
- not affect a build when that node is absent from the selected plan;
- participate only when the node is within the invocation's proof-instrumentation scope;
- remain execution/debug policy rather than part of the semantic action key.

For the example above, building `AppTheory` should assign:

```text
AppTheory   2.5s
SlowTheory  30.0s
BaseTheory  2.5s
```

Node-local overrides should allow disabling the timeout for one theory using the same `0` convention as the existing timeout settings.

If multiple policy sources apply directly to the same node, precedence should be explicit. A conservative initial rule would be:

1. an invocation-wide `--tactic-timeout` continues to override manifest policy, preserving current CLI behavior;
2. otherwise a node-local `theory_tactic_timeouts` value overrides the manifest/default timeout for that node;
3. otherwise existing entry-point policy supplies the timeout.

Issue #1576: Join a shared thread without a prior clone

## Why

A Heddle thread is the unit of work. Sharing one today still assumes the joiner already has the repository (`heddle clone` of a native or Git remote, then `start`). That is the GitHub-shaped path. The agent-native path is: you open a thread share and we materialize a checkout. No prior clone of origin.

Delta ships this (join creates per-machine checkouts of the thread's worktrees; you do not need the git repo first). We already have the cheap materializer they never published (`materialized` reflink / `virtualized` FUSE). We should hang join on that, not on a full `clone`.

Came out of the 2026-08-26 Delta pass. Steal join-without-clone. Reject their ACL (share-a-thread grants the whole repo's worktree history).

## Product lock

- **Thread is the unit.** Join is "I was invited to this thread," not "I cloned the repo." `clone` stays for "I want the spool / Git remote."
- **No new everyday verb.** Hang this on `start` (and tapestry join). Do not add `join` to the ~23.
- **CoW lives in heddle, not sley.** Sley is the Git-format engine. Materialize with `heddle-fs-prims` / `heddle-repo` (`ThreadMode::{Materialized,Virtualized,Solid}`). Do not invent a sley CoW / git-worktree stand-in.
- **Grant the thread, not the spool.** Sharing a thread must not open every other thread's history on that repository (Delta's documented miss).
- **Human still signs `ready`.** Join materializes a checkout. It does not land.

## What

1. A share/invite for a thread is enough for a machine that has never seen the spool to `heddle start` (or tapestry open) a checkout of that thread's tree.
2. Weft serves the objects needed to materialize that thread (page/stream, O(page) RAM). No "download the world."
3. Checkout mode is the existing policy: `auto` → reflink CoW on capable hosts, virtualized when that is the plan, solid only when the host cannot.
4. `.gitignore` / ignore policy still bounds what is synced. Secrets and build artifacts stay on the machine that created them.
5. If the joiner later wants the full spool, that is `clone`, not a side effect of join.

## Done when

- A second machine, empty of that repo, opens a thread share and gets a usable checkout without `heddle clone`.
- Advertised proof on HEAD: the start/join path plus the materializer tests (`materialized_threads_e2e` or a new join e2e). Compile-only is not proof.
- ACL test: a thread share does not list or materialize a sibling thread's history.
- No sley CoW / `git worktree add` path.

## Out of scope

- Delta-style "everyone edits the same CRDT files" as the agent default. Isolation stays the default.
- Hosted undo (still the proposed API ADR).
- Replacing `clone`.

Issue #2982: feat(automation): convert stalled plans into epics of single-PR issues

## Motivation

The plan-review stage can lose information when an implementation plan becomes large.
`MAX_CURRENT_REVISION_CONTEXT_CHARS` limits prior plan context to 12,000 characters.
The amendment prompt truncates a plan that cannot fit in this limit.

A truncated amendment can remove decisions that earlier reviews accepted.
Later reviews can then find the same defects again.
More review cycles can increase cost without making stable progress.

The current plan-review policy permits three reviews in each of two plan cycles.
The pipeline can therefore receive six NOGO verdicts before it stops.
The pipeline does not convert an overlarge task into independently implementable work.

Issue #2706 added deterministic child creation for scope expansion during pull-request review.
Planning needs an equivalent host-owned path for task decomposition.

## Proposed Solution

Add a durable `plan_decomposition` transition to the plan-review stage.
The transition converts the source issue into an epic.
It creates and queues one GitHub issue for each decomposed work item.

Use these switch conditions:

1. **Lossless-size limit:** Before an amendment, render the complete current plan.
   Trigger decomposition when it cannot fit within the 12,000-character amendment context budget.
   A first review can still approve the large plan.
   After a NOGO verdict, do not amend from truncated context.
2. **Convergence limit:** Trigger decomposition after the fifth real NOGO verdict in one requirements epoch.
   Count NOGO verdicts across normal plan-cycle resets.
   Do not count missing verdicts, provider errors, timeouts, or other infrastructure failures.
   A GO verdict continues to implementation.
   A BLOCKED verdict retains the existing operator-owned blocked path.
3. **Epoch reset:** Reset the NOGO count only when the authoritative issue requirements change.
   Do not reset it when the pipeline starts another plan cycle.

Ask the decomposition agent to divide the complete epic into single-pull-request units of work.
Do not configure a minimum or maximum number of work items.
The required behavior and review findings determine the number of issues.

Each work item must have these properties:

- One pull request can implement, test, review, and revert the item independently.
- The item has one coherent behavior change or required enabling change.
- The item has explicit scope, acceptance criteria, verification, and failure behavior.
- The item identifies its direct prerequisites.
- The item maps to parent requirements or unresolved review findings.
- The item does not duplicate the scope of another item.

The decomposition result must include a complete dependency tree rooted at the source epic.
Every work item in the tree must become a GitHub issue.
Each issue must contain the parent epic link and its direct dependency links.
Dependency edges must form an acyclic order.
Independent branches can run concurrently after their prerequisites pass.

The decomposition must cover every parent acceptance criterion.
It must also cover every unresolved review finding.
The host must reject gaps, duplicate scope, unsafe paths, dependency cycles, and unsupported fields.

Use the existing text and payload safety limits for each issue specification.
These safety limits must not set the number of work items.
If one proposed item is too large for one pull request, the agent must divide it again before mutation.

Use an independent read-only review to approve the complete decomposition before GitHub mutation.
Model output is untrusted data.
Only the host can create markers, labels, issue links, dependency links, and queue entries.

Use this durable mutation order:

1. Record a versioned decomposition intent for the source issue and requirements epoch.
2. Validate the complete single-pull-request work tree and its requirement coverage.
3. Create or recover each work-item issue in dependency order through a deterministic marker.
4. Read back every issue and verify its exact normalized specification.
5. Publish one actor-owned parent summary with the ordered issue list and dependency tree.
6. Add `epic` and `state:skip` to the parent.
7. Remove conflicting planning-state labels from the parent.
8. Add `state:needs-plan` to each work-item issue and confirm the label transition.
9. Queue each exact work-item issue in topological layers during the current run.
10. Finish the parent as a successful non-code tracking item.

Do not change the parent title or issue body.
Keep its canonical plan and review as audit evidence.
Work-item issues inherit the parent severity.
They do not inherit `epic` or parent planning-state labels.

Each generated issue must include:

- `Part of epic #<parent>`.
- `Depends on #<issue>` for each direct prerequisite.
- The owned behavior and repository paths.
- Acceptance criteria that fit one pull request.
- Focused verification commands and expected evidence.
- The source plan revision and requirements-epoch identity.
- A deterministic host-owned recovery marker.

Retries and restarts must recover the same issue tree.
A changed plan fingerprint in the same requirements epoch must not create a second tree.
An ambiguous GitHub write must recover by an exact actor-owned marker or fail closed.

Do not use a fixed child, descendant, or tree-depth limit as the decomposition rule.
The single-pull-request scope is the leaf condition.
Use general pipeline resource controls to bound execution.
If a complete tree cannot be validated safely, apply `state:plan-blocked` and request operator action.

Do not decompose a generated issue again during the same pipeline run.
A later run can evaluate that issue from its authoritative requirements.

Dry-run must show the trigger, proposed issues, dependency tree, and parent transition.
Dry-run must not create issues, comments, labels, durable records, or queue entries.

Issue #303: RelativeDifference detection performance: reduce recursive CTE queries per upload

## Problem

`calculateRelativeDifferenceValues` uses recursive CTE queries for every domain value evaluation. Each CTE walks the value DAG to find matching fingerprint, range, and domain values. This creates O(D x W) recursive queries per upload, where D is the number of domain values and W is the window size.

### Consequences

1. **O(D x W) queries per upload**: ~2,304 recursive CTE queries per upload, each taking ~25ms. Per-upload time: 57-344s with linear growth as history accumulates.

2. **Detection count gap**: Importing 15 runs of test 113 (quarkus-spring-boot-comparison) produces 29 h5m detections vs Horreum's 15. The gap is explained by h5m having 2 RD configs per variable (different window/threshold combinations), producing ~2x detections.

## Current status (fingerprint-index branch)

The `fingerprint-index` branch addresses the performance issue with indexed queries while preserving the existing window-scanning detection semantics.

### Performance: fingerprint_id + root_id indexed queries
- New `fingerprint_entry` table for deduplicated fingerprint identities
- `fingerprint_id` and `root_id` FK columns on `value` table with compound indexes
- `findByFingerprint()` method uses simple indexed queries instead of recursive CTEs
- Batch-fetch all range and domain values for a fingerprint in 2 queries, then evaluate in-memory
- **Result: 0.1-0.9s per upload** (down from 57-344s), no linear growth with history

### Semantics: window-scanning preserved
- Fast path preserves window-scanning behavior: re-evaluates detection at domain values within the window around the uploaded value, including following values for out-of-order uploads
- Delete-then-recompute cleanup: before evaluating, deletes existing detections whose domain value falls within the evaluation scope, then re-creates only those that still trigger — prevents duplicate detections
- Scoped to the fingerprint's groupBy branch via `getAncestor(fingerprintValue, groupBy)`
- Fingerprint stamping in `ProcessingService.completeIngestion()` after all work items complete
- Legacy CTE-based path preserved as fallback for values without `fingerprint_id`

### FingerprintEntity lifecycle
- Created in `NodeService.calculateFpValues()` via `findOrCreate()` (hash-based deduplication)
- Stamped on sibling values in `ValueService.stampAllFingerprintsForRoot()` after all work items complete
- Cleaned up when a FingerprintNode is deleted: `NodeService.delete()` nullifies `fingerprint_id` on affected values and removes orphaned `fingerprint_entry` rows
- Single-fingerprint-per-group assumption: `stampFingerprintOnSiblings` uses first-writer-wins; multi-fingerprint groups fall back to the legacy CTE path (correct but slower)

### Results
- **All 812+ tests pass** with original test assertions
- **Test 113 import**: 100% label match rate, 29 detections vs Horreum's 15 (2x ratio from 2 RD configs per variable; `Averge Build Time` matches exactly: 5 vs 5)
- **Per-upload time**: 0.1-0.9s constant (no growth with history)

| Stage | h5m detections | Horreum | Notes |
|-------|---------------|---------|-------|
| Legacy path (window scan) | 12,682 | 15 | O(N) recursive CTE queries per upload |
| + fingerprint_id indexed queries | 352 | 15 | Same semantics, indexed lookups |
| + evaluate-at-upload only | 41 | 15 | Too restrictive for out-of-order uploads |
| + window-scanning restored | 53 | 15 | Correct semantics, some duplicate detections |
| + delete-then-recompute cleanup | 29 | 15 | 2x ratio from 2 RD configs per variable |

- `delete_fingerprint_node_cleans_up_fingerprint_entries`: verifies FingerprintEntity rows are deleted and `fingerprint_id` nullified when a FingerprintNode is deleted
- `calculateRelativeDifference_multi_fingerprint_uses_legacy_path`: verifies groups with multiple fingerprint nodes produce correct detections via the legacy CTE fallback

- Horreum invocation: `AlertingServiceImpl.java:625-745`

## Mission
Make higher-order world state safely revisable by tracking its evidence and claims, then provide coherent history, correction-impact and freshness semantics.

## Scope
- dependencies: event -> observation -> claim/inference -> node/relation/state -> synthesis/context/canon;
- coherent restart-safe world revisions as specified by the reconciled RFC;
- invalidation/recompute for correction, supersession, source deletion, purge and changed evidence;
- evidence lineage so copied/summarized material is not independent corroboration;
- stale/degraded health in doctor;
- bounded incremental recomputation rather than a full-vault scan for each change.

## Competitive-design additions, 5 September 2026
Study [Graphiti's temporal model](https://www.getzep.com/platform/graphiti/) and [Hindsight's freshness/consolidation pattern](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/). Borrow semantics and tests, not an automatic database replacement.

### Historical correctness
Specify valid time separately from the time Kizuki recorded a belief. Late evidence can revise today's account of yesterday without rewriting what Kizuki knew yesterday. Time bounds, retractions, supersession and lineage must survive export/restore and rebuild. Current and historical queries still use current access policy; historical time is not permission to revive purged or revoked material.

### Correction with consequences
Use the existing owner-correction and same-pass canon rewrite path. Preserve the exact targeted assertion and distinguish correcting the owner's belief from altering another person's historical statement. Expose an attributable impact receipt/read model: affected claim/object IDs, recomputed or invalidated views, unresolved work, and old assumptions no longer current. It must be safe for both human rendering and agent consumption.

A correction must not wait for #503's consolidation job. Define synchronous invalidation plus bounded recovery where semantic recomputation cannot complete immediately. Reads must not call invalidated state current. Undo follows the existing receipt semantics and never resurrects purged evidence.

### Freshness and policy
Bind external view/cursor tokens to principal, scope, purpose, relevant content and policy state. Internal global revisions may exist, but their counts/timing must not expose restricted activity to clients. Treat unavailable, incomplete, stale, invalidated and unchanged as distinct outcomes. Coordinate #490's external diff contract; do not publish a second one here.

Source freshness/coverage from #482 supports honest blind spots. An absent response in incomplete captured sources is not proof of no response. #503 owns consolidation/overlay execution; this issue owns dependency and invalidation semantics.

## UX / DX / AX
UX: show what changed, why, what downstream understanding was affected and anything still pending; no raw dependency graph required.
DX: typed dependency/impact APIs, indexed traversals, stable retry/error behavior, migrations and recovery tests.
AX: inspectable impact and freshness information under the same grant, not an unrestricted global changelog. A model revision is not a lock on the outside world; external execution must handle changes after a check.

- [ ] Copied evidence shares support lineage; repeated use does not increase truth authority/confidence.
- [ ] Revocation/purge blocks current and historical derived reads, clears managed dependent state and prevents job/rebuild resurrection.
- [ ] Restricted changes do not leak through revision counters, hashes, counts, timing-dependent metadata or impact enumeration; use noninterference fixtures for observable outputs within the threat model.
- [ ] Exact-head `bun run verify` and relevant #496 public-seam, lifecycle and resource gates pass.

Issue #1184: DCB materialized view: completed refresh of active version leaves registry CatchingUp

## Summary

A refresh of an already-active materialized-view version can leave its persisted registry status at `CatchingUp` after catch-up completes. The completion path sets the in-memory publication status to `Active`, but does not restore the registry status in the already-active branch.

Consumers that require the persisted registry to be `Active` then remain unavailable. An active pointer and populated projection rows do not resolve this readiness failure.

## Versions and source

- Observed in a local PostgreSQL/Orleans application using Sekiban DCB 10.17.0. The restored package metadata points to commit `cca3c8d64c5a5a013b8ce4e5197c160b26423864`.
- The same completion branch is present in the inspected 10.20.0 source at commit `b7f2386c41f90712ac65633efaa0f2b03b64c882`. We have not run this reproduction against 10.20.0 binaries.
- [10.17 source](https://github.com/J-Tech-Japan/Sekiban/blob/cca3c8d64c5a5a013b8ce4e5197c160b26423864/dcb/src/Sekiban.Dcb.MaterializedView.Orleans/MaterializedViewGrain.cs)
- [Inspected 10.20 source](https://github.com/J-Tech-Japan/Sekiban/blob/b7f2386c41f90712ac65633efaa0f2b03b64c882/dcb/src/Sekiban.Dcb.MaterializedView.Orleans/MaterializedViewGrain.cs)

## Source-level cause

`RunCatchUpTickAsync` persists `MvStatus.CatchingUp` through `_registryStore.UpdateStatusAsync` when it starts a catch-up cycle.

In `CompleteCatchUpAsync`, the `IMvActivationExecutor` path checks the current and target checkpoint truth. It then loads the active pointer. If `active?.ActiveVersion == _host.ViewVersion`, the branch sets `_publicationSnapshot.Status` to `Active`, clears `_isCatchUpActive` and `_needsImmediateCatchUp`, records completion, and returns.

That branch does not call `_registryStore.UpdateStatusAsync` to restore `Active`. This can leave registry readers and in-memory status readers with different lifecycle states after a successful refresh.

## Observed evidence

In a local PostgreSQL integration run:

- The active pointer selected version 3, generation 1.
- Both logical-table registry rows for that view remained `catchingup`.
- Their current checkpoint truth was known. Their target checkpoint truth was known and had `AuthoritativeTargetCapture` provenance. The current position was beyond the captured target.
- The view contained the expected projected work row.
- The persisted projection-status record was not faulted.
- The application repeatedly rejected the view at its registry readiness check. Its dependent background work did not advance during a 120-second observation window.

We did not capture the live grain flags before the test host exited. The persisted evidence and source inspection support this diagnosis, but we do not claim a standalone upstream regression test has passed or failed yet.

## Suggested minimal reproduction / regression test

These are proposed upstream test steps, not a standalone reproduction already executed by us.

1. Use the PostgreSQL materialized-view path with an `IMvActivationExecutor`.
2. Create and activate a view version. Include two logical tables to verify all registry rows.
3. Append events after activation and call `RefreshAsync` on that already-active version.
4. Let catch-up reach its authoritative target and complete.
5. Read the registry entries, active pointer, and grain status.
6. Assert that every logical-table registry row is `Active`, the active version and generation are unchanged, and the grain has no outstanding catch-up work.
7. Repeat the refresh and assertions.

Also test that incomplete catch-up, unknown checkpoint truth, an unsatisfied target, and a fault do not cause promotion to `Active`.

## Expected behavior and possible fix

A successfully completed refresh of an already-active version should restore its persisted lifecycle status to `Active`. It should preserve the active pointer and generation. It must retain the existing authoritative checkpoint and fault checks.

Please consider restoring the registry status in the already-active completion branch, with the library's normal lifecycle/concurrency guarantees. Application code should not need to repair library lifecycle metadata after an ordinary refresh.

We have an existing guarded application pattern that restores only status after checking active identity, completed catch-up, subscription health, and authoritative checkpoint truth. Extending it to the affected reader is planned, not yet verified by the failing integration journey. A library correction is preferable.

## Scope

This report concerns materialized-view lifecycle metadata. It is separate from cold event replay memory usage and from event-transport message-size limits. We have no evidence that those issues cause this registry transition defect.

Bind ordinary nullable materialized-view SQL parameters as SQL NULL without projection faults caused by Dapper inferring System.DBNull.

Preserve serialized MvParamKind.Null. A non-Null kind with null ValueJson is invalid. Explicit application DBNull input is unsupported. Null binding is untyped and depends on query/provider inference.

Reverting the null conversion makes this test fail at the actual binding boundary.

Characterize PostgreSQL uuid/timestamp/bytea and SQL Server non-text/varbinary plus MySQL/SQLite nullable text; record exact successes or provider limitations with executed commands and versions.

- AC5: Add discriminating tests for present-null, absent parameter, non-null, explicit DBNull input, and malformed non-Null wire kind with null ValueJson. Preserve failure visibility; do not swallow projection errors or weaken checkpoint guarantees.
- AC6: Document untyped-null semantics, measured provider/query limitations and explicit DBNull rejection in EN/JA materialized-view documentation.
