A maintainer on the project MrNedimBoztepe/Shonkor (C#) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #458: AP3: the traversal makes one query per node — loading all 108 731 edges costs less than 1 000 incident lookups

AP3 from the mandate. **Two variants with measured numbers, as instructed — the choice is yours, not
mine.**

> Entscheidungsregel: Lege beide Varianten mit gemessenen Zahlen aus F3 vor und lass die Wahl
> bestätigen. Nicht selbst entscheiden.

## F3 — the trigger fires, and it is worse than "one query per level"

`BlastRadiusTool` calls `GetIncidentEdgesAsync(cur)` **once per visited node** inside its BFS
(`BlastRadiusTool.cs:101`), not once per level. `ReferencesTool`'s transitive branch does the same
(`AnalyzeTools.cs:91`).

Measured on live `sitecoreMuM` (108 731 edges, 26 958 nodes):

| operation | time |
|---|---|
| `GetAllEdgesAsync` — the whole edge set | **1 018 ms**, ~70 MB retained |
| `GetIncidentEdgesAsync` × 1 000 | **1 299 ms** (1,30 ms per call), 45 083 edges seen |

**Loading every edge in the graph costs less than a thousand incident lookups**, and those thousand see
less than half the edges — with duplicates.

A depth-5 traversal reaching 7 046 nodes (the pre-AP7 figure for one real class) spends
7 046 × 1,30 ms ≈ **9,2 seconds in roundtrips alone**. After AP7's default exclusion the same traversal
reaches 92 nodes, so the cost is currently hidden by a filter rather than absent — and `includeModelEdges=true`
brings all of it back.

## Variant A — one `WITH RECURSIVE` statement

Reverse reachability plus weakest-tier aggregation in a single SQL statement.

- One roundtrip regardless of depth or breadth.
- Memory stays SQLite's problem.
- The tier/reason/model filters move into SQL. All three are already expressed as sets, so this is
  mechanical — but it puts the AP2 and AP7 semantics into a second language, and *"two ways to express
  one constraint"* is the shape that produced #399's 1 354 stranded edges.
- Recursive CTE termination on a cyclic graph needs care; the current BFS terminates via
  relax-on-improvement, which does not translate directly.

## Variant B — in-process adjacency, SQLite as persistence only

Load the edge set once, traverse in memory.

- **70 MB for the largest graph here**, loaded in 1 second. `FPM-Optimizely` is roughly half that.
- Filters stay in C#, where AP2/AP7 already live. One implementation, one set of tests.
- Cost is per *process*, not per query: the MCP stdio server pays it once at startup and every later
  traversal is free. The HTTP relay is per-request and would pay it every time — that is the case that
  decides against a naive version.
- Staleness: an in-memory copy goes stale the moment a scan writes. #449's revision marker gives a cheap
  invalidation signal, but it has to be wired.

## What I would want you to weigh

The honest asymmetry: **A** is one roundtrip but a second implementation of the filter semantics;
**B** is one implementation but a cache with a lifetime question. This project's recurring defect has
been two components disagreeing about the same thing — which argues for B — while its other recurring
defect has been state that outlives its validity, which argues for A.

I have no measurement that settles that, and the mandate says not to decide it myself.

Nothing built.

A maintainer on the project MyThingsLab/my-things-core (Python) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #145: Design: real fan-out/join topology for the fleet cycle (mypipeline + my-fleet)

## Why

`mypipeline`'s `workflows.json` declares a 13-node graph, but 11 of those nodes form a strict `after: [previous]` chain — `myplanner → fleet-dispatch → myresearcher → mytester → mychangelogger → mydocs → mydashboard → myprojector → myreporter → mypipeline-sync → mytelegrambot`. `myfleet.fleet_cycle`'s `RESOLVERS` dict and its driver (`cycle_driver.py`) only ever walk this list stage-by-stage; there is no fan-out (two independent stages after a shared prerequisite) or fan-in (a stage that waits on more than one predecessor) anywhere in the fleet today. It's a shell script's worth of ordering expressed as a graph data structure, not a DAG being used as one.

The dead handoff mechanism is a second symptom of the same gap: `mypipeline`'s two `trigger: ledger`-handoff nodes (`example-catalog-to-bibliography`, `idea-verdict-build-to-new-tool-tracking`) have fired **zero times ever** — one listens for an event (`myarchivist/catalog`) no tool has ever emitted, the other would have matched twice (2026-07-18, two `idea/verdict=build` entries) but `mypipeline sync` last ran 24 minutes before either landed and never ran again that day. The ledger-path bugs fixed this session (MyThingsLab/my-tester#21, MyThingsLab/my-changelogger#12 — `--ledger` defaulting to cwd instead of `--source`) mean the *data* those handoffs need is now landing in the right place; the *triggering* is still purely time-based (`fleet_cycle` runs `mypipeline sync` once per cycle, not on the event), so a handoff can always miss by exactly this kind of race.

## What a real topology would need

1. **`myfleet.fleet_cycle`**: stages currently execute as `for stage in ORDER: run(stage)`. A DAG driver needs: (a) independent stages after a shared prerequisite actually run in parallel (or at least, run without artificially waiting on each other), and (b) a join stage that only fires once *all* its declared predecessors have completed in this cycle — not just "sometime before, on an earlier run."
2. **`mypipeline.plan.build_plan`**: already does a real `topo_sort` (`src/mypipeline/plan.py:22`) — the topological ordering exists. What's missing is the driver consuming that order literally instead of flattening it to a list; `build_plan` would need to expose the graph's actual parallelism (e.g. group nodes into topological "waves" instead of a single ordered `PlanItem` list) for `fleet_cycle` to use.
3. **A `ledger`-trigger firing inline**, not just on the next `mypipeline sync`: either `mypipeline sync` runs immediately after any stage that could produce a matching ledger entry (not once at the end of the cycle), or handoff-eligible kinds get checked as each producing stage completes.

## Suggested first slice (concrete, not the whole redesign)

Pick one real fan-out that's actually useful today rather than redesigning the whole driver: after `myresearcher` produces a study brief, `mybibliography` (citations) and `myglossary` (terms) could run independently off the same output instead of my-glossary waiting behind an unrelated `mytester`/`mychangelogger` pass it has no dependency on. That's a 2-node fan-out + a trivial join back into the existing chain — small enough to prove the driver change without committing to the full graph-as-parallel-execution model up front.

## Repos touched

- `my-fleet` (`src/myfleet/fleet_cycle.py`, `cycle_driver.py`) — execution model
- `my-pipeline` (`src/mypipeline/plan.py`, `workflows.py`) — plan/graph contract
- `my-things-core/docs/tools/my-pipeline.md` — update once the contract changes

Labeled `needs-decision` + `core-contract` rather than `tool-build`: this changes how two existing, shipped tools' contracts compose, not a new tool.

Issue #217: [P1][performance] Make follower retrieval and diff calculation linear, bounded, and rate-limit aware

## Background

Because every cursor is fetched sequentially without an upper bound and a bidirectional `Array.includes()` diff is then performed, API request count, CPU usage, and memory usage can all grow without bound for large channels.

## Current path

- [`lib/accessTwitch.ts`](https://github.com/NPJigaK/twitch-follower-checker/blob/37c0a40dc67d70110448d28ca7f6acae600b45ce/lib/accessTwitch.ts#L63-L83): recursively fetches pages with `first=100` until the cursor is exhausted
- [`lib/accessTwitch.ts`](https://github.com/NPJigaK/twitch-follower-checker/blob/37c0a40dc67d70110448d28ca7f6acae600b45ce/lib/accessTwitch.ts#L89-L100): runs `includes` in both directions inside `filter`

Worst-case comparison counts:

- 10,000 items: approximately 200 million
- 25,000 items: approximately 1.25 billion
- 50,000 items: approximately 5 billion (approximately 9.2 seconds in an isolated Node measurement for disjoint sets)
- 100,000 items: approximately 20 billion

50,000 followers require at least 500 API pages, and 100,000 followers require 1,000 pages. This can lead to HTTP 429 responses, long main-thread blocking, memory growth, and an unresponsive browser tab.

## Implementation direction

- Use `Set` / `Map` ID lookups and make the diff O(N)
- Replace recursive pagination with an explicit loop
- Maintain a visited-cursor set
- Add page, item, and elapsed-time budgets
- Support cancellation through `AbortController`
- Display progress
- Handle `Ratelimit-Remaining` / `Ratelimit-Reset`
- Deduplicate by `user_id`
- Treat `total` as a diagnostic value because it changes dynamically
- Debounce the quick filter and benchmark large `rowData`
- Define the maximum supported item count as a product requirement

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Diff calculation is O(N) with respect to the old/current item counts
- [ ] Benchmarks for 10k / 25k / 50k / 100k fixtures are retained in CI or as performance tests
- [ ] Duplicate cursors do not cause unbounded fetching
- [ ] Duplicate users do not appear more than once in the display or diff
- [ ] No repeated requests are sent before the reset time after a 429 response
- [ ] State and baseline are not updated after cancellation
- [ ] A snapshot that exceeds the page/time budget is treated as incomplete
- [ ] Main-thread long tasks and heap usage are compared before and after the fix using a Chrome trace

## Evidence

- [Twitch API: Get Channel Followers](https://dev.twitch.tv/docs/api/reference/#get-channel-followers)
- [Twitch API: Pagination and rate limits](https://dev.twitch.tv/docs/api/guide/)
- [ECMAScript: Array.prototype.includes](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/indexed-collections.html#sec-array.prototype.includes)

A maintainer on the project NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym (Python) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #3006: Bound rollout task admission and persist completed results incrementally

## Parent workstream

[#2999 — Performance workstream: core Gym infrastructure](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/issues/2999)

## Slowdown path

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[All input rows stay materialized] --> B[All rollout coroutines become tasks]
    B --> C[Semaphore limits active requests only]
    C --> D[Rows and results accumulate until return]
```

## Current behavior

Rollout output is already incremental. For every completion, the collector serializes the result, appends it to the main JSONL or failures sidecar, and flushes the selected file immediately ([`rollout_collection.py` lines 1452–1479](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/blob/9287fb7797907ff17884963730d79f428a225639/nemo_gym/rollout_collection.py#L1452-L1479)). This issue must not reimplement persistence or describe results as buffered until shutdown.

The remaining residency comes from two places:

- `run_examples()` passes the complete iterable of rollout coroutines to `tqdm.as_completed()`. `asyncio.as_completed()` schedules the whole iterable, while the semaphore only limits how many request bodies enter the active request section ([`rollout_collection.py` lines 1876–1934](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/blob/9287fb7797907ff17884963730d79f428a225639/nemo_gym/rollout_collection.py#L1876-L1934)).
- `_run_from_config()` retains `input_rows`, appends every completed row and result to `rows` and `results`, keeps successful entries referenced again by `persisted_rows` and `persisted_results`, sorts those collections, uses them for upload and aggregation, and returns the full `results` list ([initialization at lines 1255–1280](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/blob/9287fb7797907ff17884963730d79f428a225639/nemo_gym/rollout_collection.py#L1255-L1280), [completion retention at lines 1452–1479](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/blob/9287fb7797907ff17884963730d79f428a225639/nemo_gym/rollout_collection.py#L1452-L1479), and [post-processing/return at lines 1558–1631](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/blob/9287fb7797907ff17884963730d79f428a225639/nemo_gym/rollout_collection.py#L1558-L1631)).

Implement bounded task creation, not only bounded request execution. Add explicit opt-in non-retaining semantics for callers that consume the persisted artifacts and do not need `run_from_config()` to return every rollout in memory.

## Impact and provenance

### Measured

The investigation measured 131,072 in-flight asyncio tasks at about 184 MB and 17.6K bookkeeping completions/s. It also measured a real 64K-token driver ceiling of 13–15 rollouts/s and 22–27 MB/s of JSON. These results show that task bookkeeping is not the current throughput bottleneck, but its memory cost grows with offered work.

### Expected

- Bounded creation should make coroutine/task residency scale with the configured in-flight window instead of total row count.
- Opt-in non-retaining mode should remove the dominant completed-row/result residency for artifact-oriented callers.
- Throughput should remain neutral unless lower memory pressure avoids allocator or paging overhead. Any throughput gain must be measured, not assumed.

## Implementation constraints

- Preserve the existing append-and-flush behavior, output schema, deterministic ordering, failure sidecar rules, resume behavior, token-capture finalization, upload behavior, aggregation, health checks, and coverage reporting.
- Preserve the current full-list return by default. Non-retaining behavior must be opt-in and have an explicit documented return contract.
- A non-retaining path still needs enough bounded state to aggregate, upload, and run health checks, or it must reload the persisted artifact in a defined way.
- Cancellation and exceptions must close output files and cancel only the bounded set of active tasks.
- Do not use server-side rejection as admission control; the driver should stop creating work until capacity becomes available.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] At most a configured, documented number of rollout tasks/coroutines are resident at once.
- [ ] The existing `num_samples_in_parallel` request-concurrency behavior remains compatible.
- [ ] Default `run_from_config()` behavior still returns the complete ordered result list.
- [ ] An opt-in mode avoids retaining completed rows/results and documents what `run_from_config()` returns.
- [ ] Main JSONL and failure sidecar records are still appended and flushed per completion.
- [ ] Resume, failure routing, aggregation, upload, token capture, health checks, and cancellation have focused tests.
- [ ] Artifact contents and final ordering match the retaining mode for the same deterministic run.

## Benchmark plan

1. Run deterministic synthetic collections with 8K and 128K offered rollouts at fixed active concurrency and representative small and 64K-token-shaped results.
2. Compare current behavior, bounded creation with retaining return, and bounded creation with non-retaining return.
3. Record peak RSS, Python heap, resident task count, resident row/result count, rollouts/s, event-loop lag, and output write latency.
4. Verify byte-equivalent sorted main artifacts and sidecars, then exercise resume from a partially completed run.
5. Report the configured window and actual peak task count so offered concurrency is not confused with resident concurrency.

## Related work

- [#3008](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/issues/3008) exposes connector queueing after driver admission.
- [#2999](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/issues/2999) tracks the shared driver and server-stack performance work.

    D --> E[Exception converted to no prediction]
    E --> F[Child may continue running]
    F --> G[More verifies spawn more children]
```

## Current behavior

At upstream `main` commit [`9287fb7797907ff17884963730d79f428a225639`](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/commit/9287fb7797907ff17884963730d79f428a225639), every inductive NVARC verification can call `_execute_python`. That function starts a new Python interpreter and awaits `proc.communicate()` with `asyncio.wait_for` ([source](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/blob/9287fb7797907ff17884963730d79f428a225639/resources_servers/nvarc/app.py#L299-L320)).

The timeout and broad exception handler returns `None` without terminating, killing, or waiting for the child ([source](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/blob/9287fb7797907ff17884963730d79f428a225639/resources_servers/nvarc/app.py#L321-L336)). Cancelling `communicate()` does not terminate the operating-system process. The server also has no semaphore around interpreter creation. Transductive mode does not execute this subprocess path.

## Impact and provenance

### Measured

The 2026-08-31 report at `investigations/gym-and-performance.md` was recorded against `6992a96de`. It identifies unbounded spawn and timeout leakage by code inspection; it does not provide measured NVARC throughput, leak count, or memory growth.

### Expected

Expected, not yet measured: a semaphore will bound resident interpreters under load. Reliable terminate/kill/wait cleanup will prevent timed-out children from accumulating. These are lifecycle and correctness results first; no speedup is claimed. Admission control may increase queue latency while making resource use predictable.

## Correctness and process behavior

The leaked-child path is a correctness and resource-lifecycle defect. Fix it independently of any performance optimization. A timeout, cancellation, invalid JSON result, nonzero exit, or validation failure must leave no child process behind and must preserve the current `None` prediction and zero-reward behavior.

## Implementation constraints

- Keep one fresh interpreter per untrusted submission; do not place untrusted code in a shared warm process.
- Add a positive configurable concurrency limit and document its per-worker scope.
- Include queue time in a separate metric from execution time; define whether the configured timeout starts before or after semaphore acquisition.
- On timeout or cancellation, terminate, wait briefly, kill if necessary, then wait again.
- Shield cleanup from caller cancellation so reaping completes before the coroutine exits.
- Preserve output decoding with `errors="replace"`, JSON validation, and board validation.
- Do not describe the restricted builtins/import list as a security sandbox.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Inductive interpreter concurrency never exceeds the configured limit.
- [ ] Success, timeout, cancellation, nonzero exit, empty output, invalid JSON, and invalid board paths all reap the child.
- [ ] Timeout cleanup escalates from terminate to kill when required.
- [ ] Cleanup runs from a `finally` path and is resilient to cancellation.
- [ ] Tests inspect descendants and file descriptors after repeated failures.
- [ ] Transductive verification behavior is unchanged.
- [ ] Queue wait and subprocess runtime are observable separately.
- [ ] Any performance claim is supported by the benchmark below rather than inferred from the leak fix.

## Benchmark plan

1. Compare baseline and candidate at the same pinned SHA with inductive mode only; run transductive mode as a regression control.
2. Use immediate success, controlled sleep, ignored terminate signal, syntax error, invalid JSON, invalid board, and caller-cancellation cases.
3. Run 1, 32, 256, and 8,192 offered verifies against limits 1, 4, 16, and 32.
4. Record maximum live interpreters, queue wait p50/p95/p99, execution p50/p95/p99, completion rate, timeout count, CPU, RSS, file descriptors, and descendants after quiescence.
5. Verify reward/prediction parity for all non-timeout cases.
6. Report bounded resource use and latency separately; do not label semaphore queueing as a throughput gain.

Issue #391: A temporal graph of people, places, activities and themes

From the technical review, items **3.2** (interest/entity graph), **6.1** (temporal knowledge graph) and **10.1**. Filed for v0.13, where *your rhythm* already lives, because it is the same subject seen from another side.

## What exists

Facts sit in tables that do not point at one another:

```text
stops -> outings -> anchors        a journey
captions -> subjects -> themes     what was in the frame
note_readings, page_readings       what was written and opened
profiles                           interests, with evidence references
```

An interest carries `InterestEvidence(kind, reference, observed_at)`, which is **one edge, written down as a column**. Everything else is joined by hand at query time, and only where somebody wrote the join.

## What that costs, concretely

The questions this library exists to answer are relational, and each one currently needs its own derivation:

```text
"which places do I go to for ramen?"        place -- theme
"who was I with when I went there?"         no person concept at all
"what changed about that place last year?"  place -- theme -- time
"is this interest tied to one place?"       interest -- place
```

`docs/proposals/0008`'s v0.13 says *a trip is a week that broke the pattern on purpose; a dormant place is a piece of the rhythm that stopped -- these are the same subject seen from different sides, and v0.13 says so once instead of five times.* **A graph is what "once instead of five times" looks like.**

## The temporal part is the point

Not a graph of what is related, but of **when things were related**. A place that was an anchor for two years and stopped is a different fact from a place that never was, and both are different from one that just started. That distinction is what `drift`, `lifecycle` and `suggest` each rebuild separately today.

## What has to be decided before it is built

- **Whether a person is a node at all.** ADR-0078 already settled what a prompt may say about people, and `NoteRecord`/`WebRecord` refuse labels on a `people` category. A graph with person nodes would be a materially different privacy posture and needs its own decision, not an inherited one
- **Whether this replaces the tables or sits above them.** Replacing them means rewriting every derivation; sitting above them means a second representation that can disagree with the first, which is worse
- **What it costs.** Measured: the geometry builds 100,000 photographs in **1.94 s**. A graph that made that ten seconds would still be invisible next to the hours the model takes (#381) — so this is not a performance decision, and should not be argued as one
- **A dependency, or not.** `networkx` is BSD; SQLite recursive CTEs need nothing. The domain declares no dependency and the adapters may, which #378 established the pattern for

## What this is not

Not a vector index. The review is explicit at **6.2**: *vector search は補助、symbolic fact/provenance を捨てない*. A graph keeps provenance on every edge; an embedding does not. Retrieval stays what it is (ADR-0037), and #389 already moved in this direction by giving `ask` symbolic facts beside the retrieved ones.

Issue #16358: Windows: RestoreSink::createDirectory never sets dirFd, so NAR extraction aborts on the first nested directory

## Summary

On Windows, `RestoreSink::createDirectory()` never assigns `dirFd`, but the non-root path in the callback overload asserts on it. Since assertions cannot be compiled out in Nix, extracting a NAR whose root directory contains a directory entry aborts the process.

The root case is already guarded and carries a TODO. The non-root case, three lines below it, is not guarded, even though the same branch fails to set `dirFd` in both.

## The two halves

`src/libutil/fs-sink.cc:205-209` — the Windows branch creates the directory and returns without touching `dirFd`:

```c++
#else
    auto p = append(dstPath, path);
    if (!std::filesystem::create_directory(p))
        throw Error("path '%s' already exists", p.string());
#endif
```

`src/libutil/fs-sink.cc:148-162` — the caller:

```c++
void RestoreSink::createDirectory(const CanonPath & path, DirectoryCreatedCallback callback)
{
    if (path.isRoot()) {
        createDirectory(path);
        callback(*this, path);
#ifndef _WIN32 /* TODO: Have dirFd equivalent for the root directory. */
        assert(dirFd);
        ...
#endif
        return;
    }

    createDirectory(path);
    assert(dirFd); // If that's not true the above call must have thrown an exception.
```

The comment on line 162 states the invariant precisely, and the Windows branch is the one place that breaks it: it returns normally without setting `dirFd`.

Assertions are live unconditionally — `src/libutil/util.cc:15-17` makes building with `-DNDEBUG` an `#error` — so this aborts rather than degrading.

## Reachability

`src/libutil/archive.cc:231` uses the callback overload while parsing a NAR. The callback is invoked with `CanonPath::root` (`fs-sink.cc:181`), and the entry loop recurses with

```c++
parse(dirSink, source, relDirPath / name, depth + 1);
```

so the first directory entry inside the NAR's root directory arrives as a non-root path and lands on line 162. A NAR containing only regular files and symlinks at its root does not reach it.

That covers `nix-store --restore`, substituter output, `copyPath`, and output registration after a build — most real store paths are directories containing directories.

## Why the obvious small fixes don't work

Extending the `#ifndef _WIN32` guard from line 153 down to line 162 doesn't fix it. `dirFd.get()` on line 167 would then be invalid, `openFileEnsureBeneathNoSymlinks` fails, and lines 178-179 throw `SysError("opening directory ...")`. That is a better failure mode than an abort, but it is still a failure.

Mirroring the Unix branch isn't small either. It needs `getParentFdAndName` (`fs-sink.cc:104`), which sits inside `#ifndef _WIN32` (lines 93-146) and is Unix-only. The Windows branch operates on a whole path via `std::filesystem::create_directory` rather than relative to a parent handle, so there is no parent handle to open from.

So the real fix is the Windows directory-handle equivalent that the TODO on line 153 already defers. I'm filing this rather than attempting it because that code exists to prevent symlink escape, I can't validate a change to it on Windows, and an unvalidated change there seems worse than a precise report. Happy to be pointed at the shape you'd want if someone has a view.

A smaller intermediate step, if the full fix is not near-term: replace the bare `assert` on line 162 with an explicit unimplemented-on-Windows error naming the missing directory-handle support. That turns a bare abort into something a user can act on, without pretending the feature exists.

## Evidence, and what I did not verify

Read from current `master`: all the line references above, the `NDEBUG` `#error`, and the `archive.cc` recursion.

Corroborating, and worth noting because it suggests this was already known: the test that would exercise this path is skipped on Windows. `src/libutil-tests/file-system-at.cc:82-85`:

```c++
TEST(openFileEnsureBeneathNoSymlinks, works)
{
#ifdef _WIN32
    GTEST_SKIP() << "Broken on Windows";
```

That test calls `sink.createDirectory(CanonPath("a/b"), ...)` on line 101 — a non-root path through the callback overload, which is exactly line 162. Confirmed the test is present in a MinGW cross-build and reports `[ SKIPPED ]` when run.

**Not verified: I have not observed the abort.** I tried, and could not, for a reason that is itself relevant. A cross-compiled `nix-store.exe` cannot get far enough to extract a NAR in the environment available to me: `nix-store.exe --version` exits 5 with no output at all, which is the silent static-initialisation failure described in #16356. With `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` unset it at least prints `error: XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is invalid or not set in the environment`; once that is set, the message disappears and it still exits 5. So the diagnosis above is a derivation from source, not a recorded crash. If someone has a working Windows build handy, restoring a NAR with a nested directory should settle it in one command.

Issue #101742: [Bug]: Opening a session can silently land you in a sub-agent/branch transcript — `_session_latest_descendant` follows every child


## Bug Description

The Dashboard resolves a session id to "the newest child leaf" with `_session_latest_descendant` (`hermes_cli/web_server.py:12425`). Its recursive walk over `parent_session_id` is **unfiltered**, so besides the `/model`-continuation children it was designed for, it also follows:

- sub-agent sessions created by delegation (`model_config` containing `_delegate_from`),
- tool sidecar sessions (`source = 'tool'`),
- **branches the user deliberately created** (`_branched_from`) — and those can be the newest nodes in the whole tree.

Because sub-agent sessions are created *after* a delegation batch, they are typically the newest children. Opening your main session then lands you in a sub-agent or branch transcript; the Dashboard swaps `?resume=` to that record and the real conversation appears to have vanished from the chat pane.

## Steps to Reproduce

Attached: [`Test-HermesSessionTree.py`](https://gist.github.com/ngominhduc263/c21326221ef9797a31deec246041c0e3) — builds the exact session-tree shape in SQLite and runs the query/loop verbatim from `web_server.py`:

```
python Test-HermesSessionTree.py /path/to/hermes-agent
```

Practical steps: use delegation a few times (creating `model_config = {"_delegate_from": "main"}` children), optionally create a branch, then open the parent session in the Dashboard.

Verified on a clean checkout of `main` @ `593aa74c6` (2026-09-03):

```
HERMES_TREE_FAIL: van nhay vao nhanh nguoi dung tu tach (branch-1) —
mo phien goc ma bi doi sang nhanh
("still jumps into a user-created branch (branch-1) — opening the parent session switches you to the branch")
```

## Expected Behavior

The walk follows only genuine continuation children. A branch is a deliberate fork the user navigates to on purpose; a sub-agent transcript is not the user's conversation at all. With no valid continuation child, the resolver should stay on the requested session.

## Actual Behavior

The newest child wins regardless of its kind, so the view silently switches to sub-agent sessions, tool sidecars, or user-created branches. Two surfaces of the "same session" show completely different content (the Terminal tab reads the PTY directly and shows the real conversation; the Chat tab shows the sub-agent transcript).

## Affected Component

Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory) — session tree resolution used by the Dashboard.

## Root Cause Analysis

`hermes_cli/web_server.py:12425` `_session_latest_descendant`:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE descendants(id, parent_session_id, started_at) AS (
    SELECT id, parent_session_id, started_at FROM sessions WHERE id = ?
    UNION
    SELECT s.id, s.parent_session_id, s.started_at
    FROM sessions s
    JOIN descendants d ON s.parent_session_id = d.id
)
SELECT id, parent_session_id, started_at FROM descendants
```

…followed by an unfiltered "newest child" walk:

```python
candidates.sort(key=started, reverse=True)
current = candidates[0]["id"]
```

Nothing excludes children whose `model_config` carries `_delegate_from` / `_branched_from`, or rows with `source='tool'`.

## Proposed Fix

Filter the candidate children in the walk (or in the SQL) to continuation sessions only — skip `model_config` containing `_delegate_from` / `_branched_from` markers and `source='tool'` rows. The attached test encodes that contract and passes with the fix.

## Debug Report

Regression tests (run against a checkout path; FAIL = bug present, PASS = fixed):

https://gist.github.com/ngominhduc263/c21326221ef9797a31deec246041c0e3

Note: `hermes debug share` was deliberately not used — it uploads live config and logs from a production machine running three gateways. All claims here were verified against a clean checkout of `main` @ `593aa74c6` instead, with standalone scripts that never touch user state (throwaway `HERMES_HOME` / in-memory SQLite).

### Environment

- **OS:** Windows 11
- **Python:** 3.11.16
- **Hermes version:** v0.21.0 (2026.8.31), upstream `593aa74c`

## Master
Tracked by #9 under Hosted-scale security / architecture.

## Gap
Web Pilot already has distinct canonical policy responsibilities: authorization/scopes (#42), network/SSRF (#45), filesystem/raw-code/dangerous capabilities (#46), information-flow/declassification (#80), high-impact action approvals (#81), tool/capability visibility (#67), quotas/entitlements (#50/#89), residency (#85) and sandbox requirements (#106). No current issue owns the **policy composition/runtime itself**: one versioned decision context, hierarchy, precedence, publishing/rollback, simulation, reason codes, consistency and fail-closed behavior.

## Goal
Create a deterministic policy decision service used by every protected Web Pilot action/resource path. Existing issues continue to own their domain semantics; this issue owns how those policies are represented, composed, versioned, evaluated and audited consistently.

## Acceptance criteria
### Canonical decision context
- [ ] Define typed policy-decision context with decision ID, authenticated subject/service account, workspace/project, roles/scopes, entitlement/quota state, deployment/region/worker/provider, application session/page/frame/worker IDs, origin/destination, operation/tool/action kind, resource IDs, artifact/data sensitivity/provenance, workflow/run/version, browser/provider capabilities, requested feature and relevant risk attributes.
- [ ] Context is constructed by trusted server/control-plane code from canonical resources; page/model/tool arguments cannot forge subject/workspace/policy version/trusted sensitivity labels.
- [ ] Every protected path uses the same context schema across MCP, REST/SDK, CLI, dashboard/MCP Apps, workflow workers and provider adapters.
- [ ] Context fields have explicit absent/unknown semantics; unknown security-relevant state cannot accidentally match an allow rule intended for known-safe state.

### Policy hierarchy/composition
- [ ] Define policy layers with deterministic precedence, for example mandatory product/deployment security floor -> organization/admin -> workspace/project -> workflow/session narrowing -> operation-specific rule.
- [ ] Child/workspace/session policy can **narrow** mandatory parent policy but cannot widen it unless an explicitly authorized policy type is designed as overridable. Mandatory #45/#46/#80/#106 security floors are not bypassed by user/workflow preferences.
- [ ] Entitlements (#89) and authorization (#42) grant the maximum capability envelope; policy may narrow/deny/require approval but never manufacture a permission/feature the identity/entitlement does not possess.
- [ ] Define deterministic conflict resolution (`deny`/mandatory controls override allow; `require_approval` is only possible when underlying auth/data-flow/capability policy says the action is approvable rather than forbidden).
- [ ] #80 mandatory data-flow denials cannot be converted to `require_approval`; only an explicit trusted declassification policy can change classification/sink allowance.
- [ ] #81 risk policy consumes the composed decision and produces approval requirements only after auth/egress/data/capability prerequisites pass.
- [ ] #67 tool visibility/listing uses the same effective policy so a hidden/denied tool cannot still be called directly by name.

### Decision model/result
- [ ] Standard policy outcomes include at minimum `allow`, `deny`, `require_approval`, `require_scope/step_up`, `require_human`, `quota_exceeded`, `unsupported_capability` and structured `indeterminate/error` where applicable.
- [ ] Result includes policy bundle/version, rule IDs, safe reason codes, matched layer(s), obligations/constraints (allowed origins, max bytes, artifact class, approval type, timeout, etc.), decision expiry/cacheability and whether the result may be reused.
- [ ] Caller-facing denial reason is safe/minimal; operator/audit detail can be richer without exposing policy secrets/internal network data.
- [ ] Decision result is immutable and referenced by operation/action/run/event/audit IDs; high-impact #81 approval envelope binds the policy decision/version/digest used.

### Policy definition/versioning
- [ ] Define a constrained typed policy schema/DSL/data model; policy evaluation does not execute arbitrary administrator Node/JavaScript code inside the control plane by default.
- [ ] Policies have stable IDs, immutable published versions/revisions, owner, scope, creation/update metadata, status (`draft`, `staged`, `active`, `retired`), dependencies and compatibility/schema version.
- [ ] Validate policy syntax/types/references/cycles/conflicts before publication; reject rules referencing nonexistent scopes/features/resources/categories.
- [ ] Atomic publish/rollback: a request never observes a half-updated policy bundle.
- [ ] Maintain history/diff and rollback metadata; deleting a policy version referenced by retained audit/run history does not erase the ability to explain past decisions.
- [ ] Optional external policy engines (OPA/Cedar/custom service) may be supported through a provider interface, but Web Pilot core semantics/results remain stable and no external service is mandatory for local/self-host use.

### Consistency/caching/distributed operation
- [ ] Define when a session/run pins a policy version vs when mandatory emergency/global changes take effect immediately. Security kill switches/revocations must not wait for a long session to end.
- [ ] Cache decisions only when inputs/policy allow it; cache key includes policy version + relevant subject/resource/context and has bounded TTL/size.
- [ ] Auth revocation, entitlement change, policy publish/rollback, resource sensitivity change and emer

Issue #38: P1: Add versioned reusable workflow engine with variables, branching, loops, and validation

## Master
Tracked by #9 under Commercial automation / reliability / token efficiency.

## Gap
A reusable workflow is more than a saved list of browser actions. Commercial automation needs a statically valid typed execution graph with immutable versions, bounded loops/parallelism, deterministic expressions, explicit browser/session ownership, block-level idempotency/checkpoints, error/finally paths, subworkflow contracts, secret references and clear separation between deterministic and AI-backed blocks. Otherwise every workflow becomes bespoke orchestration logic that #39 cannot safely resume/distribute.

## Goal
Create a versioned workflow definition/runtime built from canonical Web Pilot services. Deterministic blocks execute without inference; semantic blocks use #40 explicitly; every block declares inputs/outputs/side effects/retry/checkpoint semantics so #39 can run it durably.

## Acceptance criteria
### Workflow definition/version
- [ ] Define versioned workflow schema with stable workflow ID + immutable published version, workspace/project, name/description/tags, typed input/output JSON Schemas, secret/resource references, browser environment template/profile/session strategy, policy requirements and engine/schema version.
- [ ] Draft/edit/publish lifecycle is explicit. Published versions are immutable; edits create a new version. Runs always record exact version.
- [ ] Workflow version supports changelog/migration/deprecation metadata and compatibility validation against current block/schema/browser capabilities.
- [ ] Deleting/retiring a workflow version does not erase historical run explainability; active schedules/runs reference immutable version.
- [ ] Export/import is deterministic, portable where resource refs are remapped, and never embeds plaintext secret values/provider tokens/profile storage state.

### Typed execution graph
- [ ] Represent workflow as explicit DAG/control-flow graph with stable block IDs and validated edges rather than relying on array position.
- [ ] Detect unreachable blocks, missing outputs, cycles outside explicit loop constructs, invalid branch targets, recursive subworkflow cycles and incompatible schemas before publish/run.
- [ ] Support named start/end/output blocks and multiple terminal outcomes where product semantics require them.
- [ ] Define data dependency vs control dependency separately so parallelizable blocks are clear.
- [ ] Graph compilation produces immutable executable plan/version hash consumed by #39 workers; a worker does not reinterpret mutable draft definitions.

### Core deterministic blocks
- [ ] Browser: create/use/close session, navigate/history, wait/validate, click/type/fill/select/check/drag/scroll, upload/download, page/tab/frame select, evaluate/script (policy-gated), screenshot/export, storage/API request and other canonical tools as owners land.
- [ ] Data: literal/input, object/array construct, schema validate, select/map/filter/reduce, string/number/date operations, JSON transform, merge, dedupe and bounded expression evaluation.
- [ ] Control: condition/switch, sequence, parallel, loop/for-each, retry, timeout, delay, wait-event/condition, error/catch/finally/compensation and subworkflow.
- [ ] Integration: #103 connector/HTTP action, webhook/event input/output, artifact/file operations and human/approval steps via canonical services.
- [ ] AI blocks: semantic act/observe/extract/task/classify/transform only when explicitly declared; deterministic blocks never silently invoke #40.

### Expression/data model
- [ ] Workflow variables are typed values with provenance/sensitivity metadata from #80, not an untyped global dictionary.
- [ ] Define constrained deterministic expression language for conditions/transforms/interpolation; no arbitrary server JavaScript by default.
- [ ] Expressions have CPU/time/depth/output limits and explicit null/missing/type-error semantics.
- [ ] Block input mapping/output mapping is schema-validated at compile time where possible and runtime where values are dynamic.
- [ ] Secret references are opaque typed values; generic transform/log/output blocks cannot stringify/declassify them.
- [ ] Artifact/resource/session/page IDs remain typed references rather than strings that can accidentally cross resource classes.

### Branching/loops/parallelism
- [ ] Conditions/switch evaluate deterministically with recorded expression/result and selected branch; page/model content cannot alter workflow control policy outside mapped data.
- [ ] For-each/while/repeat loops require explicit max iterations and optional wall-clock/data limits; unbounded loops are rejected.
- [ ] Loop variable/output accumulation has configurable size limits and streaming/pagination path for large datasets.
- [ ] Parallel block/branch has explicit max concurrency and join strategy (`all`, `any`, `race`, bounded failures) with cancellation semantics.
- [ ] Browser mutations on the same session/page still route through #104; workflow parallelism cannot create unsafe shared-page concurrency.
- [ ] Parallel branches may intentionally use separate #12 pages/#10 sessions with #50 quota admission.

### Block contract / side effects / checkpoints
- [ ] Every block type declares side-effect class (`read_only`, `idempotent_write`, `non_idempotent`, `high_impact`), retry safety, checkpointability, timeout/cancellation support, required scopes/policies/capabilities and expected resource ownership.
- [ ] Block execution receives stable block-attempt ID and returns typed result, safe outputs, artifact/resource refs, policy/approval IDs, timing, usage and checkpoint metadata.
- [ ] Durable checkpoint is written **after** the side effect/result boundary according to block semantics; #39 never replays a committed non-idempotent block blindly after crash.
- [ ] Blocks supporting external idempotency keys derive stable attempt keys from run/block/version/checkpoint as appropriate.
- [ ] High-impact blocks integrate #81 proposal/approval diges

Issue #2354: [C7] Impose a total order on triangleAdjacency (mesh_orient.go)

Part of #2301 · class C7: Non-deterministic ordering → explicit total orders.
**Phase 1 — refactor-only (behaviour-preserving).**

## Occurrence
`kernel/ops/mesh_orient.go:57` — `triangleAdjacency`

## Problem
kernel/ops/mesh_orient.go:57 triangleAdjacency: `for _, us := range uses` (map[segKey][]use) appends orientLink entries onto adj[us[0].tri] and adj[us[1].tri], so each triangle's neighbour list order is Go map order. twoColorFaces' BFS consumes those lists in slice order; on a non-bipartite / conflicting component the parity assignment (and therefore which triangles triangleParityVolume flips and which windings the healed mesh ships) depends on that order. Go randomises map iteration order per run and sort.Slice is unstable, so the operation's output depends on the run rather than on the input — breaking byte-identical output and any golden, oracle or reference-key test that hashes the result. Target: build a []segKey of the keys and sort by the six int64 components of segKey (a total order on the quantized endpoint pair) before filling adj.

## Rule violated
> Output is byte-identical across runs and platforms: explicit total orders for every tie-break, no map-iteration or pointer/hash ordering, FMA-safe arithmetic in predicates.

([ground rules](https://github.com/Oblikovati/Oblikovati/blob/develop/CLAUDE.md#kernel--host-ground-rules-for-extension-and-refactoring))

Issue #764: Xiaomi Robot Vacuum H50 (xiaomi.vacuum.ov43gb) works on v3.0.0-alpha-24, but the map is refreshed non-stop while docked

### The problem

Two things about `xiaomi.vacuum.ov43gb` (Xiaomi Robot Vacuum H50), one good and one bad.

**1. The H50 already works on `v3.0.0-alpha-24`, with no code change.**

There is no issue, PR or README mention of this model anywhere, so I am documenting it for
anyone searching. Everything lines up with the current defaults:

- `VacuumApi.detect()` matches the `xiaomi.vacuum.` prefix, so it gets `VacuumApi.XIAOMI`
- map obj name sits at the default siid 10 / piid 1 (spec `urn:miot-spec-v2:device:vacuum:0000A006:xiaomi-ov43gb:2`)
- the derived AES key `mi.vacuum.ov43gb` is exactly 16 bytes, so it does not hit the
  "Incorrect AES key length" failures reported in #731, #732 and #733

Working log:

```
Getting map name...
Got map name: "0".
Downloading raw map from "https://awsusor1.fds.api.xiaomi.com/3irobotic-ov43gb/<user>/<did>/0?..."
Downloaded raw map (6191).
Parsing map...
Parsed map: (177 x 260)
Finished fetching xiaomi_cloud_map_extractor data in 0.948 seconds (success: True)
```

Worth noting for other H50 owners: **v2.2.5 cannot work for this model at all.**
`xiaomi.vacuum.` is not in `AVAILABLE_APIS`, so `_detect_api` returns `None`, the vacuum
falls back to `UnsupportedVacuum`, and the legacy `get_map_v1` miIO call fails with
`{'code': -9999, 'message': 'user ack timeout'}` — the H50 is MIoT-only and has no such
command. Upgrading to the v3 pre-release is the whole fix.

**2. The map is refreshed non-stop while the robot is docked.**

`should_update_map` reads the status from siid 2 / piid 1. On this model piid 1 is
`Vacuum Frameware Version` (a string) and the status is at piid 2. The version string is
compared against `idle_at`, never matches, so the vacuum never looks idle and the map is
downloaded and parsed every ~10s forever.

Measured with the robot parked on the dock the whole time:

| | download cycles | idle detected |
|---|---|---|
| as shipped | 9 | 0 |
| status read from piid 2 | 3, then stops | yes, at `OFF_UPDATES` |

With the correct piid the vacuum reports status `9` (`Charged`) and the off counter runs
1 → 4, stopping downloads exactly as intended.

Fix submitted upstream in the parser library, where `get_status_mapping` lives:
aronkahrs-us/Python-package-vacuum-map-parser-xiaomi#6

### What version of an integration has described problem?

v3.0.0-alpha-24

### What was the last working version of an integration?

None — v2.2.5 never supported this model (see above).

### What vacuum model do you have problems with?

xiaomi.vacuum.ov43gb

### What version of Home Assistant do you use?

core-2026.3.1

### What type of installation are you running?

Home Assistant Container

```yaml
# originally configured via YAML, automatically migrated to a config entry by the v3 import
camera:

    draw: ['all']

Once the library releases the fix it will not reach users until the pin is bumped —
`manifest.json` currently pins `vacuum-map-parser-xiaomi==0.1.3` while the library is
already at `0.1.4`.

There may also be a better home for this fix. `map_prop_mapping.py` was removed from the
library in February with the note "map property mapping module was moved to the extractor
integration", and landed here as `_NON_STANDARD_MAP_PROP` in #723. The status mapping is
the same kind of per-model data but stayed behind in the library. If you would rather have

One more thing that may be worth a separate issue: the YAML import path cannot handle a

Issue #32: CI migration: all R packages onto the reusable workflows — status and standard

## The standard this migration is held to

Every R package in the PredictiveEcology universe calls the **same** reusable workflow, with **as few overrides as possible**.

Four rules decide what an override is allowed to be:

1. **The pre-migration file defines the scope.** What a repo's own workflow was actually doing is the specification. Nothing new is invented, and nothing working is silently dropped.
2. **Keep what is custom and needed.** A package-specific dependency, an env var its tests genuinely read, an extra matrix leg it deliberately had.
3. **Drop what is dead, old, or defunct.** Retired runner images, R versions that can no longer be installed, hand-rolled steps the template now performs, variables nothing reads any more.
4. **Use the template — do not rewrite logic in YAML.** Matrix additions go through `extra-config`; setup commands stay in `post-install` verbatim. A caller says *what this package needs*, never *how CI works*.

A corollary that is easy to miss: **an override that restates a template default is not neutral, it is drift waiting to happen.** If the default changes, the caller silently keeps the old value. So `check-args`, `extra-repositories`, `build-args`, `error-on`, `cache-version` and `any::rcmdcheck` are removed wherever they merely repeated the default.

A maintainer on the project ProjectASAP/ASAPPlanner (Rust) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #290: Evaluate range-queryable structured summaries (QTree-style)

## Context

Split from #173 after its multi-subpopulation/Hydra portion landed. ASAPPlanner now represents shared multi-subpopulation frequency-sketch state through Hydra grouping candidates, but it still has no first-class range-queryable structured summary comparable to Algebird's `QTree`:

- state is organized over non-overlapping value ranges;
- each range carries decomposable/mergeable inner state;
- readout asks about a sub-range and may return lower/upper bounds rather than one scalar point estimate.

This issue evaluates and, if justified, models that remaining structured-summary capability. It does not reopen the already implemented Hydra grouping work.

## Required semantics

- Define range-shaped readout operations such as bounded range count/sum and range quantile.
- Define whether inner state is a closed core vocabulary or a recursively referenced mergeable summary family.
- State merge, compaction, and range-query legality must be explicit.
- Exact and approximate inner states must retain their existing accuracy contract; nesting a sketch does not make it exact.
- Runtime capability must gate candidate generation until a downstream implementation exists.

## Cost model

Compare alternatives in **cost units per second**, with state size reported independently in bytes.

For maintained structured range state:

```text
structured_cost_rate =
    update_rate * structured_update_cost
  + evaluation_rate * structured_range_read_cost
```

For recomputation from the pre-ASAP/raw path:

```text
raw_recompute_cost_rate =
    evaluation_rate * raw_range_scan_cost
```

For several repeating consumers sharing the same structured state:

```text
evaluation_rate = sum(1 / query_interval_i)
```

If one-shot and recurring work are compared over a finite horizon `H`:

```text
total_cost(H) = recurring_cost_rate * H + one_shot_cost
```

State accounting:

```text
structured_state_bytes = retained_range_nodes * bytes_per_range_node
```

Every cost must include units, input provenance, and model version. Unknown runtime/cardinality inputs remain unknown rather than being encoded as zero.

## Scope

1. Write an ADR defining the readout vocabulary, inner-state composition, accuracy semantics, and runtime contract.
2. Decide whether the capability belongs in core post-ASAP IR or behind the deployment extension interface.
3. If first-class core support is justified, add the representation and an experimental capability-gated replacement strategy.
4. Export the selected physical representation and explicit cost/provenance metadata for DAG visualization.

## Acceptance criteria

- ADR compares a first-class structured-summary type with deployment extension and ordinary raw recomputation.
- At least one range count or range sum fixture has a lossless readout representation.
- Unsupported/non-mergeable inner state does not produce a candidate.
- A deterministic cost model selects structured state for a high-frequency range workload and raw recomputation for a sufficiently cold workload.
- Tests verify `evaluation_rate = sum(1 / query_interval_i)` for shared consumers and prevent shared-state double counting.
- Accuracy targets and returned bound semantics survive representation, merge, serialization, and DAG export.
- Candidate generation is absent without runtime capability.

## Related

- Split from #173.
- General physical degrees of freedom are tracked by #152.
- Nested exact and approximate composition are #171 and #172.
- Candidate-plan search is implemented by closed #252.
- Cost annotations are tracked by #286.

Issue #18: Harden inherited b00t-cli pipeline code for external consumption

Follow-up from the final whole-branch review of the pipeline-types extraction (elasticdotventures/_b00t_#1251, branch `feat/1251-pipeline-types-extraction`). These are all pre-existing behaviors inherited verbatim from `b00t-cli`'s `pipeline_types.rs`/`pipeline_flowctl.rs`/`pipeline_secrets.rs` — correctly out of scope for a verbatim extraction — but this crate is now the published, external-facing home for this code, consumed by third-party pipeline engines that deserialize user-authored pipeline definitions. None of these block the extraction PR; they're tracked here instead.

## `PipelineDag::execution_order()` panics on a dangling edge (highest priority)

`src/pipeline_types.rs` (`topological_sort`), around the `adj.get_mut(...).unwrap()` / `in_degree.get_mut(...).unwrap()` calls. Reproduced empirically: deserializing `{"stages":[],"edges":[{"from":"ghost","to":"other","via_port":null}],...}` and calling `execution_order()` panics with `called Option::unwrap() on a None value`. `PipelineDag` is `pub` with all-`pub` fields and derives `Deserialize`; `validate()` catches dangling edges but nothing forces callers to run it first, and `execution_order() -> anyhow::Result<_>`'s signature advertises fallibility rather than a panic. Fix is mechanical — `.ok_or_else(|| anyhow!(...))?` on both `unwrap()` calls — or at minimum document the precondition on `execution_order`/`topological_sort`.

## `PipelineDag::build` always fails on default-constructed (name-only) stages

Reproduced: `PipelineDag::build(vec![StageSpec::from_name("a"), StageSpec::from_name("b")])` returns `Err("cycle detected in pipeline DAG")`. `StageSpec::from_name` gives every stage a `Bytes` in-port and `Bytes` out-port; `Bytes` is a wildcard in `StagePort::compatible_with`, so `build`'s all-pairs wiring emits both `a→b` and `b→a`. This is exactly the shape `StageEntry::Name` resolves to via `StageEntry::resolve()` — so the "backward-compatible, name-only pipeline" case `StageEntry` exists for can never actually be built with `PipelineDag::build`. `PipelineDag::from_sequential` is the intended path for that case, but nothing documents the distinction. Add a doc note on `build` pointing callers at `from_sequential` for name-only/sequential pipelines.

## `FlowControl::record_emit` allocates a zeroed buffer purely for occupancy accounting

`src/pipeline_flowctl.rs`, `record_emit`'s `Buffered` arm: `self.buffer.push_back(vec![0u8; bytes])`. A stage emitting 256 MB chunks under `Buffered { capacity: 4 }` allocates and zeroes ~1 GB of ballast nobody reads — the buffer only tracks occupancy, not content. `VecDeque<usize>` (or a plain counter) would do the same job without the allocation.

## `secure_stage_env_debug_redacts` doesn't actually test redaction

`src/pipeline_secrets.rs` — the test constructs `SecureStageEnv::new("test", vec![])`, never calls `resolve()`, and asserts only that the debug string contains `"test"` and `"store"`. There's no secret present to redact, so it can't catch a redaction regression. The real coverage for that property is `debug_does_not_print_secret_values` on `SecretStore`. Either resolve a real secret here and assert its absence from the debug string, or rename the test to reflect what it actually checks.

## Smaller items noted in the same review, bundle here if convenient

- `is_memory_intensive` (`pipeline_flowctl.rs`) is exported but unused by `auto_strategy`, and its threshold (`min_ram_gb > 16.0 || min_vram_gb > 8.0`) doesn't match `auto_strategy`'s own branching (`> 16.0` then `> 0.0`) — the helper doesn't describe the function it appears to.
- `PipelineDag` derives `Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize` but not `PartialEq`, unlike every other type in `pipeline_types.rs` — minor API asymmetry, easy test-writing friction.
- `detect_cycle` (`pipeline_types.rs`) uses unbounded recursion — stack overflow risk on a sufficiently deep/pathological pipeline chain.
- No `zeroize` on `SecretStore`'s resolved-secret `String`s (no scrubbing on drop) — standard hardening for a secrets-handling type; a deliberate design decision to flag rather than a clear defect.

publishing-v7 shipped a macOS wheel matrix that never ran: the top-level `reusable-publish-release-packages.yml` pins its sibling workflows by tag (`@publishing-v6` at the time), so the v7 tag's own wheel-builder file was unreferenced. audioif v0.1.0 burned its tag on the resulting 16-vs-21 wheel-count failure (run 33392558969). publishing-v8 fixed it by bumping all four internal refs in lockstep — but the failure class remains.

2. **Self-asserting matrix.** The wheel-builder should assert its own expected cell count (or the reusable workflow derive expected-wheel-count from the matrix × python-versions) instead of trusting the caller's literal — a consumer that re-pins without updating its count currently gets either a silent shortfall (count unchanged) or a burned tag (count raised, as audioif proved).

Issue #1674: Support distance cutoff in Dijkstra shortest-path searches

<!-- ⚠️ If you do not respect this template, your issue will be closed -->
<!-- ⚠️ Make sure to browse the opened and closed issues to confirm this idea does not exist. -->

### What is the expected enhancement?

It would be useful to support an optional distance `cutoff` for Dijkstra shortest-path-length APIs, similar to NetworkX's [single_source_dijkstra_path_length](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/algorithms/generated/networkx.algorithms.shortest_paths.weighted.single_source_dijkstra_path_length.html):

nx.single_source_dijkstra_path_length(
    graph,
    source,
    cutoff=10.0,
    weight="weight",
)
```

For example:

```python
rustworkx.dijkstra_shortest_path_lengths(
    graph,
    source,
    edge_cost_fn,
    cutoff=10.0,
)
```

The main motivation is performance.

Currently, bounded Dijkstra search can be implemented with `dijkstra_search()` and a custom `DijkstraVisitor`, but this requires user-side code and Python callbacks during traversal.

A native cutoff in the Rust implementation could terminate the search once the minimum queued distance exceeds the cutoff, avoiding unnecessary heap operations and edge relaxations.

This would also make migration from NetworkX easier for workloads that rely on `cutoff`.

Follow-up to #8583 (merged). Ref #8389.

## Problem

The session workflow surfaces derive the same projection several times per render, and each derivation rebuilds an index that is designed to be built once.

**1. The projection is computed three times per render.**
`SessionWorkflowCockpit.tsx:43` and `SessionWorkflowInspector.tsx:51` each call `buildSessionWorkflowProjection(todos, tools, tasks)`. Both are mounted at the same time — `App.tsx:10716` opens the inspector automatically when the cockpit is entered. `PlanExecutionView.tsx:531-605` then recomputes an equivalent set (`todosById`, `toolsByTodo`, `statesByTodo`, layering) a third time.

**2. `buildSessionWorkflowProjection` rebuilds the task index O(todos + tools) times.**
- `session-workflow-model.ts:127` calls `getPlanNodeState` per todo; that wrapper (`PlanExecutionView.tsx:412-424`) calls `createTaskExecutionIndex(tasks)` on every invocation.
- `session-workflow-model.ts:70` calls `nestedTasksForTool` per tool; same rebuild (`PlanExecutionView.tsx:229-234`).
- `session-workflow-model.ts:44` does a linear `tasks.find` per tool.

Net cost is O((todos + tools) × tasks). The index type already carries a `nestedByRootId` memo field, so it is meant to be built once and threaded through.

**3. Hovering any node re-runs the whole derivation.**
`PlanExecutionView.tsx:1151-1164` sets `hoveredTodoId` on `onPointerEnter`/`onPointerLeave`/`onFocus`/`onBlur`. None of the derived block at `:531-605` is memoized, so each hover re-runs `layerPlanTodos` (a topological sort, `:593`), `JSON.stringify(topology)` (`:585`), and the per-todo × per-tool attention walk. Hover only affects `data-focused` / `data-active`.

**4. `nestedAgentToolsForTool` has no cache.**
`PlanExecutionView.tsx:236-249` walks the `subTools` tree fresh on every call while its sibling `nestedTasksFromIndex` memoizes into the index. Called from `attentionAgentStatuses`, `getActiveAgents`, `renderExecution` and `getAttentionAgentTool`, which compounds (3).

**5. `measure()` is unthrottled.**
`PlanExecutionView.tsx:822` binds `measure` directly to `window.resize` while a `ResizeObserver` already observes the graph element and every node. Each run does a `getBoundingClientRect` per node and concatenates a signature string over every edge (`:815`, up to `MAX_RENDERED_PLAN_EDGES` = 500).

**6. Dependency-graph derivation is duplicated in three places.**
`PlanExecutionView.tsx:595-605` builds `dependentsByTodo`; `SessionWorkflowInspector.tsx:86` recomputes downstream with `todos.filter(t => t.blockedBy?.includes(id))`; the projection builds neither.

`utils/todos.ts:209` does a `findIndex` whose predicate calls `extractTodosFromToolCall` per tool, then a second full pass. It is memoized on `[messages, …]` (`App.tsx:8232`), so a live session re-runs it as messages grow — precisely while the workflow surface is open.

## Scope

- Build the task execution index once per projection and thread it through. The index-free exports `getPlanNodeState`, `nestedTasksForTool` and `getActiveAgents` have no callers outside `session-workflow-model.ts` and the tests, so adding index-taking entry points is contained.

- Memoize `PlanExecutionView`'s derived block so hover state changes only re-render, never re-derive. `todos` already has a stable identity via `useStableArray` (`App.tsx:8169`), so memoization will actually hit.
- Cache `nestedAgentToolsForTool`, or fold it into the index.

Callers and tests use those two surfaces; no market-specific Module may introduce its own dict wrapper or serialize internal immutable storage directly.

- Cover observations, source errors, diagnostics, evidence storage and every nested mapping/list/set-like input accepted by the current Interface.

Issue #183: M14: Boomi Runtime Observability Bridge — OTLP Ingestion, ProcessIR Correlation, and Evidence-Grounded Diagnostics

Sequence: begins after M13 closes

Parent architecture: M12 — Canonical Integration Authoring IR and Process Compiler Consolidation (#134)

Primary dependencies: M13 — Existing Integration Lift, Semantic Refactoring, and Safe Round-Trip Apply (#182); the existing `manage_runtimes` `get_observability_settings` / `update_observability_settings` actions; current `monitor_platform` and `troubleshoot_execution` surfaces

External capability: Boomi Runtime Observability / OpenTelemetry export

Size / risk: XL / high — introduces a persistent multi-tenant telemetry data plane, machine authentication, high-volume untrusted ingestion, retention costs, and cross-source correlation

## Problem

The MCP currently observes Boomi primarily through the Platform API. It can retrieve runtime metadata and counters, query `ExecutionRecord`, request process logs, and inspect process/component configuration. This is useful but remains a pull-based control-plane view:

* execution records are run-level summaries rather than a nested step trace;
* process logs are requested after an execution and may be slow, incomplete, or unavailable when a runtime is offline;
* the MCP cannot continuously observe JVM/runtime pressure, queueing, worker saturation, garbage collection, or runtime-to-platform communication failures;
* it cannot reliably distinguish connector latency from time spent waiting in the Atom execution queue;
* it cannot compare the design represented by ProcessIR with the path and timings actually observed at runtime;
* troubleshooting therefore relies too heavily on a flat execution message, downloaded text logs, and generic inference.

Boomi runtimes can now export OpenTelemetry metrics, logs, and traces over OTLP/gRPC. The repository already exposes Platform API actions to read and update runtime observability settings, but it has no endpoint that can safely receive those signals, no tenant-bound machine credential, no telemetry store, no versioned Boomi attribute adapter, and no MCP query contract that joins runtime evidence with the Platform API, M12 ProcessIR, or M13 imported-process provenance.

Pointing a runtime at `/mcp` is not a solution. MCP is a request/response tool protocol authenticated for interactive clients; it is not a durable telemetry ingestion protocol. Sharing that path would couple high-volume machine traffic to MCP sessions, request limits, user OAuth, Cloud Run latency, and the interactive control plane.

M14 must add an optional telemetry bridge without weakening any existing authority or isolation boundary.

## Goal

Allow a customer-managed Boomi Atom to send OTLP metrics, logs, and traces to a dedicated service endpoint owned by this project, then expose bounded, tenant-safe, evidence-grounded runtime analysis through the existing MCP tools.

The first complete M14 workflow is:

1. An authenticated MCP user selects a saved Boomi profile and local Atom.
2. The MCP inspects the current `RuntimeObservabilitySettings` and reports any configuration conflict.
3. The service provisions a runtime-bound telemetry channel and machine credential.
4. Through an explicit prepare/apply operation, the MCP configures the Atom to export selected signals to the dedicated OTLP/gRPC endpoint.
5. The service verifies signal arrival without exposing the credential in logs or ordinary MCP responses.
6. A process is executed on that Atom.
7. The MCP joins the Platform API execution record with the received trace tree, nearby runtime metrics, relevant sanitized log events, the deployed process identity, and—where identifiers permit—the corresponding M12 ProcessIR or M13 observed graph nodes.
8. `troubleshoot_execution` explains the observed failure or latency using cited evidence, correlation confidence, and explicit telemetry-coverage limitations.
9. Large trace/log datasets remain server-side or are delivered through a bounded file-backed evidence export; they are not dumped into an MCP response.

The resulting product view is:

```text
ProcessIR / LiftedIntegration = what the integration is designed to do
Platform API                 = what is configured, deployed, and recorded
OpenTelemetry                = what the runtime and execution actually did
MCP diagnostic surface       = the evidence-grounded joined explanation
```

The production proof must use a customer-managed local Atom. The architecture may support other eligible runtime types later, but M14 does not depend on Boomi-hosted cloud rollout or availability.

## Architecture decision

M14 separates the interactive control plane from the telemetry data plane.

```text
Boomi local Atom
    │
    │ OTLP/gRPC over TLS
    │ runtime-bound bearer/custom-header credential
    ▼
Dedicated telemetry ingress
    ├─ authenticate channel before persistence
    ├─ bind server-side tenant/profile/account/runtime scope
    ├─ validate size/cardinality/time bounds
    ├─ redact/filter before durable storage
    ├─ batch, backpressure, deduplicate, and count drops
    ▼
Telemetry backend
    ├─ traces and span events
    ├─ sanitized logs
    ├─ runtime metrics
    └─ channel/coverage metadata
              ▲
              │ tenant-scoped typed queries
              │
Boomi MCP control plane
    ├─ RuntimeObservabilitySettings via manage_runtimes
    ├─ ExecutionRecord / deployments / runtime metadata
    ├─ M12 ProcessIR + materialization attestation
    ├─ M13 ObservedProcessGraph / lifted provenance
    ├─ monitor_platform aggregates
    └─ troubleshoot_execution evidence bundles
```

The telemetry ingress may live in the same repository and cloud project, but it must be independently deployable, independently scalable, and separately rate-limited. It must not run inside the `/mcp` request handler or require an open MCP/SSE session.

The exact telemetry backend is selected by a mandatory M14.00 ADR after live signal and volume capture. The ADR must evaluate queryability, tenant isolation, retention deletion, operating cost, OpenTelemetry compat

`packages/rocketchat-livechat/.app`

which no longer exists in the current repository structure.

This would allow the plugin to work directly with the current Livechat build output and avoid recursively spawning another Meteor build.

Issue #145: [P0] Constrain destructive runtime cleanup to Ralph-owned paths

## Summary

RalphDex allows `artifactRetentionPath` to resolve outside `.ralph/`, including absolute paths, but destructive runtime-maintenance paths trust the resolved directory and recursively delete from it.

Reviewed against `main` at `5c83d423f2b933cc202e0da3aa6192e6648edc7e`.

## Current behavior

`RalphStateManager.resetRuntimeState()` resolves the configured paths and then recursively removes `paths.artifactDir` along with Ralph's normal prompt/run/handoff/log directories.

Because `artifactRetentionPath` is operator-configurable and may be absolute, configurations such as:

```text
artifactRetentionPath = "."
artifactRetentionPath = ".."
artifactRetentionPath = "/shared/path"
```

can make **Reset Runtime State** recursively delete unrelated workspace or external data.

Retention cleanup has the same underlying trust problem: it scans the configured artifact root and recursively removes Ralph-looking entries such as `iteration-N` directories selected by the retention plan. If the root is not exclusively Ralph-owned, unrelated directories that match those names can be pruned.

The Reset confirmation describes Ralph runtime artifacts rather than surfacing the exact resolved destructive root, so the operator may not realize the configured artifact path broadens the deletion scope.

## Impact

- recursive deletion of unrelated repository files;
- recursive deletion outside the repository when an absolute artifact path is configured;
- retention cleanup can remove unrelated `iteration-N` directories from a shared root;
- confirmation UI can understate the actual destructive scope.

## Relevant code

- `src/ralph/stateManager.ts`
  - `resetRuntimeState`
  - `cleanupRuntimeArtifacts`
- `src/ralph/artifactRetention.ts`
- `src/ralph/pathResolver.ts`
- `src/commands/artifactCommands.ts`
- `ralphCodex.artifactRetentionPath` configuration

## Suggested direction

Introduce a managed-root ownership invariant for every destructive runtime operation.

A safe design should include:

1. resolve/canonicalize the configured artifact path;
2. require destructive targets to be an explicitly Ralph-owned directory;
3. use an ownership marker/version file or equivalent positive identification rather than trusting the directory name alone;
4. reject dangerous roots such as the workspace root, filesystem root, parent traversal, or an unowned external/shared directory;
5. show the exact resolved deletion root in destructive confirmations;
6. make retention cleanup use the same ownership guard.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Reset cannot recursively delete the workspace root, a workspace parent, filesystem root, or an arbitrary unowned absolute directory.
- [ ] Cleanup/retention refuses to delete from an artifact root that is not positively identified as Ralph-owned.
- [ ] Safe custom artifact directories remain supported, including absolute paths when explicitly initialized/owned by Ralph.
- [ ] Destructive confirmations show the resolved target path.
- [ ] Add regression tests for `.`, `..`, workspace root, filesystem/root-equivalent inputs, and an external shared directory.
- [ ] Add a regression proving unrelated `iteration-N` directories in an unowned root are never pruned.
- [ ] Document the custom artifact-root ownership contract.

Issue #13: eval gate is a source reader: intercept spawns in the eval kernels instead

PR #12 gates eval's subprocess spawns by reading the submitted source and extracting every spawn whose command is written as a literal. That closes the case that shows up in transcripts, where an agent blocked at bash rewrites the same command in Python. It does not close the case where the code hides the spawn from a source reader.

A command assembled at runtime is handled: it reads as an opaque site and raises a permission request. The gap is a spawn the reader never sees at all, which fails open:

```python
getattr(os, "sys" + "tem")(cmd)
__import__("os").system(cmd)
exec(compile(payload, "<s>", "exec"))
```

```js
globalThis[["child", "_process"].join("")]
```

None of those match a callee name, so no site is produced and nothing is judged.

## The fix

Intercept spawns inside the eval kernels rather than in the source. Every spawn then calls back to the host classifier at execution time, with the real argv, and there is nothing to hide from.

Touch points in the OMP fork:

- `packages/coding-agent/src/eval/py` — patch `subprocess` and the `os.system`/`os.exec*` family in the Python kernel.
- `packages/coding-agent/src/eval/js` — patch `child_process` and `Bun.spawn` in the worker.

The runtimes already have a host bridge (`eval/agent-bridge.ts`, `eval/tool-bridge.ts`); route the classifier call over it rather than opening a second channel.

## Cost

A fork edit plus a binary rebuild, and the patch has to survive upstream merges. That is why PR #12 took the plugin-sized version first.

## When to do this

When session logs show agents building command strings to slip past the parser. Static extraction is the cheap version and it is enough while the observed behavior is agents taking the shortest path rather than evading a gate. A run that shows reflection or string arithmetic around a spawn is the signal that this is worth the fork.
