Issue #570: The no-clone roster read depends on a human's gh session, so it works on exactly one host

DECISION: @zach ruled the direction on 2026-09-04 -- "we need to run these things without clones. that's the design. should have done it for all of them." What is open is which credential a hostless read uses, since the current answer is accidental.
DEFAULT-AFTER 14d: none -- every option is a credential decision.

`dose` already reads `schedule/ROSTER` from GitHub rather than a checkout, and says so at the top of `bin/dose-project.sh`:

> Reads schedule/ROSTER from GITHUB via `gh api`, never a local clone: a clone is stale or absent.

**That design is right and it does not actually hold.** It has a hidden dependency that makes it work on exactly one host.

## The measurement

`lib/dose-common.sh`:

```sh
gh_as() {
  if [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ] && [ -n "${SUDO_USER:-}" ] && [ "$SUDO_USER" != root ]; then
    sudo -n -u "$SUDO_USER" "$GH_BIN" "$@"
  else
    "$GH_BIN" "$@"
  fi
}
```

Under `sudo`, root drops back to `$SUDO_USER` to run `gh`. On monkey that borrows **Zach's authenticated gh session**. Verified 2026-09-04: root on monkey has no `~/.config/gh`, no `GH_TOKEN`, and a direct `sudo gh api repos/hf7y/scheduler` fails with *"To get started with GitHub CLI, please run: gh auth login"* -- while `sudo dose <project> --check` succeeds, because it is not really root doing the reading.

So the no-clone read works on monkey **because a human is logged in there**, not because the mechanism is hostless.

On vaporwave the same call exits BLIND. Its own App (`unattended-vaporwave`, App 4813610) authenticates and mints tokens, but its installation covers `vkv23`, `vkv`, `inv-redirects`, `vibe-kiosk`, `dog` -- **not `hf7y/scheduler`**. Correct scoping for a project App; useless for reading the roster. So `dog` is `live` in ROSTER, has no crontab, and dispatches nothing.

## Why this is a design bug and not a vaporwave bug

The estate's rule is that a fix whose only route is a checkout is a topology finding. This is the same shape one layer up: **a mechanism that claims to need no clone, but needs a human's session instead.** Both are "it works where someone already set it up by hand".

It also means the no-clone guarantee has never been tested anywhere but the host where it cannot fail.

## The options

1. **Read a public repo unauthenticated.** `hf7y/scheduler` is public (`private: false`). `gh api` refuses to try without a token, but the endpoint does not require one -- a plain HTTPS GET of the contents API works. This fixes every host at once, needs no credential anywhere, and removes the human-session dependency entirely. It stops working the day scheduler goes private, which should then be a loud refusal rather than a silent regression.
2. **Give each host a credential that can read scheduler** -- widen an App installation, or place a host token. Works for private repos too; adds a credential to every host and widens App reach to the repo that arms projects.
3. **Both** -- unauthenticated by default, a credential when one is present, with the fallback stated in the log so nobody has to guess which path ran.

Whatever is chosen, `fetch_repo_file` is the one place to change: `fetch_roster` and the `schedule/FREEZE` read already share it, and its header says the BLIND/GAP distinction must not be re-derived per caller.

## Done when

- [ ] `dose <project> --check` works on a host with no gh login and no clone.
- [ ] The path taken is visible in the output, so "it worked" and "it worked because a human was logged in" are distinguishable.
- [ ] `dog` converges on vaporwave without anyone adding a credential there.
- [ ] A witness runs it as a user with no gh session -- the case monkey structurally cannot exercise.

Issue #24: Performance: bound discovery and update learning incrementally

## Problem

The toolkit can spend more effort collecting context than answering the marketer. Opportunities launches eight requests up front, brand discovery widens across pages and patterns without a firm ceiling, and every learning refresh re-fetches the entire completed history. These paths grow with the site even when the user's request is small.

This is a source-grounded scaling concern. No current latency benchmark was run, and the June live audit is historical evidence rather than a current performance claim.

## Evidence

- [Opportunities fetch plan](https://github.com/humanmade/accelerate-ai-toolkit/blob/e136dbb0eaecf6f68135224eff05874a627da3d5/skills/accelerate-opportunities/SKILL.md#L15-L32) always requests two summaries, top content, landing pages, engagement, active experiments, source breakdown and audiences.
- [Brand ingestion](https://github.com/humanmade/accelerate-ai-toolkit/blob/e136dbb0eaecf6f68135224eff05874a627da3d5/docs/brand-pack.md#L18-L40) fetches published pages, resolves synced references and confirms pattern usage. Sufficiency rules instruct the agent to widen the sweep when coverage is thin, without fixed page/byte/time limits.
- [Test palette cache](https://github.com/humanmade/accelerate-ai-toolkit/blob/e136dbb0eaecf6f68135224eff05874a627da3d5/skills/accelerate-test/SKILL.md#L57-L63) and the separate brand-pack cache overlap. Brand-pack prose specifies seven-day reuse but notes that a writer is not yet wired up.
- [Learning fetch loop](https://github.com/humanmade/accelerate-ai-toolkit/blob/e136dbb0eaecf6f68135224eff05874a627da3d5/skills/accelerate-learn/SKILL.md#L57-L74) paginates every completed experiment, then fetches detailed results for each. [Merge logic](https://github.com/humanmade/accelerate-ai-toolkit/blob/e136dbb0eaecf6f68135224eff05874a627da3d5/skills/accelerate-learn/SKILL.md#L111-L154) appends compositions and uses a fixed temporary filename; incremental work must also handle duplicate entries and interrupted/concurrent updates.
- Producer [author-content lookup](https://github.com/humanmade/accelerate/blob/3e9f3b700ab4072f1a95ce150193a528694d7fe3/inc/abilities/author.php#L281-L295) loads all published IDs before later limiting output. [Filtered experiment discovery](https://github.com/humanmade/accelerate/blob/3e9f3b700ab4072f1a95ce150193a528694d7fe3/inc/abilities/discovery.php#L484-L488) can fetch 10,000 rows for post-filtering. Smaller toolkit result limits do not automatically bound this server work.

## Solution / approach

```text
question → minimum useful reads → answer or targeted follow-up
brand cache → bounded representative refresh → explicit coverage result
journal → new/changed experiment identities → bounded detail reads → atomic merge
```

### Implementation

1. Define explicit request, payload and elapsed-time budgets for the full weekly plan and brand ingestion. Choose documented initial defaults and evaluate them on representative small/large fixtures. Avoid a new service or general caching framework.
2. Stage opportunity retrieval: parallelise independent required reads, fetch optional sources when they can change the recommendation, and reuse equivalent site/window results within the session. Do not silently compare incompatible date windows.
3. Bound pages, resolved patterns and markup bytes during brand sampling. Deduplicate references and prevent cycles. Sample deterministically for traffic and template coverage; reaching a cap must produce honest partial coverage, not pretend the whole site was surveyed. Preserve real markup, valid tokens and existing Block Runner pre-flight.
4. Consolidate overlapping palette/brand-pack reads. Include site identity, contract/cache version and appropriate theme/context identity in invalidation. Never reuse a cache across sites; preserve a usable prior cache if refresh fails.
5. Make learning incremental by experiment identity and an available change marker. Inspect the actual listing contract before choosing a cursor: do not invent an `updated_since` argument or assume ended timestamps/annotations never change. If changed-record detection requires producer support, document that precise upstream dependency and retain a bounded reconciliation path.
6. Persist processed IDs/change fingerprints so reruns and interruption do not double-count outcomes or append duplicate compositions. Preserve the current monotonic iteration-counter semantics without treating display numbering as an identity.
7. Provide an explicit bounded rebuild path for recovery; routine refresh must not replay every historical detail. Use unique temporary files or locking/version checks as needed to prevent concurrent journal updates losing data.
8. Record local, telemetry-free measurements: request count, response bytes, elapsed time, cache hit/refresh, pages inspected and budget-exhaustion state. No phone-home.
9. Keep producer query optimisation separate: limiting author IDs before ranking can change correctness, so any upstream improvement must preserve ordering/velocity semantics. Likewise, do not silently truncate filtered experiment listings.

Own `skills/accelerate-opportunities/SKILL.md`, `skills/accelerate-learn/SKILL.md`, relevant palette/cache instructions in test/design, `docs/brand-pack.md`, `docs/self-optimising.md`, and small cache/journal helpers or fixtures.

- [ ] Optional-source failure produces a useful partial answer with provenance, without repeated failing calls.
- [ ] Brand ingestion stops within page/pattern/byte/time limits on a large fixture and preserves usable representative markup.
- [ ] Repeated synced ref

Issue #669: Orphaned/phantom action pins still live post-remediation: dtolnay ×35 repos (two orphaned SHAs), trufflehog ≥20, codeql-action ≥14

## Fourth CI fault: 111+ repos pin an **orphaned** action SHA, which makes a lockfile impossible

Found while remediating the estate for Workflow Dependency Locking (#657). Five of the first 34 repos swept failed at the same point, with the same cause.

### The error

```
1 action could not be resolved — 2 workflows affected
  dtolnay/rust-toolchain@4be9e76fd7c4901c61fb841f559994984270fce7
  no tag or branch contains this commit — a symbolic ref is required for the lockfile
```

`gh actions-lock` cannot emit an entry for a commit that no ref points at, so **no lockfile can be produced for the repo at all** — and without a lockfile, every workflow that needs one stays dead. One unresolvable pin bricks the whole repo.

### Measured

| | |
|---|---|
| commit `4be9e76f…` | **exists** upstream, dated 2025-12-16 — but **orphaned** (force-pushed off its branch) |
| tags `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` publishes | exactly one: **`v1` → `6c977a6ca407…`** |
| repos pinning the orphaned SHA | **111** (code-search floor — it undercounts, see #668) |

Known-affected so far: `jtv-lang`, `coord-tui`, `social-media-tools`, `KnotTheory.jl`, `presswerk`.

### ⚠️ Why SHA-pinning made this worse, not better

The estate pinned actions to full SHAs for supply-chain safety — correct in principle. But **a SHA is only durable if a ref keeps it alive.** When upstream force-pushes, the commit survives (GitHub keeps unreferenced objects) and workflows *kept working*, so nothing surfaced. The pin only became fatal when lockfile generation started demanding a **symbolic** ref.

So this failure was latent for eight months and was triggered by a GitHub feature rollout, not by any change here.

### The fix

Repin `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@4be9e76f…` → **`@6c977a6ca407…`** (the `v1` tag), estate-wide.

Generalised, this wants a check nobody has: **for every pinned action SHA, assert some tag or branch contains it.** That is exactly what `gh actions-lock` does internally, so the detector already exists — it just needs running as a gate rather than discovered during remediation.

### Suggested deliverables

1. Repin the 111+ references to the `v1` SHA (mechanical).
2. A sweep for *other* orphaned pins — this is unlikely to be the only one; prior estate audits found unresolvable pins in bulk.
3. A hypatia rule or CI gate: **pinned SHA must be reachable from a ref.** Cheap to implement, and it would have caught this before the rollout made it fatal.

Related: #657 (the three faults this is the fourth of), #668 (why the 111 is a floor).

Story ID: ORACLE-MODEL-D

## User Story
As a SQM user validating, transpiling, or generating Java for MODEL queries, I want every downstream layer to understand the typed clause explicitly so invalid semantics fail early and no transformation silently loses or approximates MODEL behavior.

## Scope
- Add structural validation for declarations, names, references, rule targets, selector/address arity, tuples, iteration limits, and range steps.
- Add input-row, main-model, reference-model, and post-model output scopes.
- Validate declaration resolution, quote-aware name uniqueness, model/measure/dimension references, target writability, uncorrelated reference/FOR queries, and nested-query scope isolation.
- Add Oracle semantic validation for UPDATE/UPSERT/UPSERT ALL, single/multi-cell restrictions, positional/symbolic addressing, reference-model reads, automatic order with iteration, PREVIOUS/ITERATION_NUMBER contexts, ordered rules, aggregates/analytics, nested references, and prohibited rule subqueries.
- Derive post-model schema as partition + dimension + measure columns and type-check rule values where catalog types are available.
- Validate compatibility with recursive queries, limiting, locking, and existing DML query-source positions using documented Oracle behavior.
- Add path-aware `ModelClauseUnsupportedRule` behavior: exact retention for capable Oracle targets and explicit unsupported diagnostics for incapable targets.
- Populate source dialect, target dialect, and stable node path in every MODEL `TranspileProblem`; discover nested clauses in subqueries, CTEs, reference queries, and existing DML query sources.
- Do not approximate MODEL with CTEs, joins, windows, PIVOT, procedural SQL, or client code.
- Extend `SqmDslVisitor` and the Maven codegen plugin for the complete public DSL.
- Preserve MODEL and its diagnostics through control and middleware pipelines.
- Update validation, transpilation, codegen, control, middleware, and downstream support documentation/tests.

- Every structural, scope, schema, and Oracle semantic rule has focused success/failure tests with stable paths.

- Future approximate rule families remain explicitly documented but are not implemented implicitly.
- Generated Java uses only public DSL/builders, compiles, reconstructs an equal tree, and renders normalized equivalent Oracle SQL.
- Control and middleware expose specific validation/transpilation failures rather than generic render errors.
- DML composition is tested without adding a MODEL-specific DML node; DDL remains absent.
- Every changed production source file has at least 80% patch coverage and every introduced class has at least 80% meaningful line coverage.

## Scope Boundaries
- Validation, exact preservation, unsupported-target diagnostics, codegen, and downstream integration are in scope.
- Cross-dialect approximation is out of scope and requires a separate proof-oriented design.
- No new DML node or DDL work is introduced.

Issue #1157: Design an opaque dynamically typed Covalence object resource

## Goal

Define one extensible host-managed Covalence object type spanning the userspace object hierarchy: checked kernels and facts, immutable bytes, checked blobs, tables/namespaces, strategy leases, callback functions, and future application objects. A future Strategy call can accept one optional object without adding a new ABI parameter for every large or structured payload.

Keep the current small control plane:

```wit
apply-tactic: async func(
  tactic-id: u64,
  arguments: list<u8>,
  object: option<covalence-object>,
  kernel: option<kernel>,
) -> result<kernel, string>;
```

The exact signature is provisional. Because a kernel is itself a Covalence object, a later uniform form might instead consume/return objects; retain the direct typed kernel path initially until ownership, ergonomics, and call overhead are understood.

This recovers large script input naturally: pass an immutable bytes object (or a checked CAS blob) as `object`, rather than copying it through `list<u8>` or permanently adding a script-specific entry point. The same mechanism can pass a rewriter callback, namespace, database handle, strategy instance, or other programmatic input.

## Representation

Prefer an opaque WIT resource, not a giant closed variant:

```wit
interface objects {
  resource covalence-object {
    type-id: func() -> list<u8>;
    type-name: func() -> option<string>; // descriptive only
  }
}
```

Typed interfaces perform checked conversion/borrowing:

```wit
bytes-as-object: func(value: bytes) -> covalence-object;
object-as-bytes: func(value: borrow<covalence-object>) -> option<bytes>;
kernel-as-object: func(value: kernel) -> covalence-object;
object-as-kernel: func(value: covalence-object>) -> result<kernel, covalence-object>;
```

Names are illustrative. Consuming downcasts are useful for linear/mutable objects; borrowing inspection is useful for immutable objects. A failed consuming downcast should return the original object rather than destroy it.

Type identity should be stable and namespaced (likely O256), while a human name is untrusted descriptive metadata. Avoid Rust `TypeId`, process-local integers, RTTI strings, or representation-dependent IDs as wire commitments.

## Authority invariant

Dynamic typing must not erase logical authority boundaries. An untrusted component cannot construct an object tagged `kernel`, `theorem`, or checked `blob` from arbitrary bytes. Only the typed checked host constructors can create those object implementations. Downcasts inspect the host-side implementation/type identity; they never trust a guest-provided tag.

An address still identifies bytes only. An object type or metadata claim does not make those bytes a checked kernel/fact.

## Object families to prototype

- immutable shared bytes (zero-copy host clones/slices);
- checked CAS blob `(address, bytes)`;
- checked mutable/exclusive kernel;
- immutable table/namespace metadata;
- Strategy instance lease from #1155;
- callback/function object;
- application-defined opaque objects registered under stable type IDs.

Not every object is serializable or content-addressable. Callbacks, live kernels, database connections, and leases are runtime capabilities. Serialization/address/clone operations should therefore be optional typed capabilities, not methods promised by the root object.

## Callbacks

A callback object should be an opaque async callable capability, not a raw guest function pointer:

```wit
resource callback {
  call: async func(
    arguments: list<u8>,
    object: option<covalence-object>,
  ) -> result<option<covalence-object>, string>;
}
```

Design explicitly for reentrancy, cancellation, recursive calls, store affinity, resource limits, traps, and cycles. A callback passed into another Wasm instance must not accidentally grant the callee all capabilities of its creator.

## Cross-instance/store problem

Wasmtime component resources ordinarily live in one Store/resource table. Strategy pooling and nested loading require a host-level representation that can be projected into several component stores without forging or losing identity. Immutable objects may use `Arc`; mutable linear objects such as kernels need exclusive leases/ownership transfer. Do not paper over this with universal `Arc<Mutex<dyn Any>>`: define clone, borrow, consume, and concurrency semantics per object family.

Pool/cache keys must not depend on process-local object handles. Dropping the last guest handle should release the host object unless another explicit owner/pool retains it. Detect or bound callback/object cycles.

## Python and WIT shape

Python should expose a common `Object` base/protocol while retaining distinct concrete classes (`Kernel`, `Bytes`, `Blob`, `Strategy`, callback wrappers). Python conversion can be ergonomic, but implicit conversion from ordinary values must remain untrusted and type-directed. `None` means no object, distinct from a process-global default capability.

WIT sees one opaque root resource plus typed adapter interfaces. Avoid a universal stringly `invoke(method, json)` surface; Strategies and other hot paths should keep typed methods and use the object only for open-ended payloads/capabilities.

## First experiment

1. Implement host-only Rust `CovObject` with stable type identity and immutable Bytes + checked Blob cases.
2. Add consuming and borrowing checked downcasts with failure-preserves-value tests.
3. Add Kernel with explicitly linear ownership and prove handles cannot alias one mutable kernel across stores.
4. Add `option<covalence-object>` to an experimental Strategy world, leaving the current world version intact.
5. Pass a large bytes script and a small callback object to a demo tactic.
6. Measure direct typed calls versus dynamic-object adaptation and cross-store projection.
7. Prototype the same hierarchy in Python before freezing WIT names.

## Acceptance criteria

- stable, documented object type identity;
- checked types cannot be forged through tags or metada

Issue #203: Bare Parquet directory: only one level of Hive partition columns discovered (list_with_delimiter is non-recursive)

## Problem

`ParquetTableReader.getTableInfo()` (used by indextables_spark's distributed Parquet-directory
companion-sync scan, `DistributedSourceScanner.scanParquetDirectory()`) only discovers **one
level** of Hive-style partition directories for a bare Parquet directory with more than one
partition column. For a directory written like `zone=east/date=2024-01-01/part-....parquet`,
`ParquetTableInfo.getPartitionColumns()` comes back as `["zone"]` — `date` is silently dropped
entirely, not just misordered.

Found while adding a regression test for indextables_spark issue #393 (declared partition-column
order) — a bare two-column-partitioned Parquet directory test failed with the second partition
segment (`date=...`) missing from the produced split path altogether, which is a more severe
symptom than the ordering bug that test was meant to cover. Root-caused to this function rather
than to anything in indextables_spark; the equivalent Delta and Iceberg companion-sync paths are
unaffected (they source declared partition columns from table metadata, not directory listing).

## Root cause

`native/src/parquet_reader/distributed.rs`, `get_table_info_async()`:

```rust
// List immediate children with delimiter (single LIST call, no recursion)
let prefix = url_to_object_path(&url);
let list_result = store
    .list_with_delimiter(Some(&prefix))
    .await
    ...

for cp in &list_result.common_prefixes {
    let dir_name = cp.as_ref();
    if let Some(last_segment) = dir_name.rsplit('/').find(|s| !s.is_empty()) {
        if last_segment.contains('=') {
            partition_directories.push(dir_name.to_string());
            if !partition_columns_found {
                // Walk the path to find all partition levels
                for segment in dir_name.split('/') {
                    if let Some(eq_pos) = segment.find('=') {
                        let key = &segment[..eq_pos];
                        if !partition_columns.contains(&key.to_string()) {
                            partition_columns.push(key.to_string());
                        }
                    }
                }
                partition_columns_found = true;
            }
        }
    }
}
```

`store.list_with_delimiter(...)` is a **non-recursive**, single-level object-store LIST — for a
table root it returns only the immediate child prefixes (e.g. `zone=east/`, `zone=west/`), never
the deeper `zone=east/date=2024-01-01/` prefixes. The `for segment in dir_name.split('/')` loop
comment ("Walk the path to find all partition levels") suggests the author intended to handle
multi-segment partition paths, but `dir_name` can never contain more than one `key=value`
segment given how `list_with_delimiter` bounds the listing — so that inner loop is effectively
dead code for anything beyond the first partition level. `partition_directories` itself is also
only ever populated with first-level prefixes, so downstream file listing
(`list_partition_files_async`, called per entry in `partition_directories`) presumably also never
descends into the second level — worth checking as part of any fix here; the exact
under-listing behavior for actual *files* (not just the reported column names) wasn't
independently verified in this report.

## Impact

- `BUILD INDEXTABLES COMPANION FOR PARQUET` against a bare Parquet directory partitioned by
  **more than one column** silently produces incomplete/incorrect partition metadata (and,
  pending verification per the note above, may also miss files under deeper partition levels
  entirely).
- Delta and Iceberg companion-sync sources are unaffected — they don't go through this
  directory-listing path.
- Every existing test in indextables_spark that partitions a bare Parquet directory uses exactly
  one partition column (e.g. `partitionBy("date")`, `partitionBy("region")`) — consistent with
  this being a real, previously-uncovered gap rather than a regression.

## Suggested fix direction

Recurse `list_with_delimiter` calls level-by-level (or use a recursive/prefix-walking listing)
until a level's `common_prefixes` stop looking like `key=value` directories, collecting one
partition column name per level in the order encountered — mirroring how
`native/src/delta_reader` and `native/src/iceberg` source declared partition order from actual
table metadata rather than directory listing. Needs a test with a 2+ column bare Parquet
directory (not currently covered anywhere in this repo's test suite either).

## Not included in this report

- A fix — this is a report only, scoped out of indextables_spark issue #393/#(this PR) since it's
  native tantivy4java code and a distinct bug (missing data, not misordering).

A maintainer on the project infinidysk/infinidysk (C#) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain: Issue #1346: Harden Remove Orphaned Files with persistent orphan confirmation and mutation-time revalidation ### Before submitting - [x] I have searched existing issues and did not find a similar request. - [x] This request relates to use with legally obtained content. ### Problem or use case Remove Orphaned Files is a destructive maintenance task that can run manually or automatically on a daily schedule. It already has several useful safety protections, but a single apparently valid library scan can still authorize permanent deletion.

Current cleanup identifies deletable WebDAV files primarily from the current Library Directory scan and database state. A Usenet file can become a deletion candidate when it:

  • has no imported symlink or STRM reference found in the current library scan,
  • has no HistoryItemId, and
  • predates the cleanup run.

The current implementation already has important safeguards that should remain, including:

  • rejecting a Library Directory inside the rclone mount,
  • requiring at least five distinct linked WebDAV IDs,
  • aborting a real run when more than 90% of the deletable population appears unlinked,
  • protecting items still associated with SAB history, and
  • excluding items created after the cleanup scan started.

The remaining problem is that these safeguards mainly protect against obviously catastrophic scans. A plausible but incomplete library view can still fall below those thresholds and be treated as authoritative.

For example:

Normal scan:
5,000 linked
1,000 unlinked

Temporary partial view:
3,500 linked
2,500 unlinked

The second result is a major change in library visibility, but it is not necessarily extreme enough to trigger the existing 90% circuit breaker.

This matters because temporary mount visibility problems, filesystem synchronization, library moves, container startup/remount conditions, or other transient states should not be able to turn one unusual scan into permanent deletion.

There is also a time-of-check/time-of-use concern in the current file-deletion path. Candidate files are selected using orphan-protection predicates, but the final file deletion is performed against the selected IDs. If protection state changes between selection and mutation, the final DELETE does not currently re-evaluate all of the predicates that originally made the file eligible.

Interestingly, the empty-directory cleanup already follows a stronger pattern by re-checking directory emptiness in the DELETE itself so a concurrent child insertion cannot result in an unsafe cascade deletion. Applying the same fail-closed principle to orphaned files would strengthen the destructive path.

This is especially important for scheduled cleanup. Unattended maintenance should be more conservative than an interactive action and should tolerate one temporary or incomplete library observation without permanently removing anything.

The goal is to make safety intrinsic to Remove Orphaned Files itself, without requiring users to manually run Dry Run before every cleanup and without making scheduled maintenance impractical. ### Proposed solution

Introduce a lightweight persistent orphan-confirmation workflow combined with a second link validation before destructive work and mutation-time database revalidation.

The intent is to build on the existing cleanup implementation rather than replace it.

1. Persist only orphan candidates, not the complete library snapshot

When an item is first observed as unlinked, record a small amount of persistent evidence, conceptually:

DavItemId
FirstSeenUnlinkedAt
LastSeenUnlinkedAt
ObservationCount
LastSuccessfulScanGeneration
ConfigFingerprint

Only currently suspicious items need rows. There should be no need to persist every linked library item or a complete filesystem snapshot.

This keeps storage overhead small even for large libraries.

2. Require both repeated evidence and elapsed time

A candidate should become eligible for deletion only when both conditions are satisfied:

  • it has been observed unlinked in at least two successful/trustworthy cleanup scans, and
  • a minimum grace interval has elapsed since it was first observed.

The exact default interval can be selected by the maintainers. A value such as 24 hours may be reasonable for daily scheduled cleanup, but the important invariant is that running the task twice immediately should not defeat the protection.

First healthy observation
        ↓
record candidate
        ↓
do not delete

Later healthy observation
        ↓
still unlinked?
        ↓
grace interval elapsed?
        ↓
eligible for destructive revalidation
3. Reset the evidence when an item is linked again

If a candidate becomes linked again, clear/reset its orphan-confirmation state.

An old observation should never be reusable months later after an unrelated future unlink event.

4. Never advance candidate evidence from an unhealthy scan

A failed or suspicious scan should:

  • delete nothing,
  • not increment ObservationCount, and
  • not update FirstSeenUnlinkedAt/LastSeenUnlinkedAt as evidence.

This should include current safety failures such as:

  • Library Directory unavailable or traversal failure,
  • Library Directory inside the rclone mount,
  • too few linked IDs,
  • the existing extreme-unlinked-ratio circuit breaker, or
  • a future historical-baseline anomaly check.
5. Keep a small last-known-good scan baseline

Persist summary information from the latest trustworthy cleanup scan, for example:

LastSuccessfulScanAt
Link

DavItem exists

Organized symlink / STRM exists

points to an InfiniDysk /.ids/<guid> target

does that DavItem still exist?

This should not be implemented as generic filesystem dangling-link detection such as find -xtype l, File.Exists(target), or an HTTP/WebDAV probe of every target.

A temporarily unavailable rclone mount can make an otherwise valid symlink fail to resolve while its DavItem is still perfectly valid. The authoritative stale-reference test should instead be:

read the stored symlink/STRM target
        ↓
is this an exact InfiniDysk-owned .ids reference?
        ↓
extract DavItemId
        ↓
does that DavItemId exist in the InfiniDysk database?

That keeps transient filesystem availability separate from actual InfiniDysk identity loss.

Add a dedicated Library Reference Integrity maintenance workflow that reuses InfiniDysk's existing organized-link and safe-cleanup primitives.

I would keep this separate from Remove Orphaned Files: the two operations are inverse consistency checks with different destructive effects. They can share a library-census abstraction, but should remain separately understandable and auditable.

The census should retain all recognized links grouped by exact DavItemId, conceptually:

DavItemId A
  → /library/Movies/A.mkv
  → /library/combined_symlinks/A.mkv

DavItemId B
  → /library/TV/Show/S01E01.mkv

Only references already positively recognized as InfiniDysk-owned should participate. Foreign/debrid/custom links, malformed targets and non-InfiniDysk STRMs should remain untouched.

Generated-output paths should follow the same ownership/exclusion rules already used by RemoveUnlinkedFilesTask, so a generated STRM output is not accidentally confused with an Arr-imported organized-library reference.

2. Compare referenced IDs to DavItems set-wise

Do not issue one database query per library link.

Collect the distinct referenced IDs and perform batched/set-based existence checks against DavItems:

recognized library DavItemIds
          MINUS
current DavItems.Id
          =
stale-reference candidate IDs

This should remain approximately O(library references + database batches), with no NNTP/provider reads required.

The existing orphan cleanup already uses batched/indexed linked-ID processing for large libraries, so large-library scalability should remain an explicit design goal.

3. Fail closed if the library census is not trustworthy

If Library Directory is missing, inside the rclone mount, unreadable, or traversal exits unsuccessfully, the task should abort without classifying or modifying links.

### Self Checks

- [x] I confirm that I am using English to submit this report.
- [x] Non-english title submitions will be closed directly.

### RAGFlow workspace code commit ID

2db8eb6c91184402e2979b6b52b77063919c7e17

### RAGFlow image version

v0.27.0

### Other environment information

- Deployment: Docker Compose (`docker/docker-compose.yml`, `ragflow-cpu` profile)
- OS type: macOS host (Docker Desktop)
- Affected area: Data Pipeline / Agent canvas editor (`category=dataflow_canvas`), frontend autosave

### Actual behavior

A Data Pipeline canvas that had a full, working definition (multiple components wired together, verified via a successful "Test Run") had its stored DSL silently replaced with an **empty** one: `components: {}` and `graph: {nodes: [], edges: []}` — every node and edge gone. This happened with no user action to delete or clear the canvas; the browser tab was simply left open across a backend restart/reconnect.

I confirmed the empty state directly in the database (`user_canvas.dsl`):

```json
{
  "components": {},
  "graph": { "nodes": [], "edges": [] },
  "globals": {...}, "variables": {...}, "messages": [...]
}
```

Root cause is in the frontend autosave, `web/src/pages/agent/hooks/use-save-graph.ts:74-107`:

```ts
export const useWatchAgentChange = (chatDrawerVisible: boolean) => {
  const nodes = useGraphStore((state) => state.nodes);
  const edges = useGraphStore((state) => state.edges);
  const { saveGraph } = useSaveGraph(false, true);
  ...
  const saveAgent = useCallback(async () => {
    if (!chatDrawerVisible) {
      const ret = await saveGraph();
      ...
    }
  }, [chatDrawerVisible, saveGraph, setSaveTime]);

  useDebounceEffect(
    () => { saveAgent(); },
    [nodes, edges],
    { wait: 1000 * 20 },
  );
  ...
};
```

`nodes`/`edges` come straight from the Zustand canvas store (`useGraphStore`). This effect fires an unconditional `saveGraph()` (→ `PUT /api/v1/agents/{id}` with `buildDslData()` → `graphToDsl` → `buildDslComponentsByGraph`, `web/src/pages/agent/utils/dsl-bridge.ts:163-197` and `web/src/pages/agent/utils.ts:604-672`) 20 seconds after **any** change to `nodes`/`edges` — including a transition to/through an empty array — with no check that:
- the initial fetch of the existing DSL has actually completed and populated the store, or
- `nodes`/`edges` are non-empty before persisting.

If the store's `nodes`/`edges` are (or become) `[]` for any reason — a component remount after the backend becomes briefly unreachable and reconnects, a route/tab re-render that resets the store before the fetched DSL is re-applied, etc. — and that empty state holds for the 20s debounce window, `buildDslComponentsByGraph([], [], ...)` returns `{}` and the empty DSL gets written over the real one. There is no confirmation prompt and no way to tell from the UI that this happened until the pipeline is run again and every component is missing.

The autosave effect should not persist an empty `nodes`/`edges` state over an existing non-empty canvas. Issue #382: lookup_lineage stops at consumed datasets: dataset ancestry (Dataset_Dataset) is data flow but never walked

## Summary

`lookup_lineage` reports `walked_complete=True` after visiting 2 executions for
a training run whose data provenance is several derivation steps deep. The
missing edge is **dataset → parent dataset**: lineage reports a consumed
dataset and stops there, never climbing to the datasets it was derived from.

This is not the orchestration question ADR-0001 settled. Dataset derivation is
data flow — a train/test split *is* how the training data came to exist — so
the current behaviour looks like an unintended gap in that decision rather than
a consequence of it.

Observed on the live `eye-ai` catalog with deriva-ml `1.60.0`.

## Reproduction

```python
lin = ml.lookup_lineage("7-ZW3P")
lin.executions_visited      # 2
lin.walked_complete         # True
[(d.rid, d.version) for d in lin.lineage.consumed_datasets]
# [('5-WEBG', '0.6.0'), ('5-ZHRE', '0.6.0'), ('5-ZMGJ', '0.6.0')]
```

The walk terminates with `walked_complete=True`, yet each consumed dataset has
recorded ancestry that is never visited:

```python
ml.lookup_dataset("5-WEBG").list_dataset_parents()   # -> 2-277G
ml.lookup_dataset("2-277G").list_dataset_parents()   # -> 2-1S12, 2-277E
```

So the real chain is `2-1S12 → 2-277E → 2-277G → 5-WEBG → 7-ZW3P`, and
`lookup_lineage` sees only the last hop.

## Why this is data flow, not orchestration

ADR-0001 decides between two edge sets — data-flow (`Dataset_Version.Execution`,
`<Asset>_Execution`) and orchestration (`Execution_Execution`) — and rejects the
latter. Every alternative it weighs (`edge_type` field, orchestration-only,
`edge_types` param) is about `Execution_Execution`. **Dataset ancestry is not
considered anywhere in it.**

But `Dataset_Dataset` is a data-derivation edge, not an orchestration one. The
ADR's own motivating example makes the gap concrete:

> "A user staring at `predictions.csv` wants to know which dataset trained the
> model that produced it, **and which dataset was loaded to produce that
> training set**."

That second clause is exactly what is missing. On `7-ZW3P` the user asks and
gets `6-MWQE` — a BlackBox backfill sentinel — while `2-1S12`, the LAC source
cohort the splits derive from, is unreachable.

## Proposal

Add an opt-in parameter, defaulting to today's behaviour:

```python
lookup_lineage(rid, *, include_dataset_ancestors: bool = False)
```

When set, expanding a dataset also walks `Dataset_Dataset` to the source
datasets, recursing with the existing `depth`/`max_executions`/cycle handling,
and includes each ancestor's producing execution as a parent.

This is mechanical: no new semantics, no policy judgement, and the traversal
already exists in `list_dataset_parents()`. It is additive and default-off, so
no existing consumer changes.

Two details worth deciding explicitly:

1. **Version pinning.** `Dataset_Dataset` records no version, so given
   `5-WEBG @ v0.6.0` there is no way to say which of `2-277G`'s 85 versions it
   derives from. The ancestor edge is therefore version-less today — worth
   noting in the response, and possibly worth a schema follow-up (this is the
   same gap raised in #367).
2. **Ancestor producers may be sentinels.** With #367's `origin_recorded` now
   available, an ancestor whose origin was never captured can be reported
   honestly rather than silently attributed.

## Not proposed: folding in the feature arc

`find_feature_producers` (#370) recovers a much larger set — on `7-ZW3P`, 13 of
17 contributing workflows arrive that way, including the optic-disc detector
that produced the bounding boxes the training images were cropped to. It is
tempting to have lineage call it too, and we deliberately do **not** propose
that:

- Feature producers are **candidates**, not ancestors. The catalog cannot say
  which features downstream code actually read (#370's own docstring says so),
  and lineage returning them as parents would assert a dependency the data does
  not support.
- Unscoped it **cascades**. Expanding each candidate's own consumed datasets
  finds more candidates whose inputs get scanned in turn; we measured 15
  datasets for one execution, 7 of them unrelated to the model's data cone,
  before scoping the walk.

That scoping is deployment-review policy and belongs in the consumer.
`find_feature_producers` being a separate, explicit call is the right shape —
this issue only asks for the mechanical ancestry edge.

## Context

Raised from `deriva-ml-model-deploy`, which builds a provenance ledger over
these primitives. It currently re-implements the ancestry walk itself
(`list_dataset_parents` + a `lookup_lineage` per ancestor). Everything else it
needed has moved upstream (#370, #371, #372); this is the last piece that is
purely mechanical rather than policy.

Issue #391: [Stage 8][Uninstall] Add versioned application inventory and exact removal coordinator

Parent: #116
Coordinates with: #159, #180, DB-009, DB-020

## Goal

Implement the accepted-runtime-owned, versioned application inventory and uninstall coordinator that safely composes exact removal effects without pulling provider, permanent-entry, setup, repository, or filesystem identities into its internal contract.

This is the primitive owner for the Temp Fast finding that DevBridge must track what it creates and must distinguish app-only removal from full exact purge. It is not authority to retire the legacy Stage-0 tree before #159 proves that cutover, and it is not authority to bypass environment lifecycle adapters.

## Assessment

Current head already contains useful lower-level bricks:

- each installed permanent-entry component has an exact content manifest;
- `ExactArtifactSet` can bind a bounded tree to filesystem identity, reject indirection/substitution, remove exact files/directories non-recursively, and re-observe absence;
- local mutation and state-store primitives support serialized replacement and exact reread;
- setup PATH ownership and provider/environment lifecycle ownership already have narrow adapters.

Missing:

- one versioned neutral inventory contract with created/adopted/foreign provenance;
- separate application-removal and full-purge plans;
- explicit preserved/protected/referenced reporting;
- a DB-009 planned -> attempted -> observed -> reconciled journal for the cross-owner operation;
- exact `REMOVE` plus plan-digest confirmation;
- producer registration from each owning layer;
- supported CLI composition.

The old `~/.devbridge/runtime` Stage-0 data and unselected experimental checkouts cannot be inferred obsolete from their names or age. Ordinary installation deliberately retains verified generations. They remain preserved until their owning cutover/retention contracts publish exact retirement authority.

## Primary-source research

- Node.js documents that promise filesystem mutations are not synchronized/threadsafe, `fsync` requests that file data be flushed with OS/device-specific behavior, rename is a separate operation, and recursive removal has retry semantics rather than ownership semantics. The implementation must serialize locally, write/flush/replace/re-read durable records, and must never use recursive removal as its authority source: https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.13.1/docs/api/fs.html
- Microsoft documents that deleting through a symbolic-link path deletes the link rather than the target, while deletion may remain pending or fail because of open handles: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-deletefilew
- Microsoft documents an explicit no-path-redirection directory-removal mode and that junction removal affects the link rather than its target. Node does not expose that flag directly, so the existing lstat/reparse/canonical-identity checks plus non-recursive removal and re-observation remain required: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-removedirectory2w
- Microsoft documents move/replace and write-through as separate flags. A plain rename must therefore be followed by exact reread; it is not itself a claim of durable acceptance: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-movefileexa

## Reassessment / ownership boundary

The Permanent Entry and Runner may publish neutral receipts for artifacts they create, but they must not own uninstall policy. The accepted runtime owns mode selection, confirmation, planning, orchestration, and reporting. Provider/environment producers expose only neutral subjects/effects; destruction remains inside their existing lifecycle adapters. The generic coordinator never sees provider names, VM/domain/disk paths, repository identities, or foreign object types.

A manifest is evidence, not permanent deletion authority. Every effect must be rebound and re-observed immediately before mutation. Foreign, ambiguous, referenced, current/LKG-required, or unregistered state is preserved and reported.

## Primitive-to-high-level plan

1. Define a small versioned inventory/removal protocol with exact keys, bounded neutral identities, provenance (`created`, `adopted`, `foreign`), retention class, references, opaque effect identities, and deterministic digest.
2. Implement read-only planning for `application` and `purge` modes. Both require literal `REMOVE` plus the exact current plan digest before effects can start. `application` excludes authority/environment state; `purge` may include only exact locally authorized created/adopted resources. Foreign/ambiguous/referenced resources are always preserved.
3. Implement a durable DB-009 journal and bounded resume/reconcile loop. Before every effect: rebuild the plan, prove digest/generation stable, bind exact effect, observe, attempt once, observe/reconcile, and record the outcome.
4. Attach filesystem removal through `ExactArtifactSet`; prune only explicitly owned empty directories. Surface sharing/lock failure distinctly. Never recursively sweep a home/config/provider root.
5. Add producer adapters in ownership order: permanent-entry/runner payload receipts, accepted-runtime/service payload receipts, setup/PATH receipts, configuration authority, then lifecycle/environment receipts. Producers own discovery and local details; the coordinator consumes only the neutral contract.
6. Add `devbridge uninstall inspect --mode <application|purge>` and explicit apply/resume UX only after every supported producer required for that mode is registered. No implicit prompt or ordinary command may enter uninstall.
7. Test normal, foreign/adopted, referenced protection, link/reparse substitution, concurrent mutation, plan drift, interruption at every phase, open-file/lock failure, non-empty parent preservation, report accuracy, and no-provider/direct-host-fallback absence.
8. Qualify application-only removal/recovery first; qualify full purge through real Hyper-V and KVM/libvirt lifecycle

A maintainer on the project jaseci-labs/jac (Jac) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #8952: /graph/data walks every reachable node with no read-access check and is mounted on the stdlib server, the scale server and the gateway with no off switch: gate it under [serve] (off in production) and route the walk through the ACL

### Summary

`GET /graph/data` serializes every node reachable from a root, field values included, through a raw storage walk that never consults the access layer. It is mounted unconditionally on the stdlib server, the scale server and the microservice gateway, and no configuration key removes it. #8755 (item 3) reports the anonymous guest-root dump, and its owner plans a config flag plus required auth. This issue records three things that plan has to cover, with a live repro, and proposes the concrete shape so the visualizer can be switched off in production and, when on, shows a caller only what they are allowed to read.

Verified live on `main` @ `c08bef250` (2026-09-04), `jac run --serve --no-client`, SQLite. Repro app and probe script at the bottom.

### 1. The walk bypasses read access, so requiring auth is not enough

`collect_node_connections` (`jac/jaclang/runtime/impl/graph_utils.impl.jac:80-112`) recurses over `sv_live_edges(...)` (`jac/jaclang/runtime/osp_graph_sv.jac:153-201`), which is the storage-level adjacency list. Nothing on that path calls `check_read_access` or `acl_read_ok`.

Normal traversal does: `jac/jaclang/runtime/graph_walk.jac:182` and `:237` drop any hop whose far node fails `acl_read_ok` whenever `access_gated()` holds. That is the layer #7860 repaired for the topology-index path. The visualizer is the one remaining reader that skips it.

Repro: `alice` (authenticated) hangs a `Secret` on `root.shared` and grants nothing. A guest walker reading `[root.shared-->]` is filtered correctly. Anonymous `GET /graph/data` is not:

```bash
# guest, ACL-aware traversal through a walker
curl -s -X POST localhost:8765/walker/read_shared -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
# {"ok": true, ..., "reports": [["Account(email='alice@example.com', api_key='sk-live-SECRET-KEY')"]]}

# guest, /graph/data
curl -s localhost:8765/graph/data
# {"nodes": [
#   {"id": "0b1a...", "label": "root"},
#   {"id": "30ea...", "label": "Account(email='alice@example.com', api_key='sk-live-SECRET-KEY')"},
#   {"id": "3be9...", "label": "Secret(owner='c573...', value='only-alice-should-read-this')"}
# ], ...}
```

Consequence: after auth is required, an authenticated user's dump still contains every node linked into their reachable set that they have no right to read: nodes other users attached to shared commons, nodes whose grant was revoked (#7860's scenario), anything reachable across a shared node. The response has to equal what the caller could traverse with `[-->]`; otherwise `/graph/data` is a read-access bypass for every logged-in user, not just for guests.

### 2. Three surfaces, one config table

- **stdlib server**: `jac/jaclang/server/impl/server.impl.jac:2393-2396` registers `/graph` and `/graph/data` unconditionally. `_graph_data` (`:2038-2085`) resolves the caller with `_auth_or_guest` (`:1922-1931`), so a missing **or invalid** token silently becomes the guest root with HTTP 200 (`Authorization: Bearer not.a.token` returns the public graph; a client holding an expired token is shown the public graph as if it were its own).
- **scale server**: `jac/jaclang/scale/server/impl/serve.static.impl.jac:380-414` registers both; `graph_data` (`:430-470`) has the same guest fallback at `:443`. `serve.core.impl.jac:513` calls `register_graph_endpoint()` with no gate, unlike the admin portal (`admin_portal.impl.jac:38-43`, `[scale.admin] enabled`) and the API docs (`serve.core.impl.jac:246`, `[scale.server] docs_enabled`).
- **gateway**: `jac/jaclang/scale/runtime/gateway/microservice_gateway.impl.jac:312-379` fans `GET /graph/data` out to every eligible service, forwards the caller's headers, and merges the fragments (`:389-394`). A flag only the service reads is still aggregated unless the gateway honors it too.

Both servers already read the project-level `[serve]` table (`serve.static.impl.jac:159-161`, `:278-282`; `server.impl.jac` throughout), so a key under `[scale.server]` would reach one surface of three. `ServeConfig` (`jac/jaclang/project/config.jac:80-89`) is where a single key covers all of them.

### 3. Labels carry contents, and docs plus tests pin the current behavior

`label: repr(node_arch)` in both handlers serializes every `has` field, so the dump is data, not topology. The docs describe anonymous access as a feature (`jac/jaclang/cli/docs/reference/plugins/jac-scale-http.md:1863-1876`, `cli/docs/tutorials/production/local.md:248`, skill `cli/skills/jac-sv-endpoints.md:79`), and two tests assert the anonymous 200 (`jac/jaclang/scale/tests/server/test_serve.jac:870-873`, `jac/tests/runtimelib/test_serve_client.jac:2353-2372`). All of these move with the fix.

### Proposal

**Config, one key, honored by all three surfaces:**

```toml
[serve]
graph_visualizer = false   # default false; `jac run --dev` turns it on unless set explicitly
```

- **Off** (production default): neither `/graph` nor `/graph/data` is registered on either server (404), and the gateway passthrough does not aggregate. Same pattern as `[scale.admin] enabled` and `[scale.server] docs_enabled`, but in `[serve]` so the stdlib server and the gateway see it.
- **On**: `/graph/data` requires a valid token and answers 401 otherwise. No guest fallback; the page's "Public Graph" mode and `?public=1` go away, which is what #8755 asks for. One startup log line ("graph visualizer enabled at /graph") so an operator can see it is mounted.
- `dev_mode` already flows into the server (`serve.core.impl.jac:189`), so `jac run --dev` keeps today's ergonomics without an explicit key.

**Walk:** `collect_node_connections` takes the same gate `[-->]` uses: when `access_gated()`, skip an edge whose far node fails `acl_read_ok` and do not recurse into it. Building the dump from the `GraphQuery` path directly would leave a single reader and no second ACL to keep in sync. `repr` labels can stay once that holds, since the caller could `report` those nodes anyway.

**Tests:** flip the two anonymous-200 assertions to 404 (off)

Measured with `live_ids()` from the current exports:

| id | in deny-set | actually live-reachable |
|---|---|---|
| `77SG9jTdVKhwMwvR` dispatcher | ✅ | ✅ |
| `S4N1LiisAqA4hpMC` spine | ✅ (floor label) | ✅ |
| `53RxDSON8P3QSN22` sub-main-processing | ❌ | ✅ |
| `tKeQUkZK5cFK9BFa` sub-resolve-and-gate | ❌ | ✅ |
| `WfZ8UCTO9bsrvilO` sub-fetch-results | ❌ | ✅ |
| `B3rBMtABou6FpY69` sub-media-intake | ❌ | ✅ |

Same for `qa4LWvPrhUnAPgjC`, `oIzFAzi3bGgn5mTH`, `NTpMPKzkLZx7pJBE`, `fr2u3e6FKg52cPvK`, `4dPJ8ykop8VIpddY`, `aaPzPW96VuLqKM7t` — i.e. the entire RS-9 second level. Every one of them has been `--yes`-deployable since the 2026-09-01 cutover (deploy C on 2026-09-02 went through this hole too).

## Cause (`scripts/deploy.py`, `live_ids()`)

```python
live = set(LIVE_LABELED_IDS)            # floor ids pre-seeded into the RESULT set …
stack = [roots …]
while stack:
    wid = stack.pop()
    …
    live.add(wid)
    if wid in graphs:
        for c in graphs[wid][3]:
            if c not in live:           # … and the same set is used as the VISITED set
                stack.append(c)
```

`S4N1…` is in `LIVE_LABELED_IDS` (label starts with `LIVE`), so when the dispatcher's callee `S4N1…` is examined, `c not in live` is False and it is never pushed → its own `executeWorkflow` callees are never walked. The floor silently truncates the closure at every floor id. The two early `continue` guards inside the loop compound it (a floor id that IS exported still gets skipped if it arrives on the stack).

Second weakness: `KNOWN_ID_LABELS` entries like `"sub-resolve-and-gate (LIVE lineage — live-reachable via S4N1)"` do not start with `LIVE`, so the floor does not cover them either.

## Fix (one change)

Keep a separate `visited` set; seed the stack with roots AND every floor id that has an export; add to `live` on visit; push callees `not in visited`. Then `live_ids()` returns the true transitive closure and the floor only adds unexported ids.

Regression guard: `tests/unit/deploy_gates_test.py` case — build a 3-export toy tree `root(ingress, active) → A (floor-labelled) → B` and assert `B in live_ids(tmp_root)`. RED on today's code.

## Until fixed

Treat every id in the table as LIVE by hand: never pass `--yes` for them; always `--i-know-this-is-live` + interactive `y`. The #80 live deploy is being run that way.

Issue #1161: [security] Four new unbounded-recursion-in-error-rendering instances on the Rust server (extends #1117)

Filed from the 2026-08-31 security review (`docs/security-reports/2026-08-31.md`, finding **C9**). Not fixed in this pass — review/document/file only. Extends the standing #1117 bug class (unbounded recursion in Rust error-message renderers, no BSON nesting-depth cap anywhere on the Rust wire/decode path) rather than duplicating it — #1117's original two sites (`argtypes.rs::render_stage_value`, `update.rs::render_value`) are still open and unfixed; this issue tracks four *additional* sites, three of which are net-new this window.

## Findings

1. **`crates/secantus-core/src/aggregate.rs:286` (`render_value_compact`, new this window)** recurses into `Bson::Array`/`Bson::Document` with no depth cap (lines 320-333). Called from `redact_runtime_error` (line 351) to render mongod's `17053` error when a `$redact` expression evaluates to a non-`$$KEEP`/`$$PRUNE`/`$$DESCEND` value.
   - **Trigger:** `aggregate([{$redact: {$literal: <a BSON array nested tens of thousands of levels deep>}}])` against a collection with at least one document. No auth, no prior state beyond one document existing.

2. **`crates/secantus-core/src/aggregate.rs:264` (`redact_list`, new this window)** widens `$redact`'s array handling to recurse into nested arrays via a `redact_subdoc`/`redact_descend`/`redact_list` mutual recursion (previously nested arrays were copied verbatim and never walked — this is a genuine correctness fix, but it opens a second, independent unbounded-recursion surface). Even when every value in the document is a proper decision (so finding 1 above is never reached), a document containing a self-nested array deep enough recurses the evaluator itself past the stack limit.

3. **`crates/secantus-commands/src/bulkwrite.rs:67` (`render_op`)** calls the already-known-unbounded `argtypes::render_stage_value` (the exact function #1117 already flags) the moment a `bulkWrite` op entry doesn't contain a supported `insert`/`update`/`delete` key.

4. **`crates/secantus-commands/src/bulkwrite.rs:121` (inline call)** calls `render_stage_value` the moment a `bulkWrite` `ops[]` entry isn't a BSON document at all — reads the raw array entry and stringifies it recursively before any other validation runs.
   - **Trigger for 3/4:** a `bulkWrite` command whose `ops` array contains one entry that is itself a deeply-nested BSON array (not an object). The type check that would reject it calls `render_stage_value` on the offending value first, to build the error message.

## Root cause (shared with #1117)

No BSON nesting-depth cap anywhere on the Rust wire/decode path — re-confirmed this cycle by grepping the full `crates/` tree for `max_depth`/`MAX_DEPTH`/`recursion_limit`/`nesting` (only unrelated hits: `$graphLookup`'s `maxDepth` pipeline option, SQL-parser depth counters).

## Impact

A Rust stack overflow aborts the whole process rather than unwinding through `catch_unwind` in `secantus-server`. Each site above is an independent, unauthenticated, single-request denial-of-service on the Rust server — same severity class as #995 and #1117.

## Suggested fix

Rather than patching each renderer individually as new ones get added (this is the second review cycle to find new instances of the same pattern), reject BSON past a nesting-depth cap at decode time everywhere on the Rust server (mongod's own default is ~100–200 levels). That closes this issue, #1117, and any future instance in one place.

A maintainer on the project jdrumgoole/SecantusDB (Python) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #1357: [security] Unbounded recursion in explain.rs's canonical_match family — stack-overflow DoS via any explain() filter

Filed from the 2026-09-07 security review (`docs/security-reports/2026-09-07.md`). Not fixed in this pass — review/document/file only.

## Finding

`crates/secantus-core/src/explain.rs` (new file, 511 lines, this cycle) implements mongod's `parsedQuery`/stage-tree normalisation for the `explain` command. Its core functions — `canonical_match`, `clauses`, `field_clauses`, `canonical_children`, `negate`, `clauses_of_canonical` — mutually recurse to flatten nested `$and`/`$or`/`$nor`/`$elemMatch`/`$all` filter documents, with no depth cap anywhere in the recursion:

- `canonical_match` (line 376) calls `clauses` (line 310)
- `clauses` recurses into `$and` children directly (line 322: `out.extend(clauses(d))`), and into `$or`/`$nor` via `canonical_children` (line 360), which calls `canonical_match` again per child (line 366) — a mutual recursion with no depth counter
- `field_clauses` (line 192) recurses into `canonical_match` again for `$elemMatch` and `$all`'s `$elemMatch` members (lines 231, 247)

Reachable from the `explain` command's `filter` field: `crates/secantus-commands/src/admin.rs:449` (`let canonical = secantus_core::canonical_match(&Bson::Document(filter.clone()));`) and `:514`. `explain` is an ordinary command any client can send (`db.collection.find(<filter>).explain()`), with no auth required by default (`--auth` is opt-in per CLAUDE.md).

## Trigger

```js
db.runCommand({
  explain: { find: "c", filter: { $and: [ /* nested $and tens of thousands of levels deep */ ] } },
  verbosity: "queryPlanner"
})
```

## Impact

A Rust stack overflow aborts the whole Rust Mongo-wire server process. Unauthenticated (by default), single-request, whole-server denial of service.

## Root cause (shared with #1117/#1161/#1192/#1193, #1355, and the pgtypes issue filed alongside this one)

Same standing class: no BSON-nesting-depth cap anywhere on the Rust decode/render/normalise path. This is the third new instance found in this single review cycle, all from the same missing guard.

## Fix suggestion

Add a depth parameter (or a shared depth-limited traversal helper) to `clauses`/`canonical_match`/`field_clauses`/`canonical_children`, and return a bounded-nesting error or fall back to echoing the filter unchanged past a sane limit (mongod itself caps BSON nesting depth at parse time — 100 by default — so filters this cycle's normalisation logic would ever legitimately see are already bounded; the fix is to make this code enforce the same limit rather than trust the caller).

Not fixing in this pass per the security-review process — review, document, and track only.

A maintainer on the project jdschleicher/Salesforce-Data-Treecipe (TypeScript) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #104: calculateLevelsRecursively is exponential in graph depth

## Problem Statement

`RelationshipService.calculateLevelsRecursively` re-walks an object once per distinct path that reaches it. On a layered graph — the shape an org has when several objects share a child lookup — that is exponential:

| objects | depth | recursive calls |
|---|---|---|
| 30 | 10 | 88,572 |
| 36 | 12 | 797,160 |
| 42 | 14 | **7,174,452** |

#98 (`10d1ce7`) removed the *allocation* half of this: the method was handing every child a **copy** of the visited set, so those millions of calls were also millions of `Set` allocations. That was the cause of a jest worker exhausting a 4 GB heap in CI, and it is fixed — 2.0-2.3x faster, verified semantics-identical.

**The exponential call count itself was deliberately left in place.** A real org with a deep enough lookup chain would still spend seconds here, inside `Generate Treecipe`, on the extension host thread.

## User Story

As a developer generating a Treecipe against an org with deeply chained lookups, I want relationship levels computed in polynomial time, so that generation does not hang on graph shape.

## Why the obvious fix was reverted, and what it costs to do properly

The standard fix is longest-path relaxation: if an object has already been visited at a level greater than or equal to the one now proposed, nothing beneath it can be raised, so the re-walk is skipped.

```ts
const isLevelRaised = relationshipDetail.level < proposedLevel;
if (!isLevelRaised && relationshipDetail.isProcessed) { return; }
```

That was implemented during #98 and **reverted**, because a differential run over 600 random graphs showed it changing the level of **1,531 objects** — every one of them in a graph containing a **cycle**.

In a cyclic graph the current implementation's path-based visited set lets a node be re-entered along a different path and keep incrementing, settling at levels far above the object count (13 and 17 were observed in a ~10-object graph). The relaxation stops that, producing lower and arguably more sensible levels — but *different* ones.

Those levels decide **which objects go in which Treecipe file and in what insertion order**. Changing them changes generated data for any org with circular lookups, which Salesforce orgs genuinely have. That is a deliberate behavior change needing its own fixtures and its own decision, not a side effect of a performance fix.

## The question this issue has to answer first

**What should the level of an object in a dependency cycle be?** The current implementation's answer — keep climbing until the path guard stops you — looks like an artifact rather than a decision. Until that is settled, no fix can be verified, because there is nothing to verify against.

Suggested order:
1. Decide and document the intended semantics for cyclic graphs
2. Write fixtures that pin those semantics
3. Then make it polynomial, checking against the fixtures rather than against the old implementation

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Intended level semantics for graphs containing cycles are decided and written down, with the reasoning
- [ ] Fixtures pin those semantics — at minimum a two-object cycle, a three-object cycle, and a cycle with a tail hanging off it
- [ ] `calculateLevelsRecursively` is polynomial in graph size; the 42-object / depth-14 graph completes in a bounded number of visits rather than 7,174,452
- [ ] A differential or property check shows levels for **acyclic** graphs are unchanged from today
- [ ] Any change to cyclic-graph levels is stated explicitly in `CHANGELOG.md` as a behavior change affecting generated recipe order
- [ ] A test asserts a deep layered graph completes without a heap or time blowup
- [ ] The existing tests added in #98 (layered graph levels, two-object cycle termination) still pass or are consciously updated
- [ ] `npm run compile`, `npm run lint`, `npm run jest-test` all clean; coverage does not regress

## Affected Areas

| Area | File | Change |
|---|---|---|
| Traversal | `src/treecipe/src/RelationshipService/RelationshipService.ts` | Modify |
| Fixtures and tests | `src/treecipe/src/RelationshipService/tests/` | Modify |
| Docs | `CHANGELOG.md`, possibly `CLAUDE.md` relationship-grouping note | Modify |

## Out of Scope

- The allocation fix — already landed in #98
- Any change to how relationship trees are grouped into files once levels are known

## Context

Measured and reverted during #98. The reverted patch and the differential harness that caught it are described in `10d1ce7`.

Issue #273: Extend the conformance kit to the Queue interface, paired with a real second implementation

## Context

Split out of #252, which asked, as part of its own scope, "whether the kit also covers the `Queue` interface, which has the same shape of problem — jinaga-server has `postgres-queue.ts` with no shared suite." PR #269 extracted `describeStorageConformance` and left that sub-question open for a maintainer decision, on the reasoning that `Queue` has no second implementation *in this repository* to exercise a suite against.

The decision, recorded on #252: yes, the kit should cover `Queue` — but not as a sixth step on #252, and not ahead of a second implementation to run it against. This issue carries it.

## The contract is real, and none of it is in the signature

`Queue` (`src/storage.ts:65`) is three methods:

```ts
export interface Queue {
    peek(): Promise<FactEnvelope[]>;
    enqueue(envelopes: FactEnvelope[]): Promise<void>;
    dequeue(envelopes: FactEnvelope[]): Promise<void>;
}
```

The behaviour callers actually depend on, read off `IndexedDBQueue` (`src/indexeddb/indexeddb-queue.ts`), the only real implementation anywhere:

- **`enqueue`** is an idempotent upsert keyed on the fact's type and hash (`put(envelope, factKey(envelope.fact))`, line 144), so re-enqueueing a known fact replaces it rather than duplicating it.
- **`peek`** returns the queued envelopes **plus the transitive ancestor closure** of every queued fact — deduplicated, with facts already in the queue excluded from the ancestor set — sorted in topological order, and validated: it throws on a cycle and on a predecessor missing from the result.
- **`dequeue`** deletes by that same key (line 155) and must tolerate envelopes that were never enqueued, because `WebClientSaver` dequeues whole batches taken from `peek` (`src/fork/web-client-saver.ts:166`) and those batches contain ancestor envelopes the queue never held.

An implementation returning only the queued rows, in insertion order, type-checks and satisfies a naive round-trip test while silently breaking the outbound path. `WebClientSaver.save` (`web-client-saver.ts:148`) sends exactly what `peek` returns, and a fact sent without its predecessors leaves a dangling reference upstream — the same hazard that method's own comment describes for the batching case, arriving through the queue instead.

## Why it is worth writing down

Because the second implementation already exists and conforms to nothing. `PostgresQueue` in jinaga-server returns `[]` from `peek` and no-ops both writes, which makes a server configured with `pgStore` plus `upstreamReplicators` accept writes and never forward them, silently — jinaga/jinaga-server#184.

That is not a hypothetical divergence a suite would have to be invented to catch. It is the exact case a conformance kit exists for, and it has been live since `cc526d2`.

## Proposal

Add to the kit, alongside `describeStorageConformance`:

```ts
export function describeQueueConformance(
    name: string,
    createQueue: () => Queue | Promise<Queue>,
    teardown?: (queue: Queue) => void | Promise<void>
): void;
```

Cases, which are the contract above made executable:

- **round trip** — `enqueue` then `peek` returns what was enqueued
- **idempotency** — enqueueing the same envelope twice yields one entry
- **ancestor closure** — `peek` carries predecessors that were never themselves enqueued
- **no duplication** — an ancestor that is also queued appears once
- **topological order** — every predecessor strictly precedes its successor in the returned array
- **cycle detection** — a cyclic graph throws rather than returning a bad order
- **selective dequeue** — removes only what it names, leaves the rest peekable
- **tolerant dequeue** — an envelope that was never enqueued is not an error
- **empty queue** — `peek` returns `[]`

`test/indexeddb/indexeddbQueueSpec.ts` and `test/indexeddb/indexeddbQueueTopologicalSpec.ts` already cover most of this against `IndexedDBQueue` and are the source material — the same relationship the duplicated `queryGivenConditions` pair had to step 1 of #252. Note the difference, though: there is no duplicated pair to collapse here, so this is a forward investment rather than an immediate reduction in lines.

## Sequencing

**Do this together with implementing `PostgresQueue`, test-first**, rather than now. A suite extracted from the single implementation it describes mostly restates that implementation; the same suite written just ahead of a second one is a specification the second has to satisfy. The paired work is jinaga/jinaga-server#184, whose own suggested fix currently proposes insertion order and envelope payload only — which is the divergence this suite would catch on its first run.

Not a blocker for #252's remaining steps 3 and 5.

Issue #2: Exploit disconnected block structure: active-component pruning vs a full component solver portfolio

## Summary

CMG correctly supports disconnected graph Laplacians, including component-wise RHS compatibility and deterministic zero-mean normalization. It does not yet fully exploit the exact block-diagonal structure of a disconnected system for hierarchy construction, terminal solves, Krylov convergence, or scheduling.

Track a general solver improvement with two possible implementation levels:

1. **Active-component pruning inside one CMG hierarchy**: retain one global PCG recurrence and one logical preconditioner, but remove components from deeper hierarchy work as soon as they have reached a component-local terminal.
2. **A full component solver portfolio**: partition the graph before setup, route each connected component to an appropriate direct or CMG solver, and schedule work across both components and right-hand sides.

The two options are not mutually exclusive. Active pruning is the smaller intervention and may remove most of the currently observed waste. A full portfolio has a higher ceiling and improves more parts of the solver, but requires a larger API, memory, scheduling, and diagnostics redesign.

This is a general CMG issue, not an econometrics-specific feature. A downstream motivating case is `fereg` issue #20:

https://github.com/johannes-schmieder/fereg/issues/20

The work is orthogonal to #1. Fused RHS lanes exploit shared structural traversals across independent RHS solves; this issue exploits exact independence across graph components.

## Motivation

For a graph with connected components `G_1, ..., G_C`, a deterministic vertex permutation gives

```text
L = diag(L_1, L_2, ..., L_C).
```

Consequently,

```text
L^+ = diag(L_1^+, L_2^+, ..., L_C^+).
```

Every component can therefore be treated independently without approximation. This applies to arbitrary weighted graph Laplacians; it does not depend on bipartiteness, worker-firm structure, or any downstream estimator.

The current implementation uses component metadata for correctness and centering, but builds one hierarchy over the complete submitted graph and applies one global preconditioner/PCG workflow. This can leave substantial work on the table when component sizes are heterogeneous.

A representative problematic shape is:

- one or a few large components that require a deep hierarchy;
- hundreds or thousands of tiny components that contract immediately or become edgeless after shallow coarsening.

The large component determines the global hierarchy depth. Tiny-component representatives may remain present in deeper vectors and repeated centering, smoothing, restriction, prolongation, and recursive-cycle work even though their local graph work is already finished.

A downstream controlled experiment found the important distinction:

- thousands of uniformly tiny components can already be a very good CMG case;
- component count alone is therefore not a valid rejection rule;
- the bad case is a **mixture of a material component and many tiny components**;
- hierarchy setup and outer PCG iteration counts can look ordinary while recursive preconditioner work grows sharply.

The appropriate response is not a hard component-count cutoff. It is to represent and execute the exact block structure more faithfully.

## General opportunities

A component-aware implementation could improve CMG in several settings:

- disconnected meshes or image masks;
- batches of independent graph problems submitted as one block-diagonal system;
- worker-firm and other network models with many connected sets;
- repeated Laplacian solves for randomized projections, leverage, or effective-resistance calculations;
- sparse RHS vectors that touch only a subset of components;
- block-diagonal SDDM systems whose independence can be partly hidden by augmentation;
- one-RHS workloads with several material components, where component-level parallelism is available even when across-RHS parallelism is not.

It should not be marketed as a universal acceleration. A connected graph has no exact decomposition, and the one-component path should retain essentially the current cost and behavior.

## Current architectural pressure points

### One hierarchy and one recurrence

`CmgHierarchy`, `CmgPreconditioner`, and `ParallelPcgSolver` currently represent one submitted graph, one hierarchy, and one top-level PCG solve or batch policy. `ParallelPcgSolver` chooses among serial execution, planned parallel work within one solve, and independent execution across right-hand sides. It has no component-level execution strategy.

### Global direct terminal

`GroundedLdl` grounds one vertex per connected component, but constructs one grounded matrix over the combined active dimension. That matrix is block diagonal in exact arithmetic, yet the present dense assembly/factorization path does not exploit separate block dimensions.

If grounded component dimensions are `d_c`, a componentwise factorization changes dense work from being governed by the aggregate dimension `sum_c d_c` to a sum of per-block costs. This can be a very large difference for many small components.

### SDDM augmentation

An SDDM matrix may be block diagonal in its original off-diagonal sparsity graph.
