## Current XTRM baseline

Observed on `xtrm-dev/core@main` commit `4b1a5933aff84c69bfc8a5443090897cd2593cf1`.

### Managed-package path

`cli/src/core/pi-runtime.ts`:

- `MANAGED_PACKAGES` contains `{ id: 'npm:pi-mcp-adapter', ..., required: true }`;
- `getExpectedPiPackageVersion()` executes `npm view <package> version` against npmjs;
- `assureXtManagedPiPackages()` classifies any installed version unequal to current registry latest as outdated and invokes `pi install npm:pi-mcp-adapter`;
- `xt update --apply` runs this global package assurance once after repository reconciliation.

Therefore the source baseline has **no pinned adapter version or accepted range**. Its desired version is time-dependent npm `latest`.

`.xtrm/config/pi/install-schema.json` also lists `npm:pi-mcp-adapter`. `cli/test/pi-packages-parity.test.ts` explicitly permits it to be absent from `package.json` and settings because it is treated as a runtime-managed exception.

### Direct MCP-server launch path

`.xtrm/config/pi.mcp.json` is the canonical Pi MCP server source. It launches:

```text
deepwiki
  npx -y pi-mcp-adapter https://mcp.deepwiki.com/mcp

github-grep
  npx -y pi-mcp-adapter https://mcp.grep.app
```

`docs/mcp-servers.md` documents those entries as canonical and synchronized into project `.pi/mcp.json`.

Those commands do not reference the Pi-managed package copy and contain no immutable version. A clean start can therefore select a newer adapter than the one last assured by Core.

### Related implementation boundaries

- `scripts/patch-external-pi-tools.mjs` patches Serena/GitNexus behavior only. It does not establish adapter version identity.
- Core's managed package flow owns installation/update policy.
- The adapter owns MCP transport/lifecycle mechanics. It must not become XTRM workflow or authorization authority.

## Impact analysis

### What can change without a Core commit

Today, npm publication can change:

- remote MCP startup/retry behavior;
- direct/gateway tool advertisement;
- authentication/credential-refresh behavior;
- progress and metadata semantics;
- runtime extension registration;
- schema-validation behavior;
- non-TUI host behavior.

A later `xt update --apply` can also advance the Pi-managed package independently of an already-materialized `.pi/mcp.json` launch path.

### Reliability consequence

Two adapter versions can be relevant to one operator environment. Failure/recovery evidence can then be impossible to reproduce from the Core Git SHA alone. A reconnect, restart or clean install can silently change behavior.

### Security consequence

`2.28.0` fixes an OAuth concurrency race in which stale refresh/invalidation state could remove credentials written by another Pi process. XTRM must not accidentally regress such fixes through an uncontrolled second resolution path or rollback to an unrecorded version.

### Performance/operations consequence

Unversioned `npx` can add network/cache work at MCP process start. A single installed version authority should avoid duplicate fetch/resolution where practical and make offline/restart behavior deterministic.

### What remains unchanged

- Core remains owner of Pi runtime

A maintainer on the project yanet-platform/yanet2 (Go) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #2461: feat(tun64): ipv4-in-ipv6 tunnel module with externally sourced mappings

## Goal

A yanet2 installation can tunnel IPv4 traffic inside IPv6 (IPIP) using a per-host mapping table. Packets destined into configured prefixes are encapsulated toward the IPv6 address their mapping names, the return IPIP traffic is decapsulated, mappings track an external export service without operator intervention, and per-mapping traffic is observable.

No module in yanet2 provides this today, so installations that depend on the capability have nowhere to go.

## Scope

A `tun64` packet-processing module in the canonical module layout — dataplane, control-plane service, CLI — and an operator that keeps its mapping table fresh from an external export service over HTTPS.

The wire behaviour the children implement:

**Encapsulation.** For an IPv4 packet whose destination is inside the configured IPv4 gating prefixes, the destination is looked up in the mapping table as an exact `/32`. On a hit an outer IPv6 header is prepended:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| version | 6 |
| traffic class | the inner IPv4 TOS byte in full — DSCP and ECN |
| flow label | 0 |
| payload length | the inner IPv4 total length |
| next header | `IPPROTO_IPIP` (4) |
| hop limit | configured, default 64 |
| source | the configured tunnel source, optionally randomised |
| destination | the mapping IPv6 address |

The inner packet is not modified: no TTL decrement, no checksum recompute. On a miss the packet is dropped. A destination outside the gating prefixes passes through untouched.

**Source randomisation.** When enabled — the default — bytes 8..11 of the outer IPv6 source are overwritten, not ORed, with the four raw bytes of the inner IPv4 source, giving downstream ECMP entropy.

**Decapsulation.** For an IPv6 packet whose destination is inside the configured IPv6 gating prefixes, whose next header is IPIP, and which is not fragmented, the outer IPv6 header and every extension header are stripped and the inner IPv4 packet emitted. The mapping lookup on the inner IPv4 source is statistics-only: a miss increments a counter and the packet is still forwarded. Outer traffic class and hop limit are discarded. Anything failing the gate passes through untouched.

**Mapping document.** A JSON object keyed by IPv4 address, each value carrying an `addr6` IPv6 address; other fields are ignored.

```json
{ "1.1.1.1": { "addr6": "1234:abcd::1" } }
```

### Out of scope

- DSCP marking. It is delivered by chaining the existing `dscp` module after `tun64`.
- A web UI.
- Prefix-valued mappings: keys are exact `/32` host addresses.

Issue #304: [Bug]: Recursive watcher swallows inotify registration failures and stays healthy with incomplete coverage

## Bug Description

`watcher.addRecursive` logs and suppresses failures from `fsnotify.Watcher.Add`. If Linux inotify resources are exhausted (`ENOSPC: no space left on device`), grepai remains running and the workspace can continue to report as healthy/ready even though new directories are not being watched. Runtime-created directory trees can therefore become permanently invisible to the watcher without a process-level failure or degraded status.

This is not filesystem free-space exhaustion. In the observed incident, the user had exactly `65,536 / 65,536` inotify watches allocated. grepai held 4,919 legitimate watches and encountered ENOSPC after another process later consumed the remaining user quota.

Production log excerpts:

```text
2026/09/05 21:57:08 Failed to watch .../MM32/src/log: no space left on device
2026/09/05 21:57:08 Failed to watch .../MM32/src/log/playtests: no space left on device
2026/09/06 07:24:17 Failed to watch .../MM32/src/log: no space left on device
```

The process stayed alive and continued handling other events. The affected directories were not retried until the entire workspace watcher was manually restarted. After freeing inotify headroom and restarting, grepai registered 4,926 watches with no errors.

The current behavior exists in two paths:

- recursive startup registration (`watcher/watcher.go:addRecursive`)
- runtime directory-create handling (`handleEvent` calls `addRecursive` and only logs the returned error)

The runtime path is essential: the watcher may start successfully and exhaust the shared per-user quota later because another application allocates watches.

Nested workspace roots were investigated but were **not** duplicated in this incident: the three grepai inotify instances had zero duplicate `(device,inode)` registrations because the parent project's `.gitignore` already excludes the two nested project roots.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On Linux, run grepai watch on a project with recursive directories.
2. Consume `fs.inotify.max_user_watches` using another process after grepai has started.
3. Create a new directory tree beneath the watched project.
4. Observe `Failed to watch ...: no space left on device` in the grepai log.
5. Observe that grepai remains alive/ready and never receives changes under the failed directory until restarted.

The same silent-partial state can be reproduced during startup by exhausting the limit before `Watcher.Start()` recursively registers directories.

## Expected Behavior

- A fatal watch-registration error such as `ENOSPC`, `EMFILE`, or `ENFILE` is propagated as a typed/actionable error identifying the path and explaining likely inotify exhaustion.
- Startup failure does not write a ready marker and releases watches already registered.
- A fatal runtime registration error terminates/degrades the watcher rather than silently continuing with incomplete coverage.
- Transient `ENOENT` from directories created and removed during traversal may remain non-fatal.

## Actual Behavior

The error is logged and discarded. The watcher remains running with incomplete directory coverage and no machine-readable degraded state.

## grepai Version

Observed with a main-based development build corresponding to the current 0.36.x code. The relevant watcher implementation is unchanged on current `main`.

## Operating System

Linux (Ubuntu 22.04 host, kernel 5.15)

## Embedding Provider

Ollama

The full retained grepai watcher log contains repeated `Failed to watch ... no space left on device` messages while the process stayed alive. Per-process `/proc/*/fdinfo` accounting at diagnosis:

```text
fs.inotify.max_user_watches = 65536
total watches             = 65536
grepai workspace watcher  = 4919 (3 instances)
```

## Configuration

Workspace mode with three projects and a PostgreSQL vector store. The failure is independent of storage backend.

Issue #399: Epic: Late-arrival scanning at the reception desk (te-laatregistratie)

## Summary

**Epic.** Use the Account Manager to register students who arrive late at school. A handheld QR scanner reads the student card (WISA ID + Enter), the operator picks a reason from a button row, a ticket prints for the student to take to class, and the "Te laat" presence is written to Smartschool in the background.

The operators are the same people who already manage accounts, working on the same data, so this lives in the existing app as a separate tab rather than in a separate application.

## Workflow

1. Operator scans the student card. The scanner is a keyboard wedge: it types the WISA ID and presses Enter.
2. The app resolves that WISA ID **locally** from the materialized state — no network call — and shows name + class immediately.
3. Operator taps one of the reason buttons.
4. The registration is appended to a durable journal, the ticket prints, and the input is freed for the next scan.
5. A background worker drains the journal to Smartschool's Presence module.

## Settled decisions

- **The identity bridge already exists.** `SmartschoolAccount.accountId` (Internnummer) holds the student's WISA ID by operator convention, and `internalUserId` — derived from `referenceIdentifier` (#138) — is exactly the internal `userID` that Smartschool's Presence module needs. The scan path is a pure lookup in the materialized state; no new linking is required.
- **Presence writes go through `flutter_smartschool`.** `PresenceService.setLate()` (repo `yvanvds/dartschool`) already implements the internal `savePupilsPresences` endpoint. The reception account has `userCanRecord` over all classes — confirmed with the school.
- **Smartschool is never in the hot path.** Every registration is written to a durable journal *before* the ticket prints; the Smartschool write is a background drain with retry. A slow or expired Smartschool session must never stall the desk.
- **Recovery is required.** Between the scan and a successful write, the app holds the only record of who arrived late. The journal is local (survives an app crash) and mirrored to Cosmos (survives a dead laptop — a colleague steps in with her own machine).
- **FIFO per student.** A presence save *updates* the existing half-day cell rather than appending a row, so writes are last-write-wins. A second scan of the same student is deliberately allowed and must win, which means the drain has to preserve order per student.
- **No photos.** Name and class are enough.
- **Reasons are one flat row of buttons**, including "zonder geldige reden" — a different call under the hood, but just another button to the operator. The list is shared and editable, not per-machine, so the motivation text stays consistent across desks.
- **The arrival time goes into the motivation field.** Smartschool's Presence module only knows am/pm half-days, so the exact time can only be carried as free text. Fixed format `HH:mm – reden`, always (including for "zonder geldige reden"), so the field stays parseable later.
- **`DayPart` is always `morning`.** A student arriving at 12:15 is not late — that is a morning absence, and is not scanned.
- **An unresolved scan shows "leerling onbekend"**; the operator enters the absence in Smartschool by hand and the case is reviewed afterwards.
- **A new scan while the previous one is still unconfirmed is refused**, with a low, long square-wave beep clearly distinguishable from the scanner's own beep. The second student rescans.
- **Ticket printing is ESC/POS over TCP port 9100** to an Epson TM-m30III on the network — no Windows driver, and fire-and-forget.

## Explicitly out of scope

- Photos of students.
- Afternoon (`pm`) registrations.
- Claiming/ownership of queue entries across machines. The odds of a takeover *and* a Smartschool outage at the same moment are negligible, the operators know how to resolve it, and presences are reviewed afterwards anyway.
- Reporting and statistics on late arrivals. The fixed `HH:mm – reden` format keeps that possible later.

A maintainer on the project ziggornif/gimme (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #122: Browse a package by folder instead of one flat list of full object keys

## Problem

The package listing is flat. `GET /gimme/<pkg>@<version>` renders one row per object, each labelled with the full object key, and there is no way to descend into a subdirectory. On a package with any depth the page is a wall of paths rather than something you can navigate.

After #84 the page is paginated (default 50 visible files, keyset cursor), which bounds the response — but pagination bounds the *size* of the wall, it does not give it a shape.

## Evidence

Measured against `@mui/icons-material@5.15.21` (31 843 files), uploaded into a local instance backed by Garage v1.3.1, on the #84 branch:

| Request | Size | Total |
|---|---|---|
| `/gimme/mui-icons@5.15.21` (default limit 50) | 105 130 B | 0.053 s |

Every row reads `mui-icons@5.15.21/AccessAlarm.js` — the package and version are repeated on all fifty lines, and the two directories the package actually has are invisible.

For comparison, the same package's real tree, counted from jsDelivr's own data API (`https://data.jsdelivr.com/v1/packages/npm/@mui/icons-material@5.15.21`):

```
/            files=21229  directories=2
/esm         files=10612  directories=1
/esm/utils   files=1
/utils       files=1
total = 31843
```

## A folder view is necessary but not sufficient

Worth stating up front, because it is the obvious trap: a folder view does **not** on its own make this package browsable. Its root holds 21 229 files directly, so a delimited listing of the root still returns 21 231 entries. jsDelivr shows a folder view for this package and its root list is just as long — they virtualise or paginate it client-side.

So the two are complementary, not alternatives: **folder view for shape, pagination for bound**. Any implementation here must keep the keyset pagination #84 established and apply it *within* a folder level.

## The storage primitive already exists

#84 added `ObjectStorageManager.ListCommonPrefixes(ctx, prefix)`, a non-recursive (delimited) list that returns one common prefix per immediate child. That is exactly the call a folder view needs — #84 uses it on `pkg@` to enumerate versions; a folder browse is the same call on `pkg@version/sub/path/`. Verified in minio-go v7.3.0: with `Recursive: false` the client sets delimiter `/` and yields each `CommonPrefix` as `ObjectInfo{Key: prefix}`.

No new storage work should be needed. The work is routing, rendering and the listing contract.

## Scope

- A route that addresses a folder inside a package, and a listing that returns the immediate children of that folder — subdirectories first, then files.
- Rows show the basename, not the full object key. The package and version belong in the header, where #84 already renders the resolved version.
- Breadcrumbs back up the tree.
- Keyset pagination from #84 applies per folder level, since a single level can be huge (21 231 entries here).
- The JSON representation gains the same shape, so a consumer can walk the tree. This is the same contract conversation as #49 — settle it once.

## Relation to other issues

- **#84** — landed the pagination contract and `ListCommonPrefixes`. Reuse both; do not invent a second cursor.
- **#49** (`GET /packages` and version listing) — shares the browse surface and the listing contract. These two should agree, and may be worth doing in one pass.
- **#85** — unrelated, but also reuses `ListCommonPrefixes`.

## Out of scope

Client-side virtualisation of a long level, a search/filter box, and lightening the per-row markup (each row currently inlines an SVG icon plus copy and SRI buttons, ~2 KB per row). Those are real, and separate.

A maintainer on the project zzet/gortex (Go) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #763: TypeScript: same-line nested receiver call becomes false recursion labeled lsp_resolved

## Bug

When the method declaration and its body share a line, a nested receiver call `this.leaf.serialize()` is rebound to the enclosing class's own `serialize()` method. This creates a false recursive call, and the returned edge is labeled **`lsp_resolved`**. Restricting the query to compiler-resolved edges therefore does not protect against this false positive.

All names and source below are synthetic. No application repository or private dependencies are needed.

Environment: Gortex `v0.64.0+aa0da6b` (official darwin/arm64 release), macOS arm64, tsgo `7.0.0-dev.20260505.1` available on PATH. Default semantic settings.

## Reproduce

```sh
repro_dir=$(mktemp -d)
export XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$repro_dir/config"
export XDG_DATA_HOME="$repro_dir/data"
export XDG_CACHE_HOME="$repro_dir/cache"
mkdir -p "$repro_dir/nested-receiver"
cd "$repro_dir/nested-receiver"
cat > package.json <<'EOF'
{"name": "nested-receiver", "version": "1.0.0", "private": true}
EOF
cat > tsconfig.json <<'EOF'
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "Bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": [
    "src"
  ]
}
EOF
mkdir -p src
cat > src/models.ts <<'EOF'
export class Leaf {
  serialize() { return { value: 1 }; }
}
export class Box {
  leaf: Leaf;
  constructor(leaf: Leaf) { this.leaf = leaf; }
  serialize() { return this.leaf.serialize(); }
}
EOF
gortex daemon start --detach
gortex track "$PWD" --wait
```
```sh
gortex call get_call_chain --index "$repro_dir/nested-receiver" \
  --arg symbol_id=nested-receiver/src/models.ts::Box.serialize \
  --arg depth=1 --arg limit=10
```

## Actual

```json
{
  "from": "nested-receiver/src/models.ts::Box.serialize",
  "to": "nested-receiver/src/models.ts::Box.serialize",
  "kind": "calls",
  "line": 7,
  "origin": "lsp_resolved",
  "tier": "lsp",
  "confidence_label": "EXTRACTED"
}
```

The response has one node and one self-edge. The same wrong self-edge survives:

```sh
gortex call get_call_chain --index "$repro_dir/nested-receiver" \
  --arg symbol_id=nested-receiver/src/models.ts::Box.serialize \
  --arg depth=1 --arg limit=10 --arg min_tier=lsp_resolved
```

## Expected

`Box.serialize` calls `Leaf.serialize`, with no recursive edge. The field is explicitly typed `Leaf`; TypeScript resolves the call to `Leaf.serialize` at `src/models.ts:2`. The fixture typechecks without errors.

The same tiny fixture indexed fresh with the method body on a separate line resolves correctly:

```ts
serialize() {
  return this.leaf.serialize();
}
```

So the one-line method shape in the reproduction is significant. This suggests a call-site position/receiver-attribution problem, but the internal cause has not been established.

This can introduce false cycles and distort callers, flow tracing, and impact analysis. A regression should verify both the destination ID and the claimed evidence tier for multi-segment receivers, not just that a call edge exists.

Cleanup for this isolated example: `gortex daemon stop`. Its config/index are under the temporary XDG directories.
